" TENTHSOCIETY SIFTATE ": A Social Brochure. —By ALEXANDER WADDELL. Excerpts from some of the many Press opinions : " The writer urges the necessity and the pleasure of spiritual intercourse with GOD."—Liverpool Mercury, April 15, 1891. "Mr. Waddell writes in a pleasant and earnest style, sifting the experiences he has had in various parts of the country with a view to presenting something to the reader which is well worth considering."—Warrington Examiner, Tune 27th, 1891.

"The papers are written from a remarkable knowledge of Scripture, and recommend themselves by their quiet earnest- ness of style."—Scotsman, March 23rd, 1891. "With this key to the character of the work, the pages which follow prove interesting reading, and reveal the author as a close and appreciative observer of nature, and one who sees sermons in stones, books in the running brooks, and good in everything."—Preston Heritad, April 4th, 1891. "A deep religious tone pervades the book, and as the writer has evidently travelled far and near, his anecdotes and description of places are both telling and interesting."— The Isle of Wight Times, May 7th, 1891. '"The Tenth Society Siftate' de.Qerves, e.nd should have, a wide circulation."—Northampton Herald, May 2nd, 1891. . .

"There is the ring of sound common sense In all the writer says. He sets up before young men a high ideal of life. ** * It is bright and interesting and in many parts, especially the first chapter, it is humorous."—Christlan Union, April 18,1891. Extract from letter received by the author from his friend, the Rev. J. Lewellyn Roberts, M.A., vicar of Spratton, and Hon. Canon of Peterborough, March 22nd, 1891.—" There is something so chattyand cheerful, so kindly and friendly, that one takes up the book and lays it down again, and dips in here and dips in there, and finds that one has learned a good deal, or received many a happy suggestion, all by way of a pleasant talk." "It is not often that an unprofessional author writes with such tact and skill, with such ease and grace, and yet with such masterly for it the author of the Tenth Society Siftate. i The treatise has n t all the traits of that originality and piquancy that makesa social brochure popular and fascin- ating."—The Christian Union (2nd Notice), June 20th, 1891,

MADE out of hole cloth—Porous Plasters. WORKING like a horse—A lawyer drawing a con- veyance. FAILURE in the yarn trade—Writing unsuccessful novels.
THE only dairy which does not use water to excess is the dromedary: A JOKER tells of a capitalist so timid that he will not let well enough a loan without good security.

_ _ "MAMMA," said a little girl, "I've slept just sixteen hours. I went to bed at eight and got up at eight." THE little girl with the economical papa says that she is entirely opposed to the few doll (feudal) system.

A PLUMMER never asks: "Is it warm enough for you 2" He just hands you his bill and watches the perspiration trickle. A WOMAN recently refused to lend her husband her umbrella, because she said that she had noticed that he was always fond of a cold duck. THE man who fell off the fence into the brambles was much nettled by the occurrence. "We hope thistle be appreciated," says a punster. "IT is really very odd, my dear," said an old lady, one very hot day, to a friend. "I can't bear the heat in summer, and in winter I love it." A WOMAN in California is reported to have con- fessed to marrying eight husbands. There are not many women who possess her power to fasten eight men.
A CERTAIN rich man says of his wealth: "This is what I have often sighed for, even cried for, sometimes lied for, and nearly died for; what should I let it slide for?'
TiE stingiest man in this Union is said to be a miserable old bachelor who talks through his nose so as to save the wear and tear of his voice on his false teeth.

MRS. POPINJAY wants to know if the "editorial sallies" she hears so much about are the sisters of the printers' devils. "SHAVING DONE HERE," was the sign the barber put up, and when he was succeeded by a broker the, sign was not changed. BOOKBINDER—" Will you have this book bound in turkey or morocco ?" Purchaser—" Oh, mercy, no! What is the use sending it way off there! Have it bound in New York„"

"STRAWS show which way the wind blows," said an old toper. "Yes," responded a wit, look- ing at the speaker's red nose, "and straws show which way the sherry cobbler goes, too." "A PERSON in a public company accusing the Irish nation of being the most unpolished in the world, was answered mildly by a witty Irish gen- tleman, that 4 it ought to be otherwise, for the Irish meet with hard rubs enough to polish any nation on earth." _ _ _ _
WIFE (looking up from her book)—" You know a great many things, John. Now, what do you Ibink should be done in a case of drowning?" Husband —" Have a funeral, of course." _ _ _

"Is your vessel your home I" asked a lady, ad- dressing a man-of-war's-man. "It is, ma'am," replied the seaman, "in times of peace, but when we're in close action we're only boarders." SAID a gentleman to a neighbour: "I hear that our friend Griswold is sinking slowly." "Well— yes," was the reply: "you could not expect him to sink rapidly. He's had no doctor as yet." "AND she jilted you, did she 7 " inquired Rufus of Adolphus. "Me deah boy," replied Adolphus hastily, "never use that dweadful wohd again. Call it boycott, me deah boy—call it a boycott. EXPLAINED RATION-ALLY.--" Why, My dear," asked a governess of her little charge, "do we pray for our 'daily' bread? Why don't we ask for bread enough for four or five days or a week 7" "Because we want it fresh, you know," replied the ingenious child.

"I HAVE been married now," boasted a prosy old fellow, "more than thirty years, and have never given my wife a cross word." "That's because you never dared, uncle," said a little nephew who lived with them. "If you had, auntie would have made you jump." THERE'S THE 111313.—" No," said the man who was shot in the head by his friend while they were out hunting, lost the most of an ear, and was scratched considerably, "I don't mind the wounds so much, but it breaks my heart to have my head mistaken by my most intimate friend for a polecat." "As between a dog and a dude for a summer resort pet," said a young lady, as a young man left her side, "give me the dog." "Why 1" asked her companion. "The dog never says anything." "Neither does the dude, does he I" "No, he never says anything, but he makes me tired talking so much."

AN inexperienced young man from the country, at his first hotel dinner, found a "programme" printed in French; and after examining the bill of fare intently from top to bottom, he called to the waiter, and pointing to the word menu at the top, said: "Fetch me a dish of that for a starter.' LITTLE Johnny was a thoughtful child of four years. His little new brother had such powerful lungs, and used his vocal powers so obstreperously that Johnny became wearied by the nursery music, and one day said: "Ma, little brother came from heaven, didn't he ? " "Yes, he did, my dear; what of it 7 " " Nothing ; only I don't blame the angels for bouncing him. Do you?" "GENTLEMEN," said a condemned Texan stage- robber to the reporters, as the sheriff was adjusting the rope to his neck—" Gentlemen, will you grant me one last request before I die 7" The reporters to a man solemnly said they would. "Then, gentle- men, write me down as having been hanged, not • lapnched into eternity.' I'm no dude." It was hard on the boys, but they kept their word.

A MAN once went to a Turkish neighbour and solicited the loan of a rope. The Turk went into his house, and after a delay of several minutes, returned and told the borrower that the rope was In use tying up flour. "What do you mean 7" said the neighbour. "How can a rope be used to bind up flour ?" " A rope may be applied to any use,' replied the Turk, "when I do not wish to lend it."

THE Rev. Sydney Smith, being once asked by a friend for a reserved seat in St. Paul's, said: "To go to St. Paul's is certain death. The thermometer is several degrees below zero. My sentences are frozen as they come out of my mouth, and are thawed in the course of the summer, making strange noises and unexpected assertions in various parts of the church."

ONE stormy day, not long ago, a sloop was load- ing potatoes at a port in Maine. A cart from the country came alongside of her, and the driver pro- ceeded to empty his load in the vessel's hold. When he had finished, he was invited by the mate to warm and dry himself at the galley-fire, and eat a piece of pork and a ship's biscuit, the latter as hard as a flint. The driver ate the pork with a relish, without touching the biscuit. When he had finished, he handed back the indigestible biscuit to the mate, with the remark, "Here, sailor-man, many thanks; and there s your plate !"

ONE of Baron Rothschild's friends of the third degree—a sort of banker—came to borrow five hundred pounds. "Here it is," said the baron; "but remember that, as a rule, I lend only to crowned heads." The baron never dreamed of seeing his money again, but at the end of a month the ladrrower came back with his five hundred pounds. A month later the borrower reappeared, asking for the loan of one thousand pounds. "No no," said the baron; "you disappointed me once by paying me that money. I do not want to be disappointed again." SAMUEL WARREN, of "Ten Thousand a Year" fame, had a great liking for great people. Once, when sitting in the court by the side of a brother barrister, he said to him: "1 must go now David- son, as lam going to dine witl- Lord Lyndhurst.' "So am I," returned Davison. Warren looked somewhat disconcerted, but went out of court and quickly came in again, and said to Davidson: "When I said I was going to dine with Lord Lynd- hurst, I was joking." "Well," acknowledged Davidson, "so was I.'

AN Italian organ-grinder had been playing before the house of a very irascible old gentleman, who furiously and 4ith wild gesticulations ordered him to "move on." The organ-grinder stolidly ground on, and was arrested for his disturbance. At the police-court the magistrate asked him why he did not leave when requested. "Me no understan' mooch Inglese," was the reply. "Well," said the magistrate, "but you must have understood his gestures—his motions." "I tinkee he come to dance." was the rejoinder.

" CAPITAL " CHAT.
Mr. Isaac Sharp, one of the oldest ministers in the Society of Friends, intends to leave England at the end of this month on a missionary journey round the world.
Prince George of Wales is to be promoted to the command of the royal yacht Osborne. The rumour is once more current that the dukedom of York is to be revived in favour of" Our Sailor Prince."
Mr. Oscar Wilde is decorating a room for Mrs. Langtry in her new house in Pont-st. Fans (hand- painted) are to be the chief decorations. Mrs. Oscar IVilde is staying with friends in the country.

The Prince of Wales is taking things easily When serenaded at Heidelberg the other day (accor- ding to the "Neue Preuss Zeitung" of Berlin) he asked the performers to oblige with Watch on the Rhine." But what will our French friends say? asks a correspondent. Well, they will probably re- member that H.R.H. is a German.

John Burns is now on his " holidays." On Satur- day he journeyed to Devonshire for the purpose of taking part in a laboar demonstration there. Thence he will proceed to Nottingham, and will address meetings there. Afterwards he will journey to Newcastle and attend the opening meeting of the Trade Union Congress as a member of the Par- liamentary Committee of the union. When the congress is over, he will pay a visit to Scotland and address the Ayrshire miners.

According to a Melbourne correspondent, it seems that the veritable Arthur Orton, has turned up in a lunatic asylum, and interest in the famous Tich- borne case is once more being revived. The asylum in which he is supposed to be is at Parramatta, but in order to test the accuracy of the matter, Warder Carroll, of Ballarat, left on the 10th ult., for Sydney. Carroll, it appears, formerly served in the Carbineers, in which Sir Roger Tich borne was an officer, and was an important witness in the original trial of the great Tich borne case at Westminster.

An interesting case of bone-grafting is recorded by a surgeon. In the course of an operation it was found necessary to remove a portion of the frontal bone, and this left a large breach of bony surface. To make good the deficiency the hipbone of a newly killed dog was taken, the bone divided into small fragments, and the pieces transplanted to the gap in the frontal bone of the patient. Immediate and complete union ensued, without pain or reaction, and the patient was discharged from the hospital quite convalescent ten days after the operation. Three months subsequently he was still in perfect health. _ .

Sir Charles Dilke, in an interview with a reporter of the " Gaulois " who found him at "Docket," stated as his opinion that the Libelals would quit Egypt after they had been some time in power. "We will," he said, "make certain arrangements with the Powers, as in 1884 with France, and make Egypt neutral territory. "I am" (he added) "abso- lutely on the side of the French in this question of Egypt. Although I find that on certaix secondary questions,such as that of Newfoundland,the French trouble us unnecessarily, I believe in this question of Egypt you are right to reproach us for having not kept our promise."

A young lady left England on Friday in the British India is. Mombasa bent on a similar mission to that to which Sister Rose Gertrude devoted her life. Her name is Miss Edmeades, her home Winchester, her distination Upper Burmah. She has obtained a diploma in medicine, and is looking forward to a useful life of work in connec- tion with the Wesleyan Missionary Society, which has opened at Mandalay a home for the lepers. The society is under the superintendence of the Rev. A. H. Bestall and ispatronised by Government. Miss Edmeades means to change her name at Rangoon, where an interesting ceremony, in which Mr. Beatall will figure as bridegroom, will be celebrated.

Sir Donald Currie may not be a brilliant success as a politician, but, whether in his business transac- tions or in his everyday, non-commercial life, he appears to posses the Midas-like faculty of turning everything he handles into gold. in opening a bazaar at Dunkeld the other day he remarked that "he had never opened a bazaar which was not a success, and where there was not more money received than was really required.' Sir Donald— whose epitaph might run, a la Johnson on Gold- smith, "He touched nothing that he did not aurify '"—is another successful" Greenock laddie," his grandfather, who brought him up, having been a respectable barber in that malodorous Clyde seaport.

The Suffragan Bishop of Shrewsbury, who, as re- ported in Saturday's" Star," took a prominent part in urging on the agitation against Earl Shrewsbury's license to sell drink in the grounds of Alton Towers, is himself a baronet, to wit, Sir Lovelace Stamen He comes of a fierce Orange stock, his grandfather having been Mayor of Dublin, in 1809. He was edu- cated at Trinity College, Cambridge, and took a second class in classics. In the Potteries where he lives he is very popular, as he takes an entt usiastic interest in temperance work and social reform. His second son, the Rev. F. Stamer, who was for some time a Shrewsbury curate; but whose views are of a narrower type than his father's, recently married Miss Donovan.

Mr. Percy Harrison, one of the well-known Bir- mingham musical firm of Harrison and Harrison, under whose auspices Madame Patti begins a tour of England and Ireland at the midland capital on 20th October, enjoys the rare credit of getting on better with the diva than any other living manager who ever had to do business with her. Great singers are, as a rule,.fearfully fitful—capriciousness in fact, seems a large part of their nature. And woe to the poor manager who dares oppose their slightest whim ! Mr. Harrison, therefore, has something to boast of in his remarkable success with the Queen of Song. His intimacy with Madarne Patti goes far beyond mete business relations. He is admitted within the charmed circle as one of her personal friends—perhaps it is not too much to say that he is almost one of the family circle. He has just returned to business after a visit to Craig-y- Nos.

Mr. Christie Murray says that the Australian uses strong language, drinks strong tea and strong liquor. He has an original way of brewing his tea. "In all up-country places," says Mr. Murray in his second article on " The Antipodeans " in the Contemporary, " men drink tea. They drink it all day long and at every meal in amazing quantities and at a most unwholesome strength. The method of preparation is simple, and one would think that if the aim were to brew a concoction altogether poisonous it ought to be effectual. On Sunday mornings the tea-makers starts with a cleanpot and a clean record. The pot is hung over the fire with a sufficiency of water in it for the day's brew, and when this has boiled, he pours into it enough of the fragrant herb to produce a deep coffee-coloured liquid. On Monday night removing yesterday's tea leaves he repeats the process," and so on to the end of the week. Mr. Murray's opinion of Australia comes to this: "There is no country in which so high a condition of general comfort, so lofty a standard of proved intelligence, and such large and varied means of intellectual existence exist side by side with so much turbulence, so lax a commercial morality,and such overcharged statistics of drunken ness and crimes of violence."

Not the least interesting of the many interesting objects shown to the lady members of the Institute of Journalists during their recent visit to Dublin, were Dieces of the two first poplin gowns made for her Majesty in 1838, by Messrs. Atkinson, of College Green. The ground of both these pieces is of white figured poplin, or, as it was then called," tabbinet," and the design is the shamrock, rose, and thistle. On the one gown the small pattern is wrought in gold, and carried out in festooned sprays of the national emblems. The second is much more elabo- rate, seven shades of silk appearing, as well as gold and silver threads, and the white silk of the ground- work. This pattern is also very small, and forms stripes, with a filling-in of conventional green leaves, and quaint figures worked in gold. The leaves and flowers composing the stripes are true to nature. The shamrocks are alternately produced in shaded green silks and gold. The thistles are worked in green and silver, and the roses and their leaves in old-fashioned pinks and greens. The white and gold poplin has been copied—and worn as Court trains by other ladies—but the coloured piece was made specially for her Majesty, and has never been worn by anyone else.

div.head: WHIRLPOOL RAPIDS.

A. high cloud of white vapour, and the dull con- tinuous roar of surging, seething waters proclaim the presence of the far-famed "World's Greatest Cataract." Soon after rounding the Bison city, and while skirting the frontier of the Republic, along the Niagara river, that divides the United States from Canada, all eyes are directed to the western windows of the cars through which they stead- fastly scan the landscape until the vapoury pillar is descried. But while engaged in this occupation the passengers are disturbed by a baggage-man who is anxious to check the baggage to the Falls, and to sell tickets for conveyances which his firm has the sole right of plying for hire in the depot. Visitors to Niagara would, however, ao well to avoid this man, and save their dollars by taking a quiet and pleasant walk to the beautiful spots of the neighbourhood. The drivers of these convey- ances belong to a little " ring " of hotel, restaurant, and shop keepers, and refuse to let their fares patronise any other establishment than those in the list. The Jehus deliberately drive contrary to the wishes of their patrons, and their actions are fast bringing the monopolists into disrepute. Already their conduct has been brought before the New ':ork Senate in a very strong report by the Conser- vators of the Falls.
As you enter the well-kept grounds of the Unitcd States
STATE RESERVATION,

a custodian presents you with a map and short description of the place, from which it seems that the movement for the preservation of the scenery of the Falls of Niagara originated in the State of New York, in the year 1869. On the 30th April, 1883, the State Legislature passed an Act authoriz- ing the selection of the Reservation, and another Act providing for its payment on April 30, 1885. The Feservation, which comprises a tract of 106,916 acres, was formally opened to the public July 15th, 1885. In the same year the Canadians followed suit, and the Queen Victoria Niagara Falls Park was opened to the public, May 24th, 1888. The park covers an area of 154 acres. The following

div.head: BIT OF HISTORY
div.p: BIT OF HISTORY

is from the map :—" The river road, on the mainland, Commanding views of the Rapids, the islands, and the Canadian shore, extends up stream along the river bank to the old French Landing-at the eastern boundary of the Reservation. From this road many historical points on the Niagara frontier are visible. At the mouth of the Cayuga Creek, five miles above the Falls, on the Ameri- can side, Robert Cavelier de La Salle, in 1679, built and launched the Griffin,the first vessel that sailed the upper lakes. Further down at the Old French Landing,within the Reservation, La Salle and the missionary, Louis Hennepin, embarked after the portage of their canoe from Lewiston, a point on the river seven miles below the Falls. The landing place was used by the early French and British Traders, and before their zoming by the Indians of the Neutral nation and their successors the Senecas. The wooded shores of Navy and Buckhorn Islands are visible, noted for occurrences in the French and British wars. About a mile above the ;Falls is the site of the French Fort du Portage,destroyed by Joncaire before his retreat in 1759. The chimney of the French barracks built in 1753 is yet standing, and the outlines of Fort Schlosser, built by the British in 1761, are visible. December 29th, 1837, during the "Patriot Rebellion "the steamer Caroline was seized at Schlosser Landing about two miles above the Falls, towed out into the river, set on fire, and allowed to drift with the cur- rent over the Falls. Further down upon the river bank, within the Reservation, where the bluff termin- ates near Mill-st. is the site of the saw mill erected by De Pevster, a British officer, in 1767, and used in prepar- ing timber for stockades along the river. Immediately below are the sites of the Stedman and Porter mills, the first structures of the kind erected on the western fron- tier. On the opposite shore of the river is the Canadian village of Chippewa, the site of the battle of Chippewa, July sth, 1814, and on the height on the Canadian side, west of the Horseshoe Fall, the battle of Lundy's Lane, took place, July 25th,1814."
COMPARING NOTES

I had no intention of publishing my impressions of the Falls, or attempting any description of the cataract,but I have been reminded that this series of letters would be incomplete without some reference to Niagara. I have, therefore, thought the best way to deal with the subject would be in the form of an actual conversation that took place between a Liverpool gentleman and myself. It seems" Mr. Jones" sailed from the Mersey the day I did, but in another vessel ; and when he learned this fact he was most anxious to "compare notes." lie pulled out his pocket book, in which he had religiously recorded the position of the ship when the day's run was made up, and, evidently thinking:l should do the same, remarked —" Now the first day ?" "Oh, be bothered to the first day. I've got no notes only what are in my head. What interest is it to any- body to know that on such a day we were in lat.—long.—? All people generally want to know is, how far the ship sailed in a given time." "Oh, well, did you have any rough weather ?" We did, but we got it 24 hours before Mr. Jones, and taking the voyage altogether Mr. Jones's party had a very similar experience to ours. We had a burial at sea, and so had they; but they ploughed several hours through a field of ice, which we fortunately escaped. " Well now, as to Niagara," said Mr. Jones, "what was your first impression ?" "One of dreadful disappointment. I first saw it from the Suspension Bridge,and the ravine was so small, com- pared to what I had anticipated that I felt as if I could jump across it. I had pictured the whole place on such a large scale that I was really dreadfully disappointed. "Strange to say," said Mr. Jones, that was just my feeling. "But what was your after-feeling ?" " Well, I saw

div.head: FALLS UNDEU MADE AND SUNSHINE.
div.p: THE FALLS UNDEU MADE AND SUNSHINE.
and from every point of view, and altogether my day at Niagara Falls was the most delightful I have had in America."

When I arrived rain fell heavily, and the Falls looked dark and uninviting. But raining as it was,l walked the two miles between Suspension Bridge and Niagara along a trail just on the edge of the ravine, with my eyes con- stantly towards the Falls. The track, however, led into kbarrel factory, and I walked in and stayed awhile watching the coopers knock together the casks in which American flour comes to England. Then I took the rail- road until I came to a street which led to the state reser- vation. Soon after entering here the rain ceased, and then the falling waters became iridescent with the noon- tide sun which shone gloriously for the rest of the day. Whilst contemplating the scene from Prospect Point, I made the acquaintance of a young German engraver, bound for New York, and with him I descended to the foot of the Falls, and got some idea of the tremendous weight of water pouring over the Falls every minute. but with the rain and the spray, the rocks did not afford a very safe footing, so we embarked on board the "Maid of the Mist" and steamed close in to both the American and Canadian Falls. The spray came over us in tor- rents, and we should have been speedily drenched, but for the stout oilskins provided on board. It's

div.head: RISKY SORT OF BUSINESS
div.p: A RISKY SORT OF BUSINESS

running so close tø the tumbling torrent, and the little steamer requires the nicest handling. But it safely ac- complished its voyage, and landed us on the Canadian side. Here we entered the Victoria Reservation, and came across another Lancashire man. "Where did you come from ?" said he.

"Warrington;" I replied. "Do you know Taylor's of the Norton Arms ? " "Rather." "Well, just remember me to them, when you see them. My name's Barraclough, of Bacup." Mr. Barraclough was not long in the country, and was staying at Hamilton, Ont. We had a chat on our new surroundings, and many comparisons were made with old country things for the edification of my German- American acquaintance. Meanwhile, we had viewed the magnificent Canadian Horseshoe Falls, which are far superior to Uncle Sam's; and we retraced our steps to- wards the landing stage where we parted with Mr. Bar- raclough, and crossing the water once more planted our feet in the United States. I parted with the engraver who had been over the States Reservation,and proceeded alone to make my survey of it. Looking down from Luna Island towards

THE "CAVE OF THE WINDS" I noticed that a slender wooden bridge connecting the boulders was smashed in several places, and it seemed to me a foolhardy thing to attempt to make such a pas- sage under the Falls. It was very pleasant to stand in the sunshine just on the brink of Terrapin Rock, Goat Island, and watch the ceaseless waters falling below. But it is when you visit the Three Sisters Islands, that you get the best and grandest idea of what the Falls are. When you stand on the furthest side of the Island and face the broad river, when you see the great rapids that spread right across it,falling 55 feet in three-quarters of a mile, when you reflect that

THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN
CHAPTER V. MOTT REYBOLD AND HIS FRIENDS. Mott Reybold was what is called "alone in the world."
His mother died when he was a child, and his father died some six years before this, leaving him sole heir to what was reported to be a very large fortune.

thought to be very enviable. - To be sure, there were a few old-fashioned friends of his father who shook their heads when they saw the young man aping the absurd accent and more absurd manners of the young snobs who frequently afflict this country. And they shook their head still more when rumour whispered of tile gambling table, the racing track, and a style of living which he called " high " because it is generally very low, and they said to each other;

"The father was an honest man, and he made his money by hard work and fair dealing; but it is the old story. If the son is not trained to labour and to respect labour, he cannot know the value of wealth which is the product of labour." By the time Mott Reybold had reached his twenty- fifth year, it was believed among his associates that he had "made a big hole" in the comfortable for- tune left him by his father. An excuse for this profligacy was found in the fact that the young man had never had any home training, and the additional fact that he was to marry Irene Lefferts, who as her brother had been disowned, would now be the sole heir of her father's great wealth. We have already seen the foundation for the belief in this marriage, but, it should be said, up to the conversation on the train, Mott Reybold felt as certain of winning Irene Lefferts as he was that the sun would rise on the morrow. He lived at a fashionable hotel, and the instant he had seen Irene enter the door of her own home

he started for his quarters. He went at once to his own room, threw off his coat, kicked off his boots, and with an exclamation that sounded like an oath, he jerked the bell-cord, and then flung himself on the bed. "Bring me a stiff glass of Grandy and a little soda," he said to the man who answered his call. He had finished his drink, and was in the act of lighting a cigar, by way of quieting his nerves, when a rap came to the door and his friend, Jack Hyde, entered. "Hello! Dissipating alone and at this early hour. What's up ?" asked Hyde, speaking with a strong English accent, and for the very good reason that he was a Londoner. Now, tell me all the news ;" and was reached, and after kissing his mother and Flor- Frank Lefferts leaned back in his chair, and placed ence, Allen started off with more hope in his heart his feet on the table by way of making himself corn- than he had felt for many a day. fortable. He made his way to Dr. Putnam's office in New "The latest news, that will interest you, is the York, an.l was so fortunate as to find that narrow escape from drowning of your sister, a gentleman in and evidently rejoiced to meet his few days since. But, I presume you have heard . visitor. about it 7" "When you gave me your card," said Allen, " Yes ; Finch told me. Brave fellow that Gilbert. coming directly to the object of his visit, "you I'd like to meet him and tip him to the extent of a told me to call on you if I thought you could be hundred or so; for I'm mighty fond of Irene, of service." though she don't think so," said Frank Lefferts ; and "So I did, and lam ready to keep my word," he sighed, took a drink from the glass before him, said the young doctor, Nvit,h a heartiness of manner and then angaekcd his lips, and added; "Go on with that put AlLeis.n ha es,e at ou‘s.!.

"fain a book -keeper,- an accountant, and familiar with all the departments of exchange. I read, write and speak French and German as well as I do English ; but if I cannot find a place for these acquirements, I am ready to work with my hands at anything that will give my mot ler, my sister and myself a living," said Allen, with an earnest- ness that brought back his earlier days. "Spoken like a man," said the doctor, adding with the manner of one coming down to business: "Now, Mr. Gilbert, tell me where you worked last, and why you left there. I do not ask for myself, but in these days, employers have got into the habit of requiring reference." Allen's face flushed on hearing this, and his con- fusion did not escape the young doctor's keen eyes. At length he managed to say : "Doctor. Putnam, I never did an act in my life that could bring the flush of shame to my cheek or to the cheeks of those I love; but I wish you would not press that question. Some day, when you know me better, as I hope you shall, I will explain all. For the present you must take my own word. If you are not satisfied with this very indifferent recommendation of myself, let us part." As Allen spoke he rose to his feet. : "Let that be as you say," responded the dcctor. "I flatter myself that I know men apart from their anatomy, and if I should be mistaken in you, I will never trust my judgment again. Come, sit down, .and let us talk your case over. lam not ciaious to know anything you feel like holding back." This was certainly manly, and Allen felt it. He took the doctor's proffered hand, and there were rings of moisture about his eyes when they sat down again. He told the doctor, without saying where, that he had been away for some years, and that since his return he had found his family in poverty and buried his father.

He refused to call on Mr. Lefferts at the doctor's suggestion, remarking quietly: "It would look as if I were seeking a reward for doing a common act of humanity—" "An uncommon act," interrupted the doctor. "Still I can but feel that a man who does a good act, prompted only by the hope of reward, would do a bad act from the same motive. Besides that, neither I nor mine have any good reason to like the name of Lefferts."

"They cannot say the same as to your name. Now, Mr. Gilbert, I have a plan for your benefit, but as it is not quite matured, I shall keep it to myself, and if you leave me your address, I will promise you a favourable letter to-morrow. What say you?"

eau only say, Dr. Putnam, that I must let my acts in the future speak my thanks for I cannot m find words for the now," replied Alien. With this unierstanding they parted, Allen going back to Pine Place, with the feeling that a new life was opening up to him. 1 The news he. brought his mother and Florence ! comforted them very much ; and as he put his arms about the latter, he said : "I hope that we can soon move jut') more com- fortable quarters, and then dear Florence, you neel take in no more sewing, and the roses will come back to your cheeks again." The letter that came from Dr. Putnam on the. morrow bore out these cheering expectations. He wrote that he had secured for Ailen the position of codector for himself and a number of prominent professional men and merchants. , The letter concluded as follows : ! "31y friends and myself will guarantee you fifteen ! dollars a week, for, with energy, your commissions should amount to twice or three times that sum., We have also decided to advance you one hundred dollars on acoount, which amount is now awaiting you at my ! office. Come over immediately and enter on your work at once. "Hoping that this opening may lead to better things,. ! believe me, . "Very faithfully your friend, CHARLES PUTNAM." •

When this letter was read over a second time, to make sure that they had not been dreaming the good news it brought them, tears came to the eyes of Allen and his sister; and the old mother dropped on her knees beside her chair, and silently bowed her white head on her clasped hands. As Allen hastened to New York that day his heart throbbed with a joy it had not felt for years ; his loathing for the crowds gave way to a feeling of kinspip ; and the summer sun poured down with a. splendour that thrilled him and tilled him with the glory of life's possibilities. He found the doctor awaiting him with the money and a number of letters of introduction to his employers. "See these gentlemen at once, Mr. Gilbert, that, they may be able to judge by your appearance that I have made no mistake in recommending you. That position is full of re,ponsibility, and I have per- sonally given 13Jud for the faithful performance of your duty. As soon as you can do so without loss move your family over to quarters near to your business, and if you want more money to care for your mother and sister, and to make yourself pre- sentable, do not hesitate to call on me, for I do, /sot believe in halfway friendships."

To these kindly expressions, -Allen could only mutter his thanks in a whisper, for if he had tried to speak aloud he would have broken down com- pletely. Me at once caned on his patrons, aeltverea bIB letters of introduction, and got from each a lot of bills for collection.

He would have gone to work that day, though there was no pressing need for his doing so ; but he thought, as he had money enough to snake some necessary changes in his own dress, and to move his mother and sister to New York, he would give the rest of the day to find suitable rooms near the scene of his labours.

In this effort he was successful, and then started home to tell the good news. On the street car going to South Brooklyn, Allen saw a rough look- ing man whose face seemed familiar, but he could not recall where he had met the fellow before.

When Allen left the car to go to Pine Place, the man, who had been watching him, got off, too, and followed him, but did not speak till they came to, the winding road through the lumber piles, that led to the cluster of wretched huts near the water.

" Hello!" called out the man, when there was no one within hearing but Allen, "Have you forgot me, pal?" "Forgotten you 1" exclaimed Allen, coming to a halt and facing the man whose familiarity angered him. "1 never knew you, sir." "Well, I don't say that we was reglarly intro- dooced," laughed the man; "but that wasn't necessary. Have you forgot that you and me was. sent up in the same batch to Sing Sing? Have you forgot that me and you was handcuffed together, and that I offered you tobaccG and tried to cheer you up? Have you forgot that I told you my name was Mingo—Mingo Pete, and that when we got out I wanted to know you, for you have larnin' and 1 have none—at least, not enough to brag on?" "I want to forget you, and all the past since I first saw you," said Allen, moving on.

"If you can do that you'll ha.-I,:e a stronger mind than any man I ever met up with. Forget the years in prison! Well, if they ain't burnt into yer brains, then yer ain't got any; that's all I've got to say." But, despite this assurance, the man followed Allen up, and kept up talking. " What! " he continued. "Do you, or any of your folks, hang out at Pine Place? I've got friends- there, and as I've only been out of quod since yesterday, I guess they'll be surprised to see me;, but if they ain't no gladder than you I'll have a cold show for supper and a night's lodging. But I'll stick to you. I like you, and I ain't a-goin' be shook off." And with this the man kept on doggedly by Allen's side. (To le continued.)

div.head: FAIRY TALES.
div.p: FAIRY TALES.
THE DARNING-NEEDLE.

.There was once a darning-needle who thought herself so fine that she fancied she must be fit for embroidery. "hold me tight," she would say to the fingers, when they took. her up, "don't. let me fall; if you do, I shall never be found.again, Jam so very tine."

" That is your opinion is it ?" said the fingers, as they seized her round the body. " See, I am coming with a train," said the darn- ing-needle, drawing a long thread after her; but there was no knot in the thread. _

The fingers then placed the point of the needle against the cook's slipper. There was a crack in the upper leather, which had to be sewn together. " What coarse:work !" said the darning needle, " I shall never get through. I shall break !—I tan breaking!" and sure enough she broke. "Did I not say so?" said the darning needle, " I know am too fine for such work as that.''

" This needle is quite useless for sewing now," said the fingers; but they still held It fast, and the cook dropped some sealing wax on the needle, arn•l fastened her handkerchief with it in front. "So now I am a breast-pin," said the darning needle ; " I knew I ;should come to honour some clay: merit is sure to rise ;" and she laughed, quietly to herself, for of course no one ever saw a darning needle laugh. And there she sat as proudly as if she were in a stage coach, and looked all around her. "May I be allowed to ask if you are made of gold?" she inquired of her neighbour, a pin; "you have a very pretty appearance, and a curious head, al- though you are rather small. ,You must take pains to grow, for it is not every one who has sealing wax dropped upon him ;" and as she spoke, the darning-needle drew herself up so proudly that she fell out of the hankerchief right into the sink, which the cook was cleaning. • Now lam going on a journey," said the needle, as she floated away with the dirty water, " I do hope I shall not he lost." But she really was lost in a gutter. "I am too fine for this world," said the darning-needle, as she lay in the gutter; "but I know who I am, and that is always some comfort." So the darning- needle kept up her proud het ayiour, and did not lose her good humour. Then there floated over her all sorts of things,—chips and straws, and pieces of old newspaper. "See how they sail," said the darning-needle ; "they do not know what is under them. lam here, and here I shall stick. See, there goes a chip, thinking of nothing in the world but himself—only a chip. There's a straw going hy now; how he turns and twists about! Don't be thinking too much of yourself, or you may chance to run against a stone. There swims apiece of newspaper; what is written upon it has been forgotton long ago, and yet it gives itself airs. sit here patiently and quietly. 1 know who I am, so I shall not move."

One day something lying close to the darning- needle glittered so splendidly that she thought it was a diamond ; yet it was only a piece of broken bottle. The darning-needle spoke to it, because it sparkled, and represented herqelf as a breast-pin. I.suppose you are really a diamond ?" she said.

" VlTtiy ye-s, something- of the sort," he replied ; and so each believed the other to be very valuab!e, and then they began to talk about the world, and the conceited people in it. "1 have been in a lady's work-box," said the darning-needle," and this lady was the cook. She had on each hand five fingers, and anything so con- ceited as these five fingers I have never seen; and yet they were only employed to take me out of the box and put me back again." " Were they not high-born?" . • _ _

"High-born !" said the darning-needle, "no indeed, but so haughty. They were five brother.,, all born fingers ; they kept very proudly together, though they were of different lengths. The one who stood first in the rank was named the thumb, he was short and thick, and had only one joint in his back, and could therefore make but one bow; but he said that if he were cut off from a man's hand, that man would be unfit for a soldier. Sweet-tooth, his neighbour, dipped himself into sweet or sour, pointed to the sun and moon, and formed the letters when the fingers wrote. Long- man, the middle finger, looked over the heads of all the others. Gold-band, the next finger, wore a golden circle round his waist. And little Playman did nothing at all, and seemed proud of it. They were boasters, and boasters they will remain; and therefore I left them."

" And now we sit here and glitter," said the piece of broken bottle. At the same moment more water streamed into the gutter, so that it overflowed, and the piece of , bottle was carried away. "So he is promoted," said the darning-needle, "while I remain here ; 1 am too fine, but that is my pride, and what do I care ? " And so she sat there in her pride, and had many such thoughtb as these,—" I could almost fancy that I came from a sunbeam, lam so fine. It seems as if the sunbeams were always looking for me under the water. Ah I am so fine that even my mother cannot find me. Had I still my old eye, which was broken off, I be- lieve I should weep; but no, I would not do that, it is not genteel to cry." One day a couple of street boys were paddling in the gutter, for they sometimes found old nails, farthings. and other treasures. It was dirty wink, but they took great pleasure in it. " Hallo ! " cried one,as he pricked himself with the darning-needle, "here's a fellow for you." "I am not a fellow, I am a young lady," said the darning-needle ;but no one heard her. The sealing-wax had come off, and she was quite black ; but black makes a person look slender, so she thought herself even finer than before. "Here comes an egg-shell sailing along," said one of the boys ;so they stuck the darning-needle into the egg-shell. "White walls, and lam black myself," said the darning-needle, "that looks well; now I can be seen. but I hope I shall not be sea-sick, or I shall break again." She was not sea-sick, and she did not break. " It is a good thing against sea-sickness to have a steel stomach.and not to forget one's own own importance. Now my sea-sickness has past; delicate people can bear a great deal." Crack went the egg-shell, as a wagnen passed over it. "Good heavens, how it crushes!" said the darning-needle. "I shall be sick now. I am break- ing, " but she did not break, though the waggon went over her as she lay at full length; and there let her he.

THE COMBINATION OF LABOUR.—A meeting of dele- gates representing over 40,000 workmen was held at Leeds on Monday in support of a proposal, which origi- nated in Lancashire, to form a federation of trade and labour unions. A resolution was carried in favour of such a federation being established, and a committee was appointed to tale steps for bringing the matter under the consideration of the labour societies of the country. Cooxs are often called upon to provide sweet dishes of cus- tards and blanc-mauges. at short notice, and at times when It is not convenient to obtain eggs. As a useful guide to the preparation of many choice dishes and delicious custards without eggs and half the trouble our readers should write to ALFRED BIRD AND SONS, BIRMINGHAM, for a free copy of their little book entitled "Pastry and Sweets." There is nothing to pay; a post card will bring it by, return free.—Advt.

div.head: DREADFUL FAMINE SCENES IN RUSSIA.
div.p: DREADFUL FAMINE SCENES IN RUSSIA.

Of the distress in the Government of Kasan, M. Filo- manoff, a Russian priest, gives the following account: "On my round through the village of Naredey I met within half an hour sixteen persons who were struggling with death, and one old woman died before my eyes. Most of these starving people had not seen bread for more than a week. With ashen countenances and dim eyes they looked at me, some of them not having strength to lift up their hands to beg for bread. The further I went through the village the more misery I saw. Many of the pale, emaciated objects stared straight before them, resigned. Others behaved like madmen, and in their desperation rushed from one place to another, gesticu- lating and screaming 'Bread, bread; don't let us die The mothers, many of whom have seen their children die of hunger, never cease wailing. All the eatables in the village had long since been devoured, and their sole sustenance for a fortnight had been limetree leaves, crushed in mortars, and made into a sort of porridge. The famine made such progress during last week that in. one Place alone out of 150 families 47 have died out."
