div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUXCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUXCIL.

The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Ball, on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Sutton, Holmes, Burgess, -Obandley, Wright; Councillors R. T. Fairclough, 'Cannel', Shaw-Green, Greening, Beaman, Garner, IL Roberts, Fleming, Plumpton, Jenkins, Voisey, Ashton, Bill, Heaton, Browne, Hutchinson, Monks; Messrs. J. Lyon Whittle (Town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), and Walker (assistant sur- veyor).

THE ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW. TheMAyon read a letter from the Mayor of M‘nches- ter asking the Warrington Town Council to sign an en- slosed memorial in favour of holding the Royal agricul- tural show in Manchester in 1893. Alderman BURGESS asked if it meant a subscription afterwards.

The MAYOR : It does not say so. Alderman BURGESS moved that the seal of the borough be affixed to the memorial. Alderritan CHANDLEY seconded and it was agreed to. UM STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended approval of the plans of the fcllowing buildings, Ac. :—Seven houses in Col- ling-st. for Mr. C.Langshaw ; two houses in Springfield- at. for Mr. James Gleave ; five houses in Longford-st.for Mr. J. Carradice ,• alterations and additions to premises in Sankey-st. for Messrs. J. and W. Dutton; store shed in Dallam-lane for Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, Limited ; addition to house in Manchester-road for Mr. Ghisnall.

Alderman SurroN moved, and Alderman WRIGHT se- eonded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor DixoN said he honed every step would be taken to prevent the road near Messrs. Litton's mill at Bank Quay from being stopped. The MAYOR said it would be better for the interests of the town that there should be no discussirm on that point at the present moment. The minutes were then confirmed. COUNCILLOR DIXON INTERROGATES THE CHAIR- MAN OF THE SANITARY COMMITTEE. The MAYOR called upon Alderman Burgess, as Chair- man of the Sanitary Committee, to answer the follow- ing questions which had been given notice of by Conn- eitlor Dixon, viz. :—Will the Chairman give the particu- lars of the plant said to have cost £2,160? Also where are the patent furnaces of Messrs. Bryan, Donkin & Co., which cost £132 95., and if the engine and boiler from Messrs. Marshall & Sons, which cost £174 6s. 4d., was for the special purpose of driving a fan or otherwise ? Alderman Bunouss said he did notiike the job—(laugh- ter)—but it was not a difficult one to cope with,and if it bad been anybody else who asked the question he should not have hesitated. (Laughter.) His answer to the first question was that any orders for plant that had been given bad been confirmed by that Corporation, and that what- ever had been ordered had been by the Corporiaion itself. The figure of £2,160 he did not at all understand, but if Mr. Dixon wanted information he was quite sure Mr. Chorley had provided it in his annual statement of the accounts of the borough. With reference to the second question he did not know that they had ever had those patent furnaces. It was quite new to him, and he did not know where it came from and where it was. Be (could, however, say that they had had bars for the furnaces which were already in existence and were still existing. They were DOW at Lonvford and doing their work. With reference to the third question as to whether the engine and boiler was for the "special purpose of driving a fan or otherwise," his answer to that was that it was for driving the fan and not otherwise. (Laugh- ter.) The MAYOR remarked that there could be no discussion ert that reply. THE NEW MANAGER OF THE DEPOTS.—THE INSPECTION OF

div.head: MACHINERY.
div.p: THE MACHINERY.

The Sanitary Committee recommended that George T. Norman be appointed clerk in the office of the in- r of nuisances at a salary of 18s. a week; also Z:t.t(he tender of Mr. Jacob Sankey to supply 10 tons of wheat straw at is. 91. per cwt. be accepted. It had further been resolved that the machinery and plant at Longford be periodically examined by a competent per- son, to be appointed by the Committee, and that Dar. Jas. Deas be appointed the manager of Longford depot at a salary of £2OO per annum, subject to the terms of an agreement to be prepared by the Town Clerk, and to the confirmation of his appointment by the Council. Alderman BURGEss, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the Committee meant to have an indepen- dent examination of the machinery periodically. They did not state how often but it would be as often as they thought necessary. The gentleman who had been ap- pointed the manager of the Longford depot knew that this was the determination of the Committee before he was appointed. With reference to the appointment itself, the Committee had, in response to the advertise- ment, a very large number of applications for the post. He thought they numbered about 130, and out of that number eleven were selected, and the choice of the Com- mittee ultimately fell upon Mr. Dees. Out of .the ten memlans of the Committee, there were seven present when the appointment was made, and the appointment was unanimous. The testirbonials they had from Mr. Deas were of a highly satisfactory character. He had testi- monials from hislate employer,and from the Lord Provost of Perth, who wrote ot him in a very flattering manner. Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Church-street, Warrington, strongly recommended Mr. Deas. and said, should there be nothing else in the way, they would feel it a compli- ment almost to themselves if the Committee gave Mr. Dens the appointment. He hoped the minutes would be confirmed, and that they would have a manager who would give them as a Committee less trouble and anxiety and cause them to occupy a somewhat higher position in the estimation of the Council with regard to their work than they seemed to be in at the present time. They should place the new manager in charge with the fullest confidence that he will do what he undertakes to do, and they should leave him to do it, and if he did not do it the periodical examinations which would be made would discover whether he was allowing the machinery to go wrong. On the other hand, if the inspections proved his work to be satisfactory, there would be al confirmation of the value of the servant they had ap- pointed. Alderman SurroN seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said that to present a report only once in twelve months was not often. enough. (Hear, hear.) It would be much better to have inspectors four times a year. and the inspections should also include the intercepting depots. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS: Our resolution does not mention any time. Councillor B. T. FAIVCLOUGH : You said periodi- *ally. Alderman BURGESS: Yes, periodically; but the in- spection may be made four or five times a year. Councillor FAIRCLOUGH said he knew in business mat- ters, if no definite time was fixed, the work was never done. He would prefer. a fixed time--say no fewer than four times a year. Councillor BEAMAN said they intended to have an ex- amination at least four times a year. Councillor DIXON said his experience taught him that It was preferable to have a person thoroughly acquainted with the alkali trade rather than a mechanic and ongineer in charge of such works as those at Longford. Alderman BURGESS said the work of the new manager would not be cenfined to Longford, but he would have to look after the intercepting depots, and he would be responsible to the Committee and to the Council for the control of all the places.
The minutes were passed. PAYING AND SEWERAGE 001111 I TTEE. -THE REPAIR OF

FOOTPATHS. At a meeting of this Committee, it was resolved that the sum of £1,062 be paid to the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity of the Warrington Union in respect of sewers taken over by the Corporation, and that the tender of Mr. Jos. Mounfield to erect and complete boundary wall on the east side of the store yard at Rowley, at £lO3 55., be ac- cepted. The Town Clerk reported that the matter in dispute between the Corporation and the county of Lancaster with respect to the liability of the County Council under the contract of the 18th August, 1887, for the repair of Latchford and Wilderspool Causeways had been referred to counsel, who had advised that the liabi- lity under the contract had been transferred hy the operation of the Local Government Act, 1888, to the County Council, and that they were liable to the Cor- poration for the payment of the money. The London and North-Western Railway Com. footpath running be- tween yhaving repudiated their liability to repair the public their property and the river Mersey at Bank Quay, and which footpath had been previously kept in repair by the company, a resolution .was passed to the effect that the Borough Surveyor repair the footpath, the same being in a dangerous condition. Alderman WRIGHT moved the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor R.T. FAIRCLOUGH took exception to the minute relating to the footpath at Bank Quay. The London and North-Western Railway Company were bound to provide a towing path or a bridge, and he thought the town was going to incur an expense on that footpath they had no right to incur. Councillor JENKINS complained of the condition of Dickenson and Forsha w-sts., adjoining Orford-lane. Alderman BURGESS remarked with regard to the foot- path to which reference had been made by Councillor Fairclough, that they should act with extreme caution as it was not unlikely Councillor Fairclough was right.

Councillor Drxort observed that if the Committee com- municated with Mr. Glazebrook Rvlands they would be able to get much valuable information from him with respect to ancient towing paths.— - - - Alderman WRIGHT said the Committee Chad been ad- vised by their legal adviser that tbe highway in question was a public highway, and as guardians of the public highways, the Committee felt it to be their duty to re- pair the footpath. This was a temporary matter; the footpath was in a dangerous condition, and they were spending only a few shillings upon it, but if it was the feeling of the Council that they should repudiate their liability in the repair of the footpath' they would take I the matter into consideration. The London and North- Western Railway Co. said that if the Committee held them liable to repair the footpath they would expect them to allow them to block it up at each end. That the Committee did not intend to allow for a moment. With regard to Dickenson and Forshaw-sts., they were new streets. The Committee would pay attention to them as soon as possible, but they must first pay atten- tion to those which were the oldest. (Hear, hear.) ' The minutes were then agreed to. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTER. From the report of the Inspector to The Committee it appeared that 38 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 35 cases for 90 children. That 22 cases had been taken before the magistrates. and fines inflicted in 19 cases, 1 case adjourned, and 2 boys committed to an Industrial School. The report of the deputation to the Clio, published last week, was also in the minutes. Councillor Flemixei moved the adoption of the minutes. He mentioned that the Clio training ship had been established 14 years, and 900 boys had passed through the ship during that time, 600 of whom had gone to sea, and 300 to other occupations ; 92 per cent. were doing well, some of them in very lucrative and high positions. That spoke much for the skip, and in fact it was quite a model ship. He should be glad if there could be a ship established for the Catholic boys, as well as the Clio. It would be ona of the grandest things they could have. For sending boys to Liverpool they had to pay 23. 6d. a week, whereas if they had a ship like the Clio they could get them on board for almost i.ext to nothing. Councillor SHAW-GREEN seconded. The new Educa- tion Act, he observed, had now come into force, and the Committee were very anxious that school managers should take it into their careful consideration, and en- deavour to make the schools free, as far as possible. The Committee, were, with that object, in communication with them, and were hoping to bring about the desired result. The minutes were confirme4l. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, ARTS, AND TECHNICAL INSTPITCTION

div.head: COMMITTEE.-THE COUNTY COUNCIL GRANTS.
div.p: COMMITTEE.-THE COUNTY COUNCIL GRANTS.

The -minutes of this Committee have already been pub- lished excepting the following :—The return for the Library and Museum was as follows :—Visitors to the Museum, 1,841, decrease, 35 per cent., compared with July, 1890; books issued in reading-room, 924, decrease, 15 per cent., compared with July, 189); books issued in lending department, 924, increase 4 per cent., compared with July 1890. A report of the following gifts, far which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors was submitted :—Moth—Salyrion pieri, from Lago Maggiore, from Mr. R. Davies; box of insects from Japan, from Mr. C. Holmes, F.L.S. ; ants found in timber from Central America. from Mr. W. Mounfield ; starfish—oreaster reticulatus, from Mr. Kendrick; young weasel, from Mr. J. Peers; crabs (7 specimens) and fishes (2) from Mauritius, from Mr. L. Greening'; model of Jeru- salem, from Mr. R. Heaton; token of "Nathan Abraham, Warrington, 1666," from N. Heywood; "Stories of sen- timent," by Kains-Jackson, from Mr. T. Robinson; "The Education of Man," by J. G. Speed, from the author. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved the adoption of the minutes of this Committee. The Council would ob- serve, he said, that the Committee had proceeded with the preliminary arrangements for formation of technical instruction classes during the coming season. A circalar was sent out not very long ago by the County Council to all institutions which in any degree carried out the pur- pose of the Technical Instruction Act, inviting them to make applications for grants to them in aid of technical instruction. Recently the Committee were in a position to inform the Corporation that the County. Council had allocated for the purpose to Warrington £6lO, but the circular left it very uncertain whether this sum would come directly into the hands of the Corporation or that a portion of it would come into their hands and the other portions to other institutions. Therefore the Committee decided to appeal to the County Council by deputation as to the matter, and the previous day thechairman of the Committee (Mr. Monks), the Town Clerk, Mr. Made- ley, and himself, attended at Preston upon the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Council, and as the result that Committee passed the following resolu- tion :—" Resolved that that it be a recommendation to the County Council that the sum of £6lO allocated to Warrington be paid to the Corporation for the purpose of technical instruction in accordance with the scheme of the Museum, Library, Arts,and Technical Instruction Committee." (Hear, hear,) The Committee therefore had no hesitation in asking the Council to confirm their minutes in the full assurance that they would carry through a scheme that would be creditable to the town and useful to the district, and which would not cost the ratepayers one single farthing. Councillor GREENING seconded. Alderman Sultanas asked what the grant was likely to be in the future. Councillor H. ROBERTS said the Committee's scheme was only for this year, and would be alterable from year to year, according to circumstances. They would obtain an annual grant so long as the money that had been allotted by Government was applied for this purpose by the County Council, but the present grant only related to the present year. The sum of £6lO was not all the Committee expected to get from the County Council. That authority had two years' receipts to dispose of now, and the £6lO was only Warrington's proportion for the first year's receipts. The County Council were appropriating, for the purpose of adjusting finances between themselves and different interested authorities, rather more than half the amount at their disposal, but there wriuld remain £17,000 to be disposed of as the County Council might think fit, for the purposes of technical instruction in the county, and the Committee hoped to get a considerable portion of that sum.
The minutes were adopted. CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

The Registrar's report to this Committee showed that the interments during the past four weeks were : Adults, ; minors, 42; stillborn and premature, 15 ; corresponding period last year, adults, 34 minors, 54; stillborn and premature, 11.—The receipts for the past four weeks were £9l 19s. ; corresponding period last year. 030 17s. sd. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Councillor JENKINS, seconded by Councillor HEATON.
THE NEW BATHS.-THE SCHEME Nor TO BE
ABANDONED.

The report of the Bathkeeper to the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee showed that the income from the Baths for the past four weeks was £32 35., and for the corresponding period last year. £32 2s. Bd. It wus resolved that the plan for the erection of new baths, and alteration of existing baths, now submitted by the Borough Surveyor be approved ; also that the Commit- tee, having considered the plans and tenders for new baths, are of opinion that the cost of supply* same is more than they are justified in incurring, and recom- mend that the same be postponed for the present. Alderman CHANDLILY moved the confirmation of the minutes. The Council were, he said, aware that they had authorised the Committee to obtain plans and ultim- ately estimates for new baths and alterations for the old baths. The estimates obtained were as follows :—New baths, £3,320; alteration of the old baths, £923; new Turkish baths,£l,394; engineering,£l,ooo ; total 48,637. The Committee considered these estimates were such that they ought not to take the responsibility of acting directly upon them,and sought the advice of the General Purposes Committee with a view to test their feeling and to give them more confidence in any project or proposi- tion that they might bring before the Council. The General Purpose Committee considered the matter, but they themselves were unable to come to a satisfactory conclusion. They were divided in opinion and they thought that the best course would be for the com- mittee to confirm a resolution to bring before the Coun- cil in order that the Council themselves might take the responsibility of spending or declining to spend this sum. He thought it was but right that he should place before the Council the great responsibility involved in the spending of so large a stun. He had as- certained that week that there was no complaint as to the condition of the existing baths, and that there was adequate accommodation except on Saturday afternoons and Sunday mornings, and then this deficiency only ex- isted in the hottest weather. It was therefore a matter for consideration whether the baths were really required under these circumstances. They must bear in mind that the bathers going to the existing baths did not number more than 2 per cent, of the population of War- rington, so that the Council had to consider whether they would accept the responsibility of spending say £7,000 for the accommodation of 2 per cent. of the people of the town. The Corporation must not run away with the idea that the Committee did not want new public baths. They wanted them quite as much as any other section of the Council or the community did, but the responsibility involved was a great one ; and there was not merely the first cost to be considered but also the maintenance. The Turkish baths alone, for in- stance, would involve an expenditure of £2OO a year on this account, and the attendant would have to be there and the expense would be going on if only one bather came in a week. The Committee came to the conclusion that, with the present bath accommodation, it was un- desirable at present to spend the sum of money that the estimates amounted to, but they invited expressions of opinion in the Council on the subject.

Councillor BOLTON seconded the moticn. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved an amendment that the minutes of the Committee be confirmed with the excep- tion of the second paragraph in the resolution as to the baths scheme; and further that the Committee be re- , quested to proceed with such portions of the scheme for baths extension as could be accomplished for a sum not exceeding £5,000. He was glad to know that the Com- mittee were not unanimous in their decision, but that the matter was decided by the casting vote of the Chair-

div.head: TH E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 1891.
div.p: TH E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 1891.

man of the Committee, and he said with all respect that if that gentleman had been anxious for baths extension' to be accomplished they should not have had to face that - result. —He (Mr. Roberts) did not forget that the chair- man, when the plans were first submitted to the Coun- cil a few months ago,put the matter in such a shape as to show that ke would be very glad indeed if the thing was kicked out,tthat he spersonally had no interest in bring- ing the matter.before them, and with such a spirit at the head of affairs he did not wonder at all at the course things had taken. It was now six or seven years since this matter was first before the Council. In October 1885 two schemes were submitted to the Council one in- volving an expenditure of £7OO and an alternative scheme involving an outlay of £2,000. One of tkese would have been adopted at thelirne if the Council had been in a position to borrow the necessary money. Since then a special Act had been obtained for the purpose of purchasing the Waterworks, and doing other things for the improvement of the town. A claose was inserted in that Act for the very purpose of obtaining power to borrow money to carry out the bath extension. The matter was sanctioned by the Council and afterwards by the ratepayers, and he could not understand the hesi- tation of the Committee in expending this money. He admitted there were many things .requiring to be done in Warrington, and that would have to be done soon or late, but this fact might be used as an argument against any individual improvement in any department. What the Council had to decide was did the town require ad- ditional bath accommodation? If so, they'were bound to provide it. He was astonished at the case put forward by the Chairman of the Committee as to the condition of the baths. It was beyond argument that the accommo- dation was insufficient, that the surroundings were dis- graceful, and that the whole thing was discreditable to the Corporation, and to a town of 50;000 inhabitants in the year 1891. As to the argument that only 2 per cent. of the population were bathers at the existing baths, that was almost beneath notice. It was a wonder to him that 2 per cent. availed themselves of the facili- ties then. If the Corporation made the baths attractive the people would come. There was no ieason why the expenditure for Turkish Baths should be suspended. He hoped the Council would sufficiently hold up the weak ones of the Committee and give them by their support the courage to do what was necessary in the interests of the town and neighbourhood. Councillor JENKINS seconded the amendment. He con- sidered that the improvement of the baths would be one of the greatest boons that could be conferred upon the town.

Dr. CANNELL said the Committee would be perfectly willing to spend £7,000 with the consent of the Corpora- tion, but they did not wish to take the responsibility. He thought an expenditure 0f*5,000 would be quite suf- ficient.

Councillor HILL supported the amendment, but con- sidered that an expenditure of £3,000 would be ample. Turkish baths he thought unnecessary. One reason why the Warrington baths were not better attended were that persons could not afford to pay 7d. It ought not to ex- ceed 3d. or 4d., and school children ought to be admitted for id. each on certain days. Councillor BOLTON: 6d. is the price of admission to the public. Councillor R. T. FAIRCLOI7GH mentioned that the Coroner recently, in holding an inquest on two boys drowned at Latchford, said there would be cash of drowsing as long as there were no public baths in War- rington, and the foreman of the jury had asked him (Mr. Fatrclough) to bring before the Council a :suggestion by the Coroner that open-air baths should be established, where boys could bathe instead of in the river. He thought part of the £5,000 might well be expended for this purpose. Councillor SHAW-GREEN thought an extension of the existing bath system absolutely necessary, but thought the exoenditure ought not to be more than £2500. Councillor BOLTON said the Committee thought if the thing was worth doing at all, it was worth doing well. They did not want to do that which would require tinkering now and then, but to provide for future generations. The sooner the accotnodation was increased 1 the sooner the prices would have tot be dropped. The working classes would have to have a bath at a less rate than 6d. It would be a question in a short time whether the baths like the library should not be free. Alderman WRIGHT expressed his disappointment at the conclusion of the Committee. Had he been present at the Committee meeting, he would certainly have voted for carrying out a scheme for the erection of new baths under any circumstances. He believed in giving every adult and child in Warrington every facility for bathing, though it should cost id. in the £. Councillor BROWNE supported the amendment. The present baths were a disgrace, and the swimming bath was dangerous, through the slippery condition of the floor of the bath, a well known gentleman having been I saved from drowning by other gentlemen. _ _

Alderman SurroN-said he woiild like to see new baths and new everything else that the town wanted, but he and others could not see their way to the expenditure of nearly £7OOO in the face of the very large corporate debt, and of the many improvements which would cer- tainly soon or late have to be carried out at a very large cost indeed. The rates of the borough were so high that the Corporation ought to be very careful indeed as to increasing them. Many people were prevented by them from coming to Warrington and erecting works. He did not think there was such a demand for the extension of the baths as had been represented. He believed they were capacious enough to accommodate all the bathers who desired to use them. They were good enough for him and for his family to learn to swim in. When new baths were provided the Council would have to open them free to the public. As to charging too much, in one portion of the baths now the charge was only 2d. ; and that portion could be altered at a slight expense so as to meet the requirements for years to come. Open air baths in Warrington would not prevent boys bathing in ; dangerous places; as such baths did not prevent their I doing so in other towns. Councillor HeaTon said the discussions in the Council had left them no alternative but to build the baths ; and he thought that for less than £5,000 new baths could be built second to none in Lancashire and to none he had seen in the world. His idea was not to touch the new baths at all. They were not so bad as described ; they used to be very bad but had been much improved. Councillor PLumprox supported the amendment, Alder- men Chandley and Sutton's statement that there was no demand for the baths by tne working classes of War- rington was another proof that the Aldermen did not know much of what the electors did want. If the baths were improved they would be more used. He thought there ought to be one free day a week. Good baths would not prevent manufacturers coming to the town. Alderman SITTON : The rates would. Councillor FlurcantsoN advocated spending only £2,500 to £3,000 at first. Councillor Vorsner appealed to Councillor Roberts to withdraw his amendment and allow the Committee to reconsider the matter. Baths in the open air, he remarked, could only be used at certain times of the year. Turkish 'oaths could be done without.

Councillor FLEMING supported the amendment. Alderman HOLMES supported the original resolution,on the ground of economy. The Corporation had a debt of £270,000, and they were confronted with an expenditure for the widening of Bridge-st. and other purposes, of £lOO,OOO to £200,000. He had never heard of much de- mand for these baths.
Councillor DIXON supported the confirmation of the minutes. He had never found half a dozen working-men in Warrington asking for _baths.
:Councilfor BzAmAX, who supported the amendment, asserted that the bath for which the Committee charged ed. was not worth more than 2d.

Alderman BURGESS said that although an Alderman he was not ashamed to give utterance in that room to his opinions, whether they had any weight or not with those people who preached for votes. (Laughter.) He sup- ported the Committee in their wise and modest proposal. He had known four baths in Warrington, and each one been a failure. He did not know how the Council were going to expect that more than two per cent. of the population would use the baths. In the past, baths had been a failure, and they were not going in the future to be the grand thing that many gentlemen seemed to think they would be. He would advise that they let the present baths, which were in good and useful condition, be tried fora time, and if thought advisable the charge of admission might be reduced by one half. It was note- worthy that the recent improvements had not increased the number of bathers. Alderman CHATIDLEY denied that the baths were in a disgraceful condition. He had been there that afternoon, and they were as clear as crystal. There was a school of I boys there learning to swim, under the direction of a teacher. He asked the bath attendant if any complaint had been made in any department during the past three months, and his reply was "No." The price of a season ticket was 10s.,and tickets were retailed in many parts of the town, and tickets for the first-class bath might be purchased at qd. each. He was of opinion that working-men earning from £3 to £5 a week could afford to pay 103. for a season tickst. Those who could not "do so could go to the second-class bath, the charge to which was only 2d. That bath was in a beautifully clear condition, and thoroughly clean when hesaw it that afternoon, and yet not a soul was in it. That showed that new baths were not necessary. The MAYOR advocated the erection of new baths at a cost of £4,000. He pointed out as to the remarks on the bad attendance at the second-class bath, that the sum- tiler had been a most unfavourable one for bathing. A fortnight ago he said, not a boat was to be seen in the bay of Llandudno, though it did not follow that there would always be summers like the present. If the weather became warm towards the end of the week the baths would no doubt be crowded. It was said that they could get a first class bath for 41d. That might be so, but they would have to put down a big sum to begin with-10s. ;—and, as the Alderman had said, if working-men were getting £3, £4, and £5 a week they could well afford to pay that amount. He should, however, like to be enlightened upon the subject by Councillor Beaman. He should like to know how many workmen received £3, £4, and £5 a week. He thought most of them were content with a sovereign a week, although he should be pleased to find that working-men were in the happy position which had been described by Alderman Chandley. (Hear, hear.) Is to two per cent. of the population bathing,if the baths were not made attractive people would not use them. When the baths were once finished he did not see how there could be much annual expense to the ratepayers. As to the Turkish baths, Warrington was hardly big enough for them. Councillor Hutchinson had said he should like to see baths scattered over the town, but the Legh- st. baths were as central for all as they could be. A vote was then taken, with the following result :
For the amendment. The Mayor Alderman Wright Councillor H. Roberts 19 Fleming 91 Cannell 91 Green „ Greening „ Beaman „ Ashton „ Jenkins „ Plumpton Hill „ Bolton „ Browne „ Hutchinson —l5
against it. Alderman Sutton ~ Holmes 119 Burgess „ Olandley Councilllr Dixon ~ Voisey

The MAYOR declared the amendment carried. Alderman CIIANDLEY assured the Council that the Committee would work with all zeal to promote the objects desired and spend judiciously what sum the Council thought proper. Councillor H. ROBERTS thanked Alderman Chandley for the spirit in which he had received the Council's de- cision.

Councillor PLustrrow seconded the motion. He said there should be no objection to any ratepayers in the town visiting the depots. He had made inquiries in other towns, but he did not find any mwhich the War- rington rule existed. _ _

Alderman ScrrroN suggested, that to give every rate- payer an opportunity of seeing the inside of the works, the Chairman of the Sanitary Committee should give a big banqugt there and invite them. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: What would you feed them on ? (Renewed laughter.) Alderman SurroN thought it was perfect folly to sup- pose that the ratepayers would care to go to the works for purposes of inspection. They did not care sufficiently about them to do so.

Alderman BIIRORSS said he was quite sure that the gentlemen whom Councillors Dixon and Plumpton represented would go in crowds to the place to have a feed, but it must be done at the cost of the Corporation. He wished that members of the Council would exercise more care in framing their resolutions. He contended that Councillor Dixon's motion did not comply with the Standing Orders, and he asked the Town Clerk to say whether that was so or not.
The Towx CLERK : I don't think it is strictly in order; I think it is out of order. The MAYOR: There is an end of the matter then The discussion then dropped, and the meeting . ded

This Committee reported that the total income from all sources wag £456 ss. 3d. corresponding period last year, £402 16s. 10d. Increase, £53 Bs. sd. The minutes were adopted on the motion of Councillor HUTCHINSON, seconded by Councilloi SHAW-GREEN.

GAS COMMITTEE—ACCIDENTS TO WORKMEN. This Committee reported that the average illuminating power of the gas for the four weeks preceding August 21st was equal to 18.79 catiales at both works. The tender of Messrs. Bryan. Donkin and Company, Limited, to supply a duplicate exhauster, at £155, was accepted. Alderman flocmss moved, and Councillor GREENING sec onded. the passing of the minutes. Councillor H. ROBERTS asked if the Committee had given up their policy in the Accidental Insurance Com- pany, if so what was the amount of the premium to be saved, and why the Committee had given up so essential a safeguard against claims on the part of workmen against themselves for accidents received while in their service. - _

- --- Alderman HOLMES : We have abandoned the payment of the premium, as the claims have been so very small- 30s. or 40s. during the time we have been subscribing. Instead of paying to the Accidental Insurance Company, we lay by a small sinking fund of our own, out of which to pay for accidents. A MEMBER: What is the amount of the premium? Alderman WRIGHT: Nearly £9 a year, and we are go- ing to set aside £lO per annum. Councillor Rowers would not move an amendment but thought this policy was a childish and absurd ar- rangement for business men to adopt. Alderman CII&NDLBY : We are not all so clever as you are.

_ Councillor ROBERTS: You might have a claim in one year which would swallow up the savings of ten or twelve years. (Hear, hear.) Councillor GREENING: I oppose the new arrangement very strongly. I think it was penny wise and pound foolish to run the risk of heavy claims for the sake of £9 a year. The MAYOR: It seems that the Committee think that because they have had no accident they will never have one. The minutes were adopted. • FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE.

Councillor DIXON moved :—" That the resolution passed some time ago, requiring an order from Mr. Alderman Burgess before any ratepayer or stranger can inspect the Longford Works, be suspended during the months of September, October, and November, to allow all ratepayers to inspect the works when convenient during working hours, because of their present condi- tion." He remarked that many people had a desire to visit the works, and there was a strong feeling against having to ask Alderman Burgess for the necessary order. He believed that the works at Longford were the only works of the kind which were thus shut up from the

div.head: NEWTON BREWSTER SESSIONS.
div.p: NEWTON BREWSTER SESSIONS.
SATURDAY.—Before Messre.W. F.Gooch (chairman), T. J. Gillespie, W. Mitchell, T. H. Pearson, and Captain With ington. SUPERINTENDENT'S REPORT.

Police-Superintendent Brassington read the following report :—" Gentlemen,—l have the honour to lay before you the usual returns relative to the business in connec- tion with the general annual licensing sessions. There are within the townships of Golborne and Haydock, which form the Wigan portion of the Warrington petty sessional division, 32 licensed persons, viz., 13 inn- keepers, one spirit grocer, and 18 beersellers (13 on and 5 off the premises) being the same as last year. There have been 158 persons proceeded against for drunkenness, and drunk and disorderly conduct, being an increase of 4as compared with last year. During the year one inn- keeper was summoned, and the case was dismissed. The houses generally have been well conducted, and I have no objection to any of .the licenses."

Sup-erintendent -Higinbotham submitted the following report as to the Warrington portion of the division : " Gentlemen,—l have the honour to lay before you my returns relative to the business in connection with the annual licensing session. The number of licensed victuallers is 45, 2 less than last year. The number of beersellers on premises is 16, the same as last year, and the number of beersellers off premises is 5, or 4 less than last year. The reduction in the number of these off licenses and one licensed house (the King and Queen, Warrington) is owing to the extension of War- rington borough boundary, and the other licensed house (the Ship Inn, Winwick) has been discontinued. One licensed victualler (Thomas Waywall, Blue Lion Inn, Newton) was summoned on the 28th of March, 1891, for selling drink to a drunken person, and was ordered to pay costs. Generally the licensed persons have con- ducted their houses satisfactorily, and there have been few complaints.

div.head: APPLICATIONS.
div.p: APPLICATIONS.

There were no applications for new licenses, and all those for renewal of existing licenses were acceded to. , Mr. Hopwood, solicitor, of Wigan, made an applica- tion on behalf of Mr. William Walmsley, of the New Inn, Golborne. He said his client in the beginning of the year altered his premises by adding a billiard room with- out the permission of the magistrates. The superinten- dent caused a summons to be issued against him, and the case was heard on the 30th of May last, but was dis- missed, the Bench, however, expressing an opinion that Mr. Walmsley ought to have taken them into his confi- dence, before. altering the premises. Since then the room had not been used, and the application now was for permission to use the room as a billiard room. There was no access to it from outside the house. The only communication was internally by the stairs. Permis- sion was granted.

Mr. J. b. Swift, of St. Helens, said he was instructed in a matter somewhat similar, except that as yet his client had made no alterations, and was anxious to take the Bench into his confidence.—Mr. Alfred Tunstall, of the Viaduct Inn, Earlestown, had on the ground floor of that house two small rooms, one a parlour and the other a snug, and he had been considering how his premises might be improved, and been advised by Mr. Beesley, his architect to add to the two rooms by taking down an intervening wall and annexing an adjoining cottage to the rooms, which:alteration would make the premis es more commodious. Authority was given for the alteration.

div.head: ORMAN iIIVIL WAR.
div.p: THE ORMAN iIIVIL WAR.

COMPLETE DEFEAT OF PRESIDENT BALMACEDA. The complete downfall of the Government of President Balmaceda was announced on Sunday in an official des- patch from Santiago itself. The telegram :confirms the total annihilation of the Presidential army and the:flight of Balmaceda.

The confidential agency of the Chili Congress party communicates a despatch which it has received from Iquique announcing that after landing at Valparaiso the Congressionalists won two battles, namely, at Concon on the ‘.2nd August, and at Placcilla on the 28th. At the former place the enemy lost 1,500 men in killed and wounded, 1,500 men being taken prisoners, 14 guns, 2,000 rifles,three mitrailleuses, and a large quantity of ammu- ntion, and at Placilla the whole of its artillery and 3,000 prisoners. The despatch adds: "After entering Val- paraiso, the Congressionalists seized the war vessel Almirante Lynch, the Sargent's Aldea, and all the other torpedo boats. Our losses are unimportant. Don Claudio Vicuna, the President-elect, Senores Godoy, and Danados, ex-Ministers, and Senor Veil, Prefect of Valparaiso, have taken refuge on board foreign vessels." A telegram from New York mentions an "unconfirmed report" that Balmaceda in his flight struck a muleteer, and that the man in retaliation shot him dead. No- thing appears to be known at Valparaiso of this tragic denouement. From that city, however, comes the news that two regiments of Government troops at Talcahuano revolted on hearing of the President's defeat, and shot all their officers. Order has been restored at Santiago and Valparaiso,but mob rule is said to prevail at Coronel, whither Her Majesty's sloop Daphne and the German warship Sophie have been despatched to protect the in- terests of foreigners. The German Admiral has sent the corvette Alexandrine north—it is supposed to Callao— with refugees on board. A proclamation has been issued in Chili to the effect that any person harbouring Balmacedist officials, and failing to give them up, will be shot. The feeling against the United States is very bitter, and a Washing- ton telegram says it is believed in official circles that the next Congress will order an investigation of the conduct of Patrick Egan, Minister to Chili.

NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS HO RTIC UL- TUR AL SOCIETY. ANNUAL SHOW. _

The annual exhibition of fruit, flowers and vege- tables, under the auspices of the above flowers, was held on Saturday, in a field adjoining the Newton Nurseries, kindly lent for the occasion by Ur. J. E. Pardey. The day opened rather dull, and there were one or two showers, which augured badly for the success of the show, so far as the attendance of the public was concerned, but as the day wore on, it cleared up, and during the remainder of the after- noon, the weather was all that could be desired. The attendance, though fairly good, was not so large as previously. The exhibits also were not quite up to the standard of previous years, nor were they so numerous, the bad season no doubt, being responsible for this to a great extent. The show was held in a large marquee erected in the field,a.nd the exhibits were staged on benches running the whole length of each side, and the centre of the tent, and were arranged in an artistic manner. In addition to the competitive exhibits, Mr. T. J. Gillespie sent a collection of fine ferns and stove and greenhouse plants for exhibition, which helped consider- ably to enrich the artistic decorations. The various classes of vegetables, including cabbages, turnips, and potatoes sent by Mr. J. E. Perdu, were of a remarkably fine description, Mr. E. Last of Golborne, being not a whit behind with his potatoes. Messrs. Hilton and Ran- dall showed some yery fine specimens of peas and Deans, and Mr. Wood of Brynn, an old exhibitor, displayed a ' choice collection of leeks. The tomatoes shown by Mr. C. E. Arnott, were very fine and rich in colour. In the amateur class, Mr. S. Boardman took first honours, with some fine selections of potatoes and cabbages, and Mr. Geo. Clarke, exhibited some exceedingly fine apples of his own production. 'Among the flori ul- turists Mr. Boardman showed his skill in the beaut ful specimens of phloxes and gladiolas which he displayed, and Mr. S. Wood was as usual to the fore with cut flowers. The fruit show was not by any means large, nor was it exceptionally good, the only exhibits worthy of mention being the grapes and peaches shown by Col. George McCorquodale and nectarines, by Mrs. Jones. A nicely furnished model of a house and fruit garden, was shown by Mr. R. Harrison, and Mr. J. Mussle displayed several jars of honey obtained from his hives. The staging of the 'various exhibits was carried out under the superintendence tof a Committee including Messrs. Wilson, Randall,Anderson, Berry, Wilkinson ,Williamson, Hutchins, Taylor, and VVatkin. The number of entries was 750, being 100 less than last year, but alltthese did not result in exhibits. The judges in the open classes were Messrs. Kipps, (Walton Lea), Geo. Thomp- son, Worsley Hall, near Manchester. Cottagers &C.: Mr. Skeene, Garswood, and Mr. Webster, Kenyon Hall. Gardens: Messrs. J. Wilson, H. Browne, and F. Hutch- ings. The arrangements for the success (of the show were efficiently carried out by the numerous Com- mittee, assisted by Mr. J. A. Frost, secretary, Messrs. S. Leather, and T. Unsworth, hon. secs., and Mr. R. Bar- ton, treasurer. The following is a full list of the awards :—.

The Legislative Assembly of New South Wales has negatived a motion in favour of protective import duties by sixty-one to forty-seven votes. A DOUBLR Visitnicr WANTED.—On Wednesday, at the Thames Police Court,John Lewis was again charged with the murder of Emily Adams, at a Tavern in Limehouse. The woman's husband had previously been charged with the crime and a verdict of wilful murder returned against him, but it was afterwards ascertained that he was in prison at the time of the tragedy. Lewis was the last person seen in the woman's society ; but his solicitor held that as the verdict against Adams had not been quashed the magistrates had no jurisdiction to take evi- dence against his client for the same crime. The magis- trate said he would consider the point, and the prisoner was remanded. A FRAUDULENT LOVER.—At the Marylebone Police Court, on Wednesday, Titus Crawford was charged on remand with obtaining £2lO by false pretences from Mrs. Grosutt, of the White Sheaf Inn, Portman Square, London. The prisoner, it was alleged, had represented that he was a detective, that he was coming into a large fortune, and that he could free the prosecutrix from a serious trouble. He made love to her daughter, pro- mised her all the money he was likely to possess, and said if she did not marry him he would blow her brains out. While avowing his love in this furious fashion he obtained the money from the proaecutrix, and it was found, moreover, that he was married already. He was committed for trial.

DISASTROUS COLLIERY EXPLOSION.

A disastrous colliery explosion occurred early on Mon- day morning in the Red Cow pit at Bedminster, a suburb of Bristol. The gas fired at a light one of the miners was carrying, and the explosion brought down a long stretch of roof, which buried a number of men. A search party was organised, and the explorers, pene- trating to the distant workings, succeeded in bringing out eleven bodies. Another miner has since died from the effects of after-damp. Several men seriously in- jured were rescued.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
A PASSENGER TRAFFIC SYNDICATE.

A body, to be known as the Manchester Ship Canal Passenger Steamer Syndicate, Limited, has been regis- tE red, for the purpose of developing passenger traffic up- on the various sections of the canal as they are com- pleted. The capital will be £6,500, in twenty-six shams I at £250 each. The whole of the shares have been taken up. The subscribers intend,after developing the traffic, to convert the syndicate into a limited company, with considerable capital, in sufficient time before the com- pletion of the Ship Canal to Manchester, so that a thoroughly organised and efficient service of passenger steamers will be established along the whole length of the canal immediately it is open. It is needless to say that enterprises of this class will be welcomed by the directors of the canal, and that every reasonable facility will be afforded to the promoters.
PRESENTATION TO A SHIP CANAL EMPLOYE.

On Saturday evening the men employed in pile drivingon the Manchester Ship Canal, on Rdncorn sec- tion met at the Weaver hotel, Weston Point and pre- sented their foreman Mr. C. Riva with a purse of gold, on the occasion of his severing his connection with the Company. Mr. Walter Wright made the presentation on behalf of the men.

The custom of wearing black for the dead dates back to the time of the Romans. since When it has always been popular amongst Western nations. The great mortality of this coun- try, considering its sanitary arrangements, has given birth to a number of shops exclusively for the SALE OF MOURN- ING. These shops, subsisting entirely on one department., are. compelled to charge exorbitant prices, as many a be- reaved one is able to testify. having found ta her cost when the funeral was over, that she had made a bad bargain. Whilst making these statements we wish to draw the attention of Ladies to two facts —I. That we are Manufacturers of Mantles. Costumes. and Millinery, doing a large WHOLE- SALE TRADE in these departments, and that we supply our customers at the WHOLESALE PRICES. 2. Ours being a GENERAL TRADE, with a number of depattments, we are not dependent on our Mourning Trade for the profits, and can consequently afford to sell at Lower Prices than our competitors. Our designs are copied from the latest Paris and Berlin models, modified to suit the tastes of our various customers. Every garment is thoroughly examined before being sent out, and for fit. finish, and style, we cannot we surpassed, whilst our prices will be bound nearly half of those charged elsewhere. During the sale SPECIAL PRICES will prevail in this department. Ladies requiring deep or complimentary mourning will receive every attention, and they will doubtless be astonished at the value which they receive.

Two importait demonstrations of Miners' Grievances. Miners were held on Monday ; ono

at Chesterfield, and the other at Wrexham; and on Saturday there was a gather- ing at Golborne. At all of these meetings, the question of establishing an eight hours day by Parliamentary enactment was pressed to the front. It is generally conceded that eight hours in one day is quite long enough for man or boy to work in a mine ; but there is a difference of opinion even amongst miners as to the wisddm of appe'aling to the legislature. The colliers of Northumberland and Durham have obtained an average of eight hours, or something less, and they do not see why miners in other parts of the country should not, by close organisation, secure what they have secured. But what if their brethren fail, as they have hitherto failed ? Is it not reasonable, in that case, to try another plan? There is this also to be said as to tile Parliamentary method that, if it be carried out, it will be a great reform accomplished without the friction, bad feeling, and dislocation of labour which would ensue if pressure were brought to bear upon employers by a series of strikes. It would happen, too, that the eight hours day would be obtained irregularly--the boon being first secured where organisation was most perfect, while the battle would have to be fought again and again where organisation was defective. Looking at the matter from a miner's and from a colliery-owner's point of view, it seems to us that the best way to carry the thing through is to get the legislature to enact that work in mines shall not exceed eight hours per day. This would apply to boys of course, as well as men, for, as Sir Charles Dilke remarked, "their Northumberland friends were too apt to forget that a boy had the same rights as a man." One of the grievances of Welsh miners is that they are paid fortnightly instead of weekly. Thus far employers have resisted the demand for weekly pays, urging that it will cause more book-keeping; and that it will lead to more frequent drinking bouts on the part of those who are in the habit of taking a glass too much on pay day. But this applies to a portion of the men only ; and it may be that they would be less inclined to go" on the spree "if, through weekly payments and weekly purchases, they acquired more regular and there. fore more economical habits. A workman ought to be paid for his labour within a reasonable time; and it is not reasonable to ask him to work a fort- night, or longer, before receiving wages. It leads to a system of purchase on credit, which means, in many cases, getting into debt and never getting out again. The difficulty as to accounts is scarcely worth taking into consideration ; for it is one which has long since been got over in all the great industries in the kingdom. Besides, the miners of Yorkshire are at present paid weekly; and what can be done in Yorkshire can be done in other counties.

Mr. B. PICKARD, M.P., spoke, at the Wrexham demonstration, upon the necessity of dealing with royalty rents and way leaves. He said:—" If, as he believed, close upon seven millions of money were being extracted to pay royalties from the bone and sinews of the workmen and from the

capital of the employers, it was time they tried to see whether this £7,000,000 of money was rightly applied, and for the best interests of the nation." It is certainly wrong on the face of it that a land. owner should receive rent for the use of the surface of his land, say, for agricultural purposes, and then, without doing a stroke of work, or finding a. penny for plant, put a heavy tax on the minerals which are beneath the surface. And that this tax is heavy may be gathered from the fact that as much royalty is paid upon the coal which carries a steamer across the Atlantic as would' suffice to pay the wages of the captain and the crew. Can we wonder that miners, who are familiar with these things,have a strong feeling on the question of royalty rents ? They do not see why they should work like moles in the bowels of the earth, and that the first fruits should go to some- body who, through "the accident of an accident,' is enabled to call himself owner of that which was in process of making, for the use of the whole of earth's children, thousands—perhaps millions —of years before he was born. Whatever may be thought about the nationalisation of land, there ought to be no difference of opinion about the nationalisation of royalty rents. A landowner might claim that his forefathers had done some- thing towards adding to the value of the acres which he holds; but he could not say that of the minerals beneath the surface. They belong in equity, and should be made to belong in law, to- the whole of the nation, to be used for the benefit. of the nation. The drones who fatten upon royalty rents have no pleasant future before them, for the working bees are getting their eyes opened as to where the honey goes, and they are disposed to give effect to the sound doctrine which is con- veyed in the scripture which says—" If any will not work neither shall he eat."
The Trade" WE this week print two lettersfroni "

and its persons who are specially interested Defenders, in the drink trade. We direct at- tention to them, as we are always desirous of both sides being heard on any public question; and we offer a few comments in the belief that both writers fall into a grave error in viewing the licensing question as an issue pure and simple between teetotallers and publicans. it is very much more than that: it is a citizens' question, and there is no good reason why topers and publi- • cans should not join hands with temperance men in seeking to lessen the number of licensed houses. indeed, a publican who signs himself "One of the Tied," in a letter which has gone the round of the papers, says :—" My advice is this, diminish the number of public-houses and it will be all the bet- ter for those who are left, because there will not be so much competition, and will make the publi- cans more independent, and less likely to serve the drunken men, who we all know are a nuisance and an anxiety to the publican and the public, who go for a quiet glass and smoke after their day's, hard work." Why, in face of such an expression of opinion from a brother drink-seller, should Mr.. Lawrence FLOOD, or any other publican, fall foul of teetotallers when they, too, venture to urge that it would be better all round to "diminish the number of public-houses ? " Further, many of. those who are most anxious to lessen drunkenness, by lessening the facilities for drinking, show that they are neither fanatical nor intolerant by advo- cating Local Option; they are willing as to a given district to leave it to the inhabitants themselves to say how many drink shops they will have ir. their midst. Is that not fair? Or should the decision be left to brewers and drink-sellers?

We pass Mr. FLOOD'S reference to advertising with the remark that we don't know anybody who gets himself and his place of business so much ad- vertised—" on the cheap ;" but there is a homely proverb which says, there is always the greatest. crush where there is the least room. With regard to the objection taken to seven of the licenses at Warrington, we have already. explained that they were singled out because the magistrates had themselves taken objection to them two years ago, after a visit of inspection. That the magistrates • have stultified themselves in this matter is one reason why the power to deal with licenses should' be taken out of their hands. The suggestion that the people who are found drunk in the streets may have got their liquor from the wine-merchant, the grocer, or at the club, may pass for what it is worth; but it is surely worth very little in view of the glaring evidence which everywhere abounds of the number of drunken persons who are seen to issue from drink-shops. As to grocers' licenses,. where is the temperance advocate who is not, anxious to reduce their number ? The Rv. John YONGE, who is Mr. FLOOD'S pet aversion, was em- phatic in condemning them at the public meeting on Thursday night week. Touching the laboured argument that teeto- tallers—to be consistent—should have no dealing of any kind with publicans,we have already shown that it is beside the mark on this matter of licens- ing, which is a question for all classes. But it is beside the mark in any case, for the logical issue ' of such a mode of reasoning would be to hold that teetotallers and publicans ought not to live on the same planet. There is, however, sufficient intoler- ance in the world without pleading for the exer- cise of more. For our own part, we willingly admit, if it will please our correspondents, that there are some very good publicans, and some very bad teetotallers. The hypocrites are everywhere,, and they can never be hit too hard; but what then? Shall we on that account overlook the gigantic evils of the drink trader We should be glad if Mr. FLOOD would give chapter and verse for his assertion as to the judges who have "stated publicly from the judicial bench that the quips and oddities of the 'cranks' denom- inating themselves teetotallers have done more to retard and harass them in their efforts in the path of true temperance reform, continued during many years both in and out of Parliament,. than any other cause." We know of no judge who has talked such nonsense; but we do know that Mr. Justice GRANTHAM, whom he mentions, has condemned the drink traffic in forcible terms; we do know that other judges have spoken of drink as connected with three-fourths of the crime which is committed; and it is because we know these things that we are willing to assist in lessening the operations of a traffic which is p roductive of evil and that continually.

div.head: SCHOOL SERMONS AT BURTONWOOD.
div.p: SCHOOL SERMONS AT BURTONWOOD.

The annual services in aid ot the Sunday Schools connected with St. Michael's Church, Burtonwood, took place on Sunday. The morning service was conducted by the Rev. J. Johnson, curate-in-charge, who also preached an appropriate sermon, the choir rendering the anthem, " Behold ! God is my salva- tion." The afternoon service was taken by the Rev. E. W. Wittenbury-Kaye, curate of St. John's,Earls- town, but there was only a sparse congregation. The Vicar of Golborne was expected to occupy the pulpit in the evening, but he was preventea from doing so, and the Rev. J. Johnson again officiated. The choir sang in a pleasing mannfr, the anthem, "The earth is the Lord's." The collections during the day amounted to £lO. UMBRELLAS it ECOVERED.-4. Mid W. PUTTON, Sankey-Bt., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Egypt is settling 'down and learning the ways of civilisation ; for some of her merchants—not content with importing Bass's ale and Guiness's stout—have takento selling a concoction of their own under these names, being careful to be sure to imitate the original labels and capsules. There was a time when it was thought the right thing to spoil the Egyptians; now the Egyptians are trying their hands at spoiling the English. They are certainly making progress—of a kind.

Our American cousins are bent upon "licking creation" in the World's Fair which they are pre- paring to hold at Chicago. It is part of their project to exhibit a full-sized model of Nelson's ship the Victory. They would take the original if money could purchase it; for did they not at one time contemplate buying and removing the house in which Shakespeare was born? Ah, if they could only transplant Westminster Abbey or the Tower of London, how happy they would be !

The Tories of Warrington have not forgotten the beating they got last November. Both Mr. John White and Alderman Sutton, at the Con- servative club, on Saturday, urged those present to prepare for the municipal contest. Quite right; but a warning to one side is a warning to the other when it is made publicly ; and the Lib- erals of Warrington certainly need warning. Their policy of late has been one of masterly inactivity; they must be up and doing, if they would get anything done.

The visit last year to this country of the Queen of Roumania causes special interest to be taken in the serious illness from which her Majesty is suffering. It would appear that she is distressed in 'mind as well as in body, fx. the Court is beset with intriguers: and matters have come to such a pass that the Kin.- has talked of abdicating. Can it be that Russia is at the bottom of the mischief? Does the great bear want to put its paw on Roumania?

An English summer has been described as con- sisting of three hot days and a thunderstorm. We have had the thunderstorm again and again, but nobody seems to have seen anything of the three hot days. Country people have a saying that "Good old August never deceives us ' ; but it has been something of a fraud this year—with its storms of wind and rain finishing up with frost. Yes, frost ; frost at Whitsuntide and frost in August—what a season we are having! Every- body says we are to have a fine September, and everybody of course knows all about it. , there was a " fine " gale on the first of Septem- ber.] The London "Standard" is very candid in its reference to the Free Education Act which doesn't make education free. It advises the managers of Voluntary Schools not to "sulk over the securi- ties they have lost"; and reminds them that "They have got the additional fee grant of threepence a head from the Government without the introduc- tion of popular control. Everything else fades into insignificance by the side of this capital ad- vantage." Just so; but it is an advantage which will last just so long as the Tories remain in office, and that is why Tory school managers are in the sulks. The Liberals believe in popular control, because they are Liberals; they have faith in the people.

Mr. Parnell showed himself very much interested not long ago in the case of John Daly, and other Irish political prisoners. It is wonderful how his sympathies have been stirred since he felt the ground slipping from beneath his feet. But his professions are like the song of the poet in "Patience they are "Hollow, hollow, hollow." Mr. O'Brien in a letter to the Dublin, papers says that before the present strife arose he brought the facts of John Daly's case forward, and declares that Alderman Morton, of Birmingham, who first communicated certain facts to him, had over and over again writt3rt to Mr. Parnell entreating his attention, but without ever receiving the courtesy of a reply. Mr. Parnell has made another mistake; he should have said nothing about John Daly.

Being quite sure at last of £6lO for one year from the County Council in support of their scheme of Technical Instruction, the Warrington Com- mittee can go ahead in the full assurance that, if they do good work funds will be forthcoming for the future. Let them be careful, in the first instance, not to aim too high. What is wanted is that the plan should be carried out in such a way as will be an attraction to the smartest children of the elementary schools. At present most of them are sent to work too early. They would be all the bet- ter with two years' training in a Teeknical School.

It is as we anticipated with regard to the long- standing proposal to enlarge or rebuild Public Bath i 3 for Warrington: the Baths Committee is behind public opinion. For fear of spending too much they had made up their minds not to spend anything; but they were told, on Tuesday, that this wouldn't do. They have got to do something, and they should be able to do something handsome with £5,000 at their disposal. It is a good round sum of money, and it ought to run to the provi- sion of at least one open-air bathing place.

Councillor Dixon was on the right tack in bring- ing a motion before the Town Council with a view to suspending the resolution which puts a barrier in the way of ratepayers paying a visit 'to Long- ford Works. But he was informed that his motion was out of order, and the result was that it was not even discussed. No explanation seems to have been given as to how or why it was out of order; and the ratepayers are thus left in the dark. Can it be that Councillor Dixon is under a special set of Standing Orders? However, he will per- haps be equal, at the next Council meeting, to repeating his motion, in another form.

INCREASE IN THE PRICE OF BREAD AT WIDNES. Owing to the increase in the price of flour, the Widnes bakers have desided to advance the price of bread one halfpenny per loaf. ORDINATION AT DITTON HALL. During the present week seventeen priests have been ordained at Ditton Hall College, by the Roman Catholic Bishop of Liverpool. RUNCORN PEERS ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY. The fourth ballot of the Society took place on Monday under the presidency of Mr. J. J. Speakman,and resulted in M. John Waterworth, of Brackly-st., being entitled to an advance of £lOO. WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. The usual weekly meeting was held on Sunday, Dr. O'Keeffe presiding. On the proposition of Mr. Fagarty, seconded by Mr. Williamson, the retiring officers and committee were unanimously re-elected. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS. The teachers of these schools, together with a number of friends, had their annual picnic on Wednesday, when they spent a most pleasant day at Childwall Abbey. The drive to and fro was an enjoyable feature of the pro- ceedings.
WIDNES TRADE COUNCIL.

At a meeting of the representatives of the varions trade organisations of Widnes, on Wednesday evening, it was unanimously resolved to from a Trades Council for the town and a Sub-Committee was appointed to consider the rules of similar Councils and draw up a code of rules and regulations. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. andW. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. PROMOTION OF A WIDNES SERGEANT.

Sergeant Wilcox, who has occupied the position of clerk at Widnes Police Office for the last three years, has been promoted to superintendent clerk at the Bury office, and he will be succeeded by Sergeant Neil, of Bury. Mr. Wilcox possessed the confidence and good will of his brother constables, and was much respected by the general public. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Aevt.

div.head: FALL OF A WALL AT WIDNES
div.p: FALL OF A WALL AT WIDNES

During the gale on Tuesday the gable of a shed at the Bradley Arms was blown down, and two girls—Fanny Forster (New-street),and Ellen Roberts (Albert-rd.),were buried beneath the debris. Roberts was rendered un- conscious,being much bruised about the body,but luckily no bones were broken. Forster received a severe frac- ture of the leg. Both girls are progressing satisfactorily. LAWN MOWERS.—Garland, 51. Bridge-st., Warrington. and at Earlestown.—Adut. DREADFUL BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.

MichielConnolley (54) of 9, Catherine-st., has died at the Widnes Accident Hospital, from injuries received at the Widnes Alkali Works a fortnight ago. In some manner, about which there is a difference of opinion, the deceased was covered with a large quantity of hot cinders and was terribly burned abGut the legs, body, arms, and face. The skin peeled off him as he was extricated from his awful position. An inquest was held last evening, and a verdict of "Accidental Death" was returned.
BlsslNwrrEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. ACCIDENT ON THE SHIP CANAL NEAR RUNCORN.

Robert Wilson, aged 16,50 n of Captain Wilson, of Bold- street, Runcorn, met with a serious accident on the Ship Canal at Big Field, on Tuesday afternoon. He was in the act of uncoupling a wagon, when the engine attached to the train gave a jerk backwards, and flung him to the ground. The whole of the wagon passed over him, terribly smashing his left arm and also breaking his left leg. He was at once conveyed to the Latchford Hospital, where the doctor thought it necessary to amputate the arm near the shoulder, and it is a matter of doubt yet whether the unfortunate youth will not also lose his leg. UnisfeELLAs RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

WIDNES INVENTIONS SYNDICATE, LIMITED. A new company under the above name has just been registered with a capital of £2,000 in LI shares, its object being to arrange with inventors to patent and protect inventions, and to endeavour to sell them to the best ad- vantage. The following are the preliminary directors : Mr. W. T. Husband, solicitor, Widnes; Mr. T. A. Bul- lough. A.M.1.C.E., Farnworth ; Mr. William Scott Callan- der, 16, Mersey-road, Aigburth ; Mr. J. Walwyn White, Widnes ; Mr. T. H. Thomas, Widnes; Mr. James White, Widnes; Mr. William Gibbings, Garston ; Mr. P. J. Webb, Leeds; and Mr. George J. Warner, F.C.A., Widnes.
PREMIER SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND. Warrington, —Advt.
ST. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES.

On Sunday, at St. Paul's Church, special services were held and sermons preached on behalf of the National Schools. The morning preacher was the Rev. G. H. Garnett, 8.Q., who dwelt upon the importance of re- ligious and secular education being combined. In the afternoon a children's flower service waA held,the flowers afterwards being collected and distributed amongst the hospitals in the town. An appropriate address was de- livered by Rev.G. A. Le Bert, 8.A., vicar of St. Ambrose. In the evening the Rev. Canon Diggle, of Mossley Hill, occupied the pulpit and preached a forcible sermon. The collections amounted to £25 4s. 3d., an increase of £lO on last year. UAIRRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. BUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. FAREWELL OF THE REV. A. J. JAMESON, OF WESTON. The anniversary services of Weston Church Schools were preached on Sunday,in St. John's Church,and were of a very successful character. At the morning service the Vicar (the Rev. Canon Wood) occupied the pulpit, and in the course of his sermon, which dealt with educa- tion,he made a reference to the departure of the Rev. A. J. Jameson, the curate-in-charge, of whose character, ability.and work he spoke in the highest terms of praise. In the afternoon a children's flower service was held, conducted by Mr. Jameson. The children and other members of the congregation brought bouquets of flowers, which were handed to Mr. Jameson at the altar, and afterwards despatched to the sick wards at Dutton Workhouse. In the evening Mr. Jameson preached his farewell sermon to a crowded congregatien. Taking for his text "Ye are one in Jesus Christ," he said life was Ane series of partings and separations, but might God grant that that would be for the good of both congrega- tion and pastor. The collections realised double the usual anlount.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

DRUNKENNESS.—Andrew Quinn, Mary-st. ; Jane Drury, Sankey-at. div.head: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGES.
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGES.

Ou Wednesday the village of Farnvvorth was all astir on the occasion of the marriage of two well- known and highly respected couples from the dis- trict. The first was that of Mr. T. Knowles, 8.A., of Dewsbury, and Miss Sarah Annie Hibbert, of Farnworth. The officiating clergymen were the ' Rev. T. R. Pennington, M.A. (brother-in-law of the bride), assisted by the Rev. R. H. Johnson, cousin of the bridegroom. The bride was given away by her brother,the Rev. J. A. N. Hibbert,M.A., of Manches- ter. The bridewas attired in an electric blue travell- ing dress,and was attended by Miss Knowles (sister of the bridegroom), and the Misses Pennington. Af- ter the ceremony the happy couple departed for Il- lfracombe, where the honeymoon will be spent. In the evening the bride's Sunday School class, the members of the Band of Hone and several old people of the village, in addition to the choir of the church, of which the bride had been a member for many years, sat down to a sumptuous tea provided by her. An entertainment was afterwarls given, in which Professor Wyman, conjuror, of Bootle, took part. A large number of pre- sents were received. At two o'clock another marriage was celebrated at the church, the contracting parties being Mr. F. Wareing, son of Major Wareing, of Mill Brow, and Miss Pritchard, daughter of Mr. R. Pritchard, Farnworth. The cere- mony was performed by the Rev. J. R. Jones (curate- in-charge), assisted by the Rev. J. Lee (curate.) The bi-' 70, who wore a light corduroy cashmere dress, with lilac Hungarian silk trimmings, and hat to match, was given away by her father. The presents were very numerous, and of a costly nature.

div.p: MA.RRISGF OF MISS IMISON, OF RUNCORN.

A marriage in which more than customary inte- rest was taken, was solemnised at Runcorn Parish Church, on Wednesday afternoon. The happy couple who were to be made one were Mr.W.Tunstall Newton, of Plumbley, and Miss Amelia Thisbe Imi- son, youngest daughter of the late Mr. C. C. Imison, of Runcorn, and if there is any truth in the old adage that "happy is the bride whom the sun shines on " then • Miss Imison must have been supremely happy, because the air was bright with glorious sunlight. The guests were conveyed to the church in six carriages,drawn by pairs of hand- some greys, supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros.. and when the bridal party entered the sacred edifice, the following guests had taken seats near the chan- cel :—Mrs. and Miss Newton (Southport), Mr. and Mrs, Knowles (Knutsford), Rev. a Payne (Knuts- ford), Rev. Imison, who gave her away, and she was attired in a cream corded silk dress, while her head was adorned with a wreath of orange blossoms from which depended a white flowing veil. She was attended by four bridesmaids, Miss Eva Savage, and three young nieces, Miss Kathleen M. Imi- son, Miss Dorothy Cunningham, and Miss Connie Imi- son (Widnes.) Miss Savarz'e wore a dress of muslin delaine, Miss Kathleen and Miss Connie Imison were attired in yellow silk and Miss Cunningham in blue silk. Mr. Charles Steen, of Birkenhead, was the best man. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. Canon Wood, M.A. vicar, assisted by the Rev. W. RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday. Mr. H. J. Grice presided, and there were present, Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., W. Fisher. H. White, W. Timmins, W. Mellor, S. Taylor, F. Wiswall, J. W. Lightburn, a W. Humphreys, R. Abel, W. Hankinson, J. Pritchard, Jae. Dobson. F. A. Lake (Law clerk), B. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor), Dr. McDougall (medical officer.)
HHALTH OF THE TOWN.

The medical officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during August was 21, and of these 5 were inquest cases. Of the remaining 16 deaths, 3 were due to mesenteric disease, 3to convul- sions, 2 to heart disease and one each to premature birth, gangrene, natural decay, inflammation of lining membrane of the brain, inflammation of the lungs, kidney disease, and croup. The 21 deaths showed an avorage death rate of 12.6 per 1000 exclusive of the inquest cases of 9.1. The Authority would observe with satisfaction that the death-rate of the last month was very low and that the zymotic class was unrepresented.— The Chairman: Those figures would compare favourably with any authority in the kingdom.—Dr. McDougall: I should say so. It is an exceptionally low death-rate.—The Surveyor: Lowest since 1885, when there were exactly the same number of deaths.
