Stuart for granolithic pave- ment for Victoria-road, at /Is. 3.1. per superficial square yard be accepted ; that Messrs. tlenry Heys, and Co's. price for flags, ss. per superficial square yard less 21 per cent. discount delivered be accepted.—That the follow- ing plans be approved of two cottages in Heath-road, for Mr. Thomas Leach junior ; and of a house and shop in Greenway-road for Mr. Thomas Holmes.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Fisher.— On the recommendation of the Health Committee it was resolved that notices be served on the following persons to abate nuisances specified below :—Joseph Griffin 7, Salkeld Square, overcrowding; John Flannigan, back Mersey-st., overcrowding; John Cawley, 1, Shaw-st., overcrowding ; John Glynn,accommodation of fish boxes, owners of 9, 10. and 11, Norman-road, water in cellars through want of drains, owners of houses abutting on passages behind Grove-st., and Speakman-st., filthy and dilapidated condition of such passages, and in the event of non-compliance with such notices that legal proceed- ings be taken.

div.head: DANGER OF SWINGS.
div.p: THE DANGER OF SWINGS.

The Goneral Purposes Committee recommended that five pillar lamps be fixed in Victoria-road near the Board School. That in future no portion of the Fair Ground be let for swings.—Mr. Ilankinson in moving the adop- tion of the minutes, said many lives had been sacrificed and limbs broken through swing boats,which were a dan- gerous kind of amusement, and the Committee thought it time to put a stop to them. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Light- burn seconded the motion, and drew attention to the quantity of orange peel and cabbage stalks on the path- ways, and said they constituted a danger to pedestrians. It was a matter,not for the police, but for the Board,and if the Committee could take some action, it would be a great benefit.—The Chairman suggested that the High- way Committee should deal with the subject, and the minutes were passed.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The monthiy meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Present Mr. James Pritchard (chair- man), Dr. McDougall, Mr. Samuel Taylor, and Mr. G. Moss (clerk).
FREE EDUCATION

Dr. McDougall asked if there was any information as to the attendance of children at school that day.—Mr. Moss replied that there were about 90 absentees at the Board Schools that day.—The Chairman inquired if there was any rush at the Board Schools in consequence of the small fee charged at the denominational schools.—The Clerk replied in the negative.—Dr. McDougall expressed the hope that advantage would be taken of the boon now offered, but it seemed to him that 90 absentees out of 500 was a rather large number.—The Chairman: You are taking the 'number on the rolls. We have a larger number on the rolls than we have accommodation for.— Dr. McDougall: I don't think there can be any possible excuse for parents not sending their children to school, except illness.—Mr. Taylor : I think it is rather early to raise this question. This is the first day the children are asked to go to school.—Dr. McDougall: I am only speaking for the rood of the district.—Mr. Taylor : But stid the hrst day after the holidays cannot be taken as any standard of the attendance.—The Clerk said the average at the Board Schools was between 80 and 85 per cent.—Dr. McDougall : We expect a higher average than that. But as Mr. 'Fa.ylor remarked one day, it could not be taken as a standard.—The discussion then ceased, and the accounts having been passed the meeting con- cluded.

div.head: RUNCORN COMMI&SIONERS ELECTION
div.p: RUNCORN COMMI&SIONERS ELECTION

The annual election of members to Runcorn Board of Improvement Commissioners, took place on Thursday. On the present occasion there were six vacancies to be filled, six members retiring each year. The retiring members were Messrs. J. Pritch- ard, J. Dobson,W. R. Wass, J. W. Lightburn, E. Imi- son, and W. Mellor. The two last-named did not seek re-election and issued addresses thanking the ratepayers for past suppbrt. By a printer's error Mr. Imison was made to claim 14 years' service on the Board, whereas th 6 fact is that Mr. Imison had been a member of the Board for six years. In addition to the four candidates already mentioned there sought the suffrages of the ratepayers Messrs. D. Bisbrown, T. Lea, I. Stubbs, and H. Coward, the two first-named coming out as temperance candidates. This fact infused far more excitement and interest into the contest than usual as they were practically opposing three gentlemen who are representatives of the licensed victuallers'interest although at the same time it was denied that temperance had anything to do in the election. Still the teetotal party went straight for their men' and the result will be a good guage of their strength for future battles. With the ex- ception cf Mr. Dobson the whole of the candidates issued addresses to the electors, of which extracts have already been given. The polling took place at the Market Hall,which dur- ing the whole of the day presented the appearance of a hustings of the olden time, and so long as the present system continues, polling day on a Commissioners' elec- tion cannot but be a scene of turmoil and unsatisfac- tory alike both to candidates and electors. Mr. Grice, the returning officer, was assisted in his onerous duties by Mr. F. A. Lake, the law clerk, Mr. E. Marshall, the secretary, Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, Mr Barker, surveyor, and Mr. J. D. Jones, librarian. Keeping order in the polling booth was entrusted to Mr. C. Dutton,Mr. J. Percival, and Mr. E. Austin.

The time of polling was from nine am. to four p.m., a time which Mr. Humphrevs elicited at the Board meeting on the previous day was fixed by the Commissioners' Clauses Act, and promptly at four the voting ceased. A crowd of several hundred persons assembled, and during the wait of over an hour for the declaration of the poll, behaved generally with good temper, but there was at times a little rowdiness. About a quarter-past five Mr. Gripe mounted a stall and declared the unofficial result as follows :
Lightburn ...... 922 W. R. Wass 792 Coward J. Pritchard 696 He declared that he would not announce the other figures until 'after a recount; as they were so close together. _

Mr. Lightburn afterwards proposed a vote of thanks to the returning officer. This was seconded by Mr. D. Eisbrown, duly carried, and acknowledged. The recounting of the votes took place yesterday morning, and at noon Mr. Grice published the following return at the Town Hall :
J. W. Lightburn 922 J. Pritchard 676 H. Coward
W. R. Wass 792 I. Stubbs 584
_ J. Dobson 686 T. Lea 5Bl The first six are the elected candidates. About 1,300 votes were polled, being much in excess of previous years. Last year Mr. Taylor headed the poll with 468 votes.

div.head: F RODSTIAM.
div.p: F RODSTIAM.

ALLEGED IGENIOUS FRAUD ON TRH RAILWAY COMPANY. —William Palin, butcher, Chureh-street, Frodsham was summoned before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, to answer a charge of travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Liverpool to Runcorn without having previously paid his fare.—Mr. W. J. Bland, of the solicitors' department, Lime-street, prose- cuted. The facts of the case are that on the 14th of August the defendant took a return ticket from Frod- sham to Runcorn and leaving the train at Runcorn, he gave up the outward half and re-booked single Runcorn to Liverpool. At Edge Hill he gave up the single ticket, and went into Liverpool and transacted his businsss. He afterwards returned to Lime-street and without book ing entered the 3.50 train. On the arrival of the cramn at Runcorn he alighted, walked the platform for a few moments and then re-entered his compartment. At Frodsham he gave up the return half of the ticket he had taken in the morning, and was allowed to pass through the gate. A detective followed him out and then charged him with having attempted to defraud the com- pany. There had been suspicions entertained for some time that the defendant was not acting as he should,and the detective had "shadowed "him that day from the time of leaving Frodsham until his return in the after- noon.—The defendant did not appear,his wife informing the Bench that it had made him ill to have a summons for nothing.—The Bench adjourned the case fora week and intimated that a warrant would be issued if the summons were not then obeyed.

div.head: LYIIII.
div.p: LYIIII.

FRERAIASONRY.—We understand that Past Master,John Lewis, of Alrincham, a member of the Earl of Chester Lodge, Lymm, has been nominated by the Provincial Grand Master of the Province of Chester to the position of Deputy Provincial Grand Director of Ceremonies. The members of the lodge feel highly gratified at such an honour being bestowed upon one of its members. APPOINTMENT OF WAYWARDENS FOR THELWALL.—At Sale Petty Sessions on Monday, an application was made by Mr. Joseph Burgess, district surveyor of the East Bucklow Highway Board, for the approval of the magis- trates to the appointment of Mr. William Wright as way- warden for the township of Thelwall. Mr. Wright ap- peared, and produced the certificate given by Mr. Peter Warburton, chairman of the meeting. The Bench sanc- tioned the appointment. THE FUSTIAN CtrrrEns.—Since the Manchester list of prices was adopted, the Cheshire cutters have resumed work, after a strike of many weeks. The Lymm cutters allege that their masters have reduced their prices, and do not pay the prices agreed upon. A meeting was held oil Monday night, in the Bridgewater-rooms, with Mr. Gatley as chairman. The following resolution was passed, "That this conference send a delegation to the Lan- cashire Union meeting." The object of the meeting was to see whether the Lymm men would join the Northern Counties' Association. The present leaders are opposed to it. The Lancashire men are of opinion that it will be for the benefit of the Cheshire cutters to come over to the Lancashire Union, and so form a strong Aociety.

An official telegram regarding the Canadian grain crop states that the quantity is immense. In Manitoba it is about half cut, and in some sections late crops have been injured by frost. At Rothesay on Thursday Duncan McLeon, a mason's labourer, was arrested on the charge of having caused the death of his wife. She would not rise to make his breakfast, and it is alleged that he struck her on the head, death resulting from the blow. The couple had been drinking.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.
BOWLING MAIN.

On Saturday afternoon,the members of the bowl- ing club held at the Stamford Arms Inn, Warring- ton, to the number of about 40, were conveyed to the Horse Shoe Inn, Croft. A main of bowls was played on the green, and shortly after five o'clock. the visitors partook of tea. . _. THE EDUCATION ACT AT CROFT. _ . _ _ _ _

The School Board has adopted the Act, and the board school is to be entirely free, as the substitu- tion of the Government grant for the fees will make little or no difference. With regard to St. Lewis's Roman Catholic School, Croft, the managers have also adopted the Act, and the school will be entirely free, being an improvement on the present receipts from all sources. The board school was re-opened on Monday morning,after the usual mid- summer holidays, when Miss Stretch, the infant mistress, was in charge, and will continue to be so until the appointment of the late Mr. Savage's suc- cessor. There are numerous applications for the appointment, and the selection of a headmaster will shortly take place, probably at the next meet- ing of the School Board.
WARRINGTON AND FREE EDUCATION,

In view of the meeting of school managers, which is to be held on Monday, the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), has issued the following circular to school managers :—" The Elementary Education Act, 1891. lam directed by the School Attendance Committee of this borough to lay before you their views on the above Act, which, as you are aware, came into force on the Ist instant, In the first place, the Committee hope that the managers of every public elementary school within the borough will at once, if they have not already done so, ac- cept the "Fee Grant" provided by the Act. The Act, as you are aware, was passed for the pur- pose of "assisting education," and the non-accep- tance of the fee grant will impos. an unnecessary burden upon the parents of the poorer scholars, and in the opinion of the Committee will greatly im- pede the discharge of the duties of the School. A- ttendance Officers. Attention is particularly directed to Section 6 of the Act, by which the munagers of two or more public elementary schools may pay the fee grant, or part thereof, received by each school, into a common fund for distribution, as may be ar- ranged by them between or among such schools. An amalgamation of the several schools under the section referred to would not only enable some of the poorer schools to be made absolutely free by the wealthier schools ceding to them part of the Fee Grant, but some of the schools with a high scale of fees t•night take the position of High Grade Schools and provide the means of education of an advanced or superior character. The Committee wish me also to point out that unless sufficient free school accommodation is provided during the next twelve months, a School Board under Section 5, may be ordered by the Education Department to be elected in order to supply it ; whereas an amal- gamation as suggested would enable the poorer schools to be made absolutely free, and would thus cut away the ground of complaint as to insufficiency of free school accommodation." THE CATHOLIC SCHOOLS.
On the morning of Tuesday, on which day the Free Education Act came into force, free educa- tion was adopted in the Su. Mary's and St. Alban's Roman Catholic Schools, Warrington.

ST. PETERS' DAY SCHOOL. At a meeting on Tuesday evening, the managers of the above school informed the parents of the children that they had decided to accept the Gov- ernment fee grant of 10s. a head in lieu of school- pence. For the future there will be no schoolpence, nor will any charge be made to the infants for books and stationery; the children in the standards will, however, be required to pay for materials. The Vicar acted as spokesman on behalf of the managers and urged upon the parents the necessity of the regular attendance of their children. The managers present were the Rev. T. Rigby, Messrs. John Roberts, J. R. Blease, and Peter Edgar.
WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT HOMING SOCIETY. TRE SEASON'S RESULTS.

Although the IVarrington and District Homing Society has been in existence but twelve months, the success which has attended the working of the club has been very marked. Commencing with but a mere handful of members,it now counts amongst its members the leading fanciers of this sport in neighbourhood. Reference has been previously made to the working of the society, and appended we give a return of the velocities for the whole of the races throughout the season. As a rule, the birds have not been favoured with good weather; but, nevertheless, some of the performances, especially those in the race from Worcester by the old birds, will bear favourable comparison with those of other Homing Societies. From the return it will be sv.en that Messrs. Locker, Forster, Burrows, Hampton, Greenough, and Buckley, occupy prominent posi- tions in all the events, a fact which points to the excellent condition in which their birds are kept. The distance traversed by the birds in the whole of their races was over 600 miles, whilst the distance of the younger birds was nearly 300. Mr. Locker, Church-st., took the society's first prize for the best average. RIVAL SCHOOLS AT PRESCOT.— The Prescot School Board held a meeting on Tuesday to consider the appli- cation of Miss Evans, of Rainhill, to the Education Department for the fee grant under the Assisted Educa- tion Act for her schools. The Education Depart- ment had written to the Board asking their opinion on the application. Miss Evans, who is well known as a benefactress throughout the district, has recently built large schools at Prescot, with the result that many of the children who had hitherto been edu- cated at the Board Schools had joined her school, which, however, had not up to now been under Government supervision. A deputation, consisting of the vicar (the Rev. H. Mitchell) and Mr. T. P. Hewitt, was appointed to wait upon Miss Evans and discuss in a friendly way with her the general question of secondary and technical education in the town with a view to the proper utilisa- tion of her schools.
WARRINGTON.
THE WOMEN .S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

In connection with the Women's Liberal Associa- tion, Miss Bertha Mason, of Ashton-under-Lyne (daughter of the late Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P.,) will address a meeting of the Liberal townswomen of Warrington at the Liberal Club, next Thursday afternoon on the subject," Women and politics."
ST. PETER'S CHOIR TRIP.

On Monday the choir of St. Peter's with a few frieryis, to the number of 35, had a most enjoyable excursion to Blackpool. About 2-30, a steady rain set in, but the choir of St. Peter's do not allow rain to interfere with either their duties or their pleasures, and defied it. Warrington was reached about 9 p.m., everybody more or less wet but happy. THE WORKMEN'S OPEN AIR TOTAL ABSTINENOE

div.head: MISSION.
div.p: MISSION.

The usual weekly meeting of the above mission was held on Sunday on the enclosed ground off Bewsey-st., when Mr. 3. Price presided, and Messrs Rigby, Drury, and Sambrook gave short addresses. The mission also held a meeting in the afternoon at the model lodging-house, Friars-Green, when short addresses were given by Messrs. J. Price, Rigby, Tanner, and Ifigginson. The meetings were well attended.

div.head: ANGLING MATCH.
div.p: ANGLING MATCH.

A joint match of the angling clubs of Warring- ton took place on Saturday at Chester, when rrizes of the aggregate value of £l3 Ss. were competed for by 40 members who entered for the contes:-, but owing to the swollen state of the river, from recent rains, the catches were very small, only 15 prizes out of 25 being won. The following were the prin- cipal prizewinne:s:-Ist, Alfred Shaw, £3; 2, Law- rence Spencer, £2; 3. John Atherton, £1 7s. (3d.; and 4, C. Basketer, £l. There were several minor prizes. A meeting was held at the Royal Exchange, on Tuesday night, at which the prizes were distri- buted. Mr. J. Knight acted as chairman, and Mr. J. Hewitt as vice-chairman. The prizes were then distributed, and a con,,olation match was fixed for September 12th, at Preston Brook.
WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE

The monthly meeting of this Committee was held yesterday, the Rev. G. F. Roberts presiding. The valuer (Mr. Owen) reported with regard to the appeal of the National Telephone Co., as to the assessment:of their wires,offices,and exchange. Dur- ing last year there were in Warrington 561; miles of wire, and there were now in Warrington in use 75 miles of wire. If they took the assessment of 7s. 61. per mile the assessment would be -£2B rateable value of 75 miles of wire, and for office. From that would have to be deducted £5 rateable in respect of wires in the rural area. The report was adopted. The appeals were mostly of a formal nature. An appeal by the Corporation against the assessment of the gas works and water- works was referred to the valuer. A CHILD BURNED TO DEATH.

An inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse, at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning, touching the death, on Monday, at the Warrington Workhouse, Hospital, of Annie Monks, aged 8 years, daughter of a ship canal labourer, who resides in Fearnhead- lane. The evidence showed the following facts:— The child's mother went out of the house for a short time, leaving the deceased in charge of two brothers and a sister. The deceased was cleaning the grate, when her pinafore caught fire. Her brother pulled the pinafore off, but her face and hands were badly burnt. She was taken to a neigh- bour's house, and Dr. Peacocke was sent for. On his arrival, he ordered the deceased to be taken to the hospital, where she died on the day above- mentioned. A verdict of "Accidental death" was recorded.
BANKRUPTCY OF A HAY AND STRAW DEALER.

Yesterday at the Warrington Bankruptcy Couit-, before the Registrar, Mr. Nicholson, James Robin- ' son, hay and straw dealer, of Broom Edge, Lymm, appeared to undergo his preliminary examination. In answer to questions by Mr. C. J. llibb, the official receiver, the debtor said that a receiving order was made on his own petition on the 2ilnd ult., and he was adjudged bankrupt. Up to 1866 he worked for his father, and in that year began business on his own account as a farmer at High Leh. Ile gave up farming in 1881, and started in business as a hay and straw dealer, which he had continued up to his bankruptcy. He attributed his ailure to the facts that his two sons had left him and to the markets having been bad. His asse;l were £57 3s. 1(1., and this it was estimated would leave a deficiency of £69 9s. 11d. The examination. was adjourned until the 16th proximo.

div.head: ORFORD SCHOOL.
div.p: ORFORD SCHOOL.

The following report of Her Majesty's Inspector upon this school has been received by the Managers: —The Master,while maintaining efficient discipline, teaches the children carefully and well, their Arithmetic, Spelling, and Handwriting, with much of their class work, being decidedly advanced and creditable. The only points not shewing to good advantage are Grammar in the third stapdard, and Reading (in respect of intelligence in the fifth standard.) In view of the drawbacks with which he has had to cope the Master deserves credit for the very satisfactory results he has produced generally." The managers have also. been informed that in the Drawing Examination recently held by Citptain Ruse, this school is again classed Excellent. Drawing is taken by the girls as well as the boys, the former also taking Cr,okery. The grants earned are :—(l) The largest principal grant 145.—(2) The largest Discipline &c., grant is. 6d.— (3) The largest Singing grant 15.—(4) Full grant for English 25.—(5) Full grant for Geography 2s. —(6) The Needlework and Cookery Grants for girls.

INQLTEST ON A DRAYMAN. An inquest was held on Wednesday, at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-st., by Mrs. S. Brighouse, coroner, concerning the death of James Grayson, aged 62, a drayma,n, in the employ of Messrs.-Greenail Whit- ley, and Co., at St. fielens brewery, which took place at the Warrington Infirmaly, on Tuesday, from in- juries sustained at Great Sankey, on the previous Friday. The ,lect,aed, was engaged at the Chapel House inn, Great Sankey, in removing empty barrels of beer from the cellar. He commenced to roll them up a slide into the road, preparatory to taking them away, when the slide slipped, caus- ing deceased to fall on his face. A barrel fell upon him, and he was severely injured. Dr. Murray was sent for, and seeing the nature of the man's injuries, ordered his removal to the Warrington Infirmary, where he was attended by the house surgeons. The case was regarded as hopeless from the first. Testimony proving these circumstances wasgiven by Sarah Jane Woods, niece of the landlord of the Chapel House Inn ; and Jane Miller, married daughter oh the de- ceased gave evidence of identification. A verdict of" Accidental death " was returned. THE SCHOOL OF ART.

The following [ire the comparative results in the Science a- ' Art Department's egxammations for 1890 and iii. in connection with the School of Art :—S,:,ence drawing, including gpmetry,build- ing construction, and machine drawing, 1890-46, 1891-56 successes. Second grade art, first classes; Third grade art, examinations 1890 —3O ; 1891-35: taken successfully in twelve subjects as compared with seven of previous year, first class excellent 1890-1 ; 1891-2; first class, 1890-21 ; 1891-20; second class, 1890-8 ; 1891, 19; totals, 1890-30; 1891-41. The marks and prizes awarded by the Science and Art Department on works executed in the schools numbered 583 this year, against 319 in 1890. In 1890 there were only five prizes of books, value 12s. each, awarded, while this year there were 23, and also 5 prizes of books,value and one National bronze medal. Seven individual students obtained full marks this year,against three in 1890, and three obtained free scholarships, none being appointed in 1890. The students who joined the classes for the year 1889-90 numbered 239, the highest in any previous year being in 1880, when there were 230. For 1890-91 there were 265. . EMPIRE THEATRE OF VARIETIES. On Monday evening this popular place of amuse- ment was opened under the new and seemingly enterprising lesseeship of Messrs. Jones and Harri- son. The theatre is to be under the sole management of Mr. Jones and has been redecorated and otherwise much improved. The i old scenery s being entirely dispensed with and new scenes are being painted by Mr. Jones i himself, but n consequence of his work being inter- rupted by an unfortunate accident which we record elsewhere, he has only been able to get sonve of these ready for use, but we may say that those exhibited on Monday night proved him to be a scenic artist of considerable merit. A full and efficient orchestra is engaged under the conductorship of Mr. Julian lialle Wilson, of Warrington, The theatre was opened under its new auspices on Monday evening. Mr. Chippendale, one of the artistes, announced on be- half of the lessees their intention to produce select entertainments and to carefully exclude all vul- garity. The programme for the week has given abundant earnest of the fulfilment of their pro- mise. On Monday evening :next several additional L talented artistes will make their appearance.

div.head: ROYAL ARTILLERY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ROYAL ARTILLERY AT WARRINGTON.

A detachment of the Royal Artillery arrived in town yesterday, at two o'clock, from Dover, and billetted at the Seven Stars, Bridge-st. Thay have the charge of four cannon and an ambulance wagon. They will stop in town during the might,and depart this morning for Glasgow.
THE GALE.

Not much Jamage is reported to have resulted from the gale which broke over the town on Tues— day morning, .Mrs. Grea-t7es, of " The Tower," Bridge-st., had between one and two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon, a large window in one of the showrooms blown out of its frame. The amount of the damage is about .El 5. ACCIDENT TO A RAILWAY SERVANT. „ . _

On Monday evening Robert (7r-oa-,--a—ii-cket col- lector, employed by the Loudon and North-West- ern Railway Company, at Arpley Station, was coming out of the gantlemen's waiting-room, when he fell and broke his left arm, there being, he says, something slippery on the floor of the room. The limb was subsequently set by Dr. Smith,

div.head: WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY,
div.p: WESLEYAN ANNIVERSARY,

The anniversary services in connection with the Wesley Chapel, Bewsey-road, were held on Sunday. The Rev. Thomas Champness, of Rochdale, editor of "Joyful News," and founder of the "Joyful News" mission, preached both morning and even- ing. A service of praise was held in the afternoon conducted by the Rev. Alfred Freeman. The Silver- st. Sunday School Band, under the leadership of Mr. F. Hendlebury gave a selection of sacred music. The collections, in aid of the trust funds, realised over £32. There were large congregations.

div.head: 1.0.G.T.
div.p: The officers and members of the "Temperance Mission" Lodge, No. 1321, paid a visit to the "Tower tof Refuge" Lodge, Lymm, on Tuesday evening. The chair was occupied by Bro. It. Kean, supported by the officers of " Temperance Mission" Lodge. An excellent programme of songs,readings, and recitations was ren(lered, the following Bros. and Sisters taking part : Bros. Pugh, Mantle, Mortimore, J. Price, Wilson, Tomlin, and Kean; Sisters Tomlin, Shaw, Mortimore. Bro. Roberts in a short address urged the members to still greater activity in fighting the good fight and "rescuing the perishing." The usual votes of thanks brought a very pleasant evening to a close.

div.head: LABOURERS UNION DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: LABOURERS UNION DEMONSTRATION.

On Saturday afternoon, a demonstration of the local branch of the General Labourers' Union was held at Warrington. The members, headed by a brass band, and with the district banner, marched in procession through Scotland-road and Mersey- street, to Bridge Foot, where a meeting was held, under the presidency of Mr. Brown, and was addressed by Mr. Leonald Hall, of Eccles; Mr. J. Price (the district secretary) and others. Subse- quently the members proceeded in procession through Bridge, Rylands, Sankey and Horsemarket- streets, to the Club-house, the Central Coffee Tavern, 27, Winwick-street, where they partook of tea. A concert was afterwards held, Mr. .T. Brown, presid- ilia, in which Mr. J. Price, Mr. L. Hall, Mr. T. Marshall, and others took part.

div.head: MORE DELAY AT THE POLICE COURT.
div.p: MORE DELAY AT THE POLICE COURT.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Thursday morning, at ten o'clock, the hour for commencing the business, there was only one magistrate present, Alderman Harrison, and he disposed by himself of all the cases that could be dealt with by a single justice, which were finished at 20 minutes past 10, he being still unrelieved. The court sat in patient silence for about 20 minutes, when Mr. Browne, solicitor, who was engaged in one of the cases yet unheard, remarked that it would be a good idea if the Watch Committee would provide a bell at the police Station to warn magistrates to come to their duties.—Aldereaan Harrison concurred in Vie sug- gestion. If that were done he said the fact that magistrates were absent would be proclaimed to everybody in the town, and a good effect might be prod uced.—Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, who was also waiting to have a case heard, observed : I dare say we could have plenty of volunteers if we wanted them.—Alderman Harrison: They don't seem to come forward.—Mr. Riley : There is no bell yet.—Alderman Harrison: Perhaps it would be more efficacious to have one of those American devils, instead of a bell, to send forth a howl of distress when we wanted magistrates, a signal of of distress.—The Chief Constable, in reply to the Alderman said two or three officers had been out since a quarter to 10 looking up magistrates. He had had a note that morning from Mr. John White to say he had been unable to attend.—Alderman Harrison :I knew he would not be here: he has gone away for four weeks.—Mr. Browne: I think at the next Council meeting I shall propose that a special officer be appointed for the purpose of going round to the magistrates to get them to attend.—Mr. Hunt: We have one who does nothing else but look after magistrates every morning, in addition to writing to them.—lnspector Spinks said Alderman Greenall was away and Mr. Garnett was engaged, but Alderman llolmes was coming.—Mr. Hunt said in a district in which he had been 14 years, no magistrate had ever to be written to during that time to get him to attend, and no one was elected Mayor who was not prepared to devote himself to the duties. All the summonses and warrants were applied for and signed in court, and never went into the hands of the complainants.—Mr. Browne said that was the practice in some courts, but it could not be carried out in Warrington.—Mr. hunt: There are many more summonses granted than there would be, because if they come next day their passion is gone and they are forgotten.—Alderman Holmes now arrived, at a quarter to 11, and the business was proceeded with. BOWLING MAIN AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.. The annual main of bowls, confined to members of the above club,was concluded on Saturday even- ing, when the prizes were distributed to the suc- cessful competitors. This interesting ceremony took place in the first class billiard room at the Conservative Club, and was performed by Mrs. John White, in the unavoidable absence of Mrs. Reynolds. The prize list is as follows :-Ist prize, timepiece, valued at ..E5 55., George Ogden ; 2nd, coffee service, .E 3 55., Thomas Horrobin ; 3rd, cruet, .£1 55., J. J. Millington; 4th (teapot presented by Mrs. Rey- nolds), £1 is., C. Cartwright; sth, travelling bag, is., Duncan Anderson; 6th, bowls and jack, £1 Is.. Joseph Dainteth ; 7th, half a dozen knives and forks, 155., James Jolley; Bth, copper kettle,l2s.6d., Thomas Bridge ; 9th, pair of carvers, 7s. 61, Walter Holden ; 10th (an umbrella given by Messrs. J. and W. Dutton), 7s. 6d., Richard Smith. There was a good attendance of members from each room during the distribution proceedings. Mr. Thomas Mason proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. White for her at- tendance, and for distributing the prizes that even- ing—a motion which he was sure would be cor- dially agreed to by everyone present. (Applause.) Conn. Muir seconded the motion,which was carried. Mr. John White, in returning thanks on behalf of his wife, said Mrs. White was a staunch Conserva- tive. He had always looked upon himself as a good Tory, but he was not in the same street with her. (Laughter.) With regard to bowling, he fancied she could beat him at that game, in which she took great pride and pleasure. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He had no doubt that probably before another 12 months had passed over their heads they would have had to go through one of the greatest political contests this country had ever witnessed. It would be a sort of life and death struggle, and they ought to lose no opportunity of preparing for it, and he was sure they would all do so in Warrington. The November municipal elections were not far away. Probably they would have to contest every ward, and looking to the winter, they must see that it would be of the utmost importance to the Conserve- live party that the time should be well utilized ; and that they did everything they could to further those principles for which the Club had been established (Applause.)—Ald. Sutton, in proposing a vote of thanks to the chairman of the Bowling Green Com- mittee, said it was very important that they should take an interest in all matters connected with regis- tration in Warrington. They would want all the assistance they could get during the November elec- tions, if they wished to maintain their position in the Town Council. The motion was carried by ac- clamation.--Mr. Roberts returned thanks, and pro- posed a vote of thanks to Mr.Higham for his care of and attention to the green.—This was seconded bv Mr. Ward, and carried, and Mr. Hi,gharn havina re- plied, the proceedings terminated. It was announced that Mrs. White would give a prize at the next main.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THE LION HOTHL.
At the Magistrates' Court, on Tuesday, a temporary authority was granted to Joseph Taylor to sell at the Lion Hotel, Bridge-st., in place of Elizabeth Hart.

. - RIDING WITHOUT A TICKET. David Briggs, upholsterer, who gave his address as 92, Knutsford-road, was charged on Monday with riding from Liverpool to Warrington without a tic- ket. David Pugh, ticket collector, said the prisoner came by train on Saturday night, and said he had lost his ticket, and refused to pay his fare. W. Higson, another official. corroborated. P.C. Cooper said the prisoner was half-an-hour in the Police Office before be would give his address. The defendant said he went by excursion train to Liverpool for some tools, as be had got work under Mr. Marsh, at. Warrington. He lost the other half of his ticket. He told the officials at War- rington he would pay if they would send some one to his lodgings. Mr. Higson said he had offered to do so. The Mayor said the excursion return was so cheap,ls.6d., it was not likely that the defendant would take a single ticket and return without a ticket. A constable was despatched to the prisoner's employer to ascertain what truth there was in his statement, and on his return stated that defendant had drawn part of his wages on Saturday, and told the foreman he was going to Liver- pool by excursion for his tools.—The prisoner was fined 55., including costs.
A COAL THIEF AND HIS NOCTTIRNAL ADVENTURE.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, Daniel Norman was charged with stealing at about a quarter past one oh Sunday morning, 1i cwt. of coal, the pro- perty of Arthur Westwell. Chief Constable Hunt said the complabant kept a coal yard in Factory-lane, which yard had a siding on the London and North-Western Railway. The prisoner was a married man residing at No. 2, Factory-lane, and his house abutted upon Mr. Westwell's coal yard. On Sunday morning about a quarter to one P.C. Newey heard a noise in the coal yard and caught the prisoner and another man stealing coal from the yard by sliding it down a plank. The pri- soner's accomplice suddenly as the officer approached said" Heigh ho," and slipped out of sight. Newey went towards Norman, and he said "You are just too late." Newey replied " Ithink lam just in time." The prisoner said a man and a woman had just gone out of a closet ,close by, on the top of which one end of the plank had been placed. Newey asked who the man was that had been with the prisoner and he said he did not know. Newey and Inspector Cox went to the prisoner's house and found a quantity of coal there, probably stolen from the yard.—Mr. Westwell said he had been much an- noyed by the theft of coals and fowls from his yard. The prisoner had been out of work, and had been occasion- ally employed by witness.—P.C. Newey gave evidence, and stated that he and Inspector Cox found over *wt. of coal in the prisoner's house.—The defendant said he got up early to see the mail coaches run, as he had never seen them run before.—lnspector Cox said the mail coaches would pass 15 to 25 minutes before the prisoner was found in the yard.—lnspector Spinks said the pri- soner had given him the names of two men who he said were with him, as witnesses, but they denied all know- ledge of him. He had said his son would come ass witness for him, but he was not now to be found.—Nor- man was sent to prison for a month's hard labour. OBSTRUCTING THE THOROUGHFARE.

Thomas Unsworth, butcher, Irlam-street, had to answer a charge on Monday of exposing certain mutton for sale so that it projected over the footway. P.C. Bell and Inspector Spinks proved the case.—The defendant: It was not mutton, it was lamb.—Alderman Harrison: It does not matter what it was.—The defendant: They say you might as well be hung for a sheep as a lamb, but I say it was lamb.—The Mayor said when people were ready to quibble about'such distinctions as these,it made the Bench less inclined to place faith in what they said. —The Chief-Constable said the Watch Committee were determined to put a stop to these obstructions. Other butchers had made their boards less, but Mr. Unsworth refused to shot ten his.—The defendant said other trades- people for instance boot and shoe dealers, were allowed to hang their goods 20 yards out, and the same rule ought to apply to butchers.—The Mayor said it was much mere objectionable to the public to have meat projecting into the street, than such things as boots and shoes, and mentioned how in one street he had got besmeared with ham fat at a butcher's dcor.—The defendant was fined 3s. 6d., the cost of the summons.—Joseph Pilling, green- grocer, Antrobus-street, and William Oakell, greengrocer, 55, Leigh-street, Earlestown, were charred with obstructing Market-street, the former on the 22nd, and the latter on the 26th inst., by allowing their horses and carts to stand longer than necessary. They were each ordered to pay the costs. .
THE WARRING- TON FOUNDLING AGAIN.-NOT AFRAID OF THE POLICE STATION.

At the magistrates' court, on Tuesday, John Warring- ton, aged 17, was 'charged with absconding from the Workhouse and taking away clothing belonging to the Union, on Saturday last. Mr. Curry, the Workhouse porter, proved the case.—P.C, Chandley deposed to ap- prehending him in a fried fish shop.—The defendant said he wonld stop in the Workhouse if they would let him have a day out every two months.—Mr. Curry, in reply to Mr. Garnett, the presiding magistrate, said an inmate must be three months in the Rouse before he could get a day's leave.—The defendant said he would like to work at the police station.—Mr. Garnett said there was no work there for him.—The defendant: Every morning I could look after the calls.—Mr. Garnett appealed to Mr. Hunt whether he could give Warrington a trial.— Mr. Hunt replied that he could do nothing with him. He would not like the fare there. They had a good birch rod there they might use on him sometimes, and he would not be so fond of being there if he once got a dose of that'. He did not believe he was always responsible for his actions.—ln the course of some further conversa- tion, Mr. Hunt said he did not think the doctors would pass the defendant now for the asylum.—The defendant said if released he would go to Manchester to look for work,—Mr. Hunt said that Warrington was very violent sametimes ; that morning he was particularly calm and quiet.—The magistrates made an order for him to go back to the Workhouse. CHARGE OF MARITAL BRUTALITY. At the Warrington County Sessions, on Wednesday, Charles Essery, who holds an important position under the Ship Canal Company, was charged with assaulting his wife Catherine Essery, a Scotchwoman, at Sankey. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the complainant and Mr. Browne for the defendant. The complainant said she was married to the defendant on April 30th. 1887, in Glamorganshire, and had been living with him at San- key. On the night of August Ist he was dragged home in a state of intoxication by one of his workmen, the sleeve being off his coat. The moment he got in he struck her on the face and called her a foul name. She left the house through fear of him and went to her parents at Ellesmere Port. She returned on August 3rd, and at night, when she was undressing for bed he told her to go with the men she had been with the night be- fore—she had been with her parents—and shook her,and struck her, and knxked her against the mantlepiece, raising a lump on her head, saying he would be hung for her, if she did not leave that night, and telling her with an oath to be off. She went out and stayed at a Mrs. Riley's all night. She had summoned him n before at illackburn.—Cross-examined by Mr. Browne the corn- plainant appeared to be mistaken as to the date of the last assault. She denied stealing 345. 6d, belonging to 'ler husband or his spirit level, his watch and chain.

She had picked up 7s. he had dropped in the back yard and taken his watch and chain when he was among a lot of blackguards outside the back door, because it was hanging loose. She admitted she had a violent temper. It was jealousy and a bad disposition that caused his conduct. She wanted not to punish him, but to have a separation order and maintenance.—Messrs. Browne and Jenkins here conferred and they with their clients. Mr. Jenkins said, as the result, the defendant would allow his wife 83. a week, pay a guinea costs,and return her clothes,which he had,on condition that she withdrew the proceedings and returned his watch and chain. This was agreed to. THEFT or A SHAWL BY A WOMAN.

At the Borough Court, on Thursday, Sarah Jane Duffy, rubbing stone hawker, a married woman, was charged with stealing, on the 20th of July, a shawl, the property of Michael and Ann Donoghue, 5, Erwood-st. The prisoner on the date in question was in the Donog- hue's house, and took up a jug, saying she would bring some beer, and put on the shawl belonging to Ann Donoghue, and went out. She did not return, and it was ascertained that she had pledged the shawl at Widnes, giving a Widnes address and the name of Ashton. She was apprehended at Market Gate, Warrington, on the 31st ult. She was fined 20s. including costs ;in default 14 days. STRANGB CASE 0/7 THEFT BY A COMPOSITOIe.g WIFB.

Elizabeth Beere, wife of Richard Beere, compositor, employed at Messrs. McCorquodale's, Earlestown, and residing at that town, was charged with stealing about 10 p.m., on the 29th of August, from the Ram's Head Hotel, Earlestown, a pair of trousers, the property of Patrick Farrell, collier, of Haydock. The facts as brought out by the evidence were as follows.—Farrell said he left the trousers in a parcel on a mantelpiece at the hotel during his absence for 10 to 15 minutes, and missed them on his return. He said he did not want to press the case as the prisoner" did not do it wilfully."— P.C. Cameron deposed to apprehending the prisoner, at home, and her sending her son with him from the police station to point out an ashpit 200 yards from her house where he discovered the trousers. She denied to him steal- ing them, but said shetook them in mistake.—W. J. Beere (14), said he and prisoner (his mother) and his brother, aged seven, were at the Ram's Head together. Soon after they came away she noticed that his little brother had a parcel under his arm, and in answer to her he said it was her parcel. She said it was not, and finding he had I brought it from the Ram's Head, took it back there, but finding the room full of men was afraid to leave it. She was going to come back again with it when the police- man came. When he knocked, his mother told him to take the parcel out mid hide it at the back, and he put it in the ashpit.—The prisoner, who was overwhelmed with emotion, piteously protested her innocence, and corro- borated her son's account except that she did not say she took the parcel back but said, "I should have taken it back." Her husband was bound over in the sum of £lO for her to come up for judgment if required.

div.head: CHARGE OF BRUTAL ASSAULT.
div.p: CHARGE OF BRUTAL ASSAULT.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, Thos. Young, of Welsh's Yard, Latchford, Elizabeth his wife, and Jas. Andrews, a neighbour, were charged with assaulting aad beating on the 30th ult. Ellen Mary Davies, wife of Wm. Davies, of Old Road, Latchford, foreman on the Ship Canal, and Davies was charged by cross-summons with assaulting Elizabeth Young on the same date. Thomas Young and Andrews did not appear. Mr Browne, solicitor, represented Davies. He :said Mrs. Young had been looking after Mrs. Davies's house while she was laid up with influenza and in consequence of what occurred during that time was forbidden to enter the house. This caused some little friction, and on Sun- day afternoon, when Davies was at the back, James Andrews rushed out and asked her if she had accused him of committing an offence au her door. She said yes, and she would inform the Inspector if he repeated it. He then struck her on the shoulder with the buckle end of his belt. She screamed and he covered her mouth with a handkerchief and struck her with his belt across the hip. She got the handkerchief off her mouth, and screamed murder. Then Mrs. Youno'carne out with the noker and hit her across the back' of the head. Mr. Davies got out of bed and came out ; and Andrews at- tacked him and cut his face open, and blood spurted out and covered everybody near. Mrs. Young also hit him and several people near with the poker, and her husband came and assaulted Mrs. Davies. There was a crowd about and they wrenched the poker from Mrs. Young and got Andrews down and took the belt from him. Ellen Mary Davies corroborated her solicitor's statement, and said that a man named Quinn who came to her assistance, was struck with the poker.—Mr. Browne applied for a remand for Mr. Young and An- drews to be brought up by warrant.—P.S. Chandley said they had been outside the Court but had gone off drinking.—The application was acceded to, and war- rants were issued.

A THIEF NICELY CAUGHT.—RINGING HIS OWN ALARITIC At the Warrington Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Major Pickmere (chairman), Alderman Sutton, and Capt. Ridgway, Thomas Young a collier, living at Preston's lodging-house, and recently discharged as he stated from the army at Belfast, was charged with stealing from the shop door of Messrs. Dolan Brothers, tailors, 11 Horse- market-st., on the previous evening, a blue serge coat, value ss. 6d .—Messrs. Dolan had attached to every article hanging at their door a string which was coanected with a bell and the prisoner was caught by that means.—He was sent to prison for 14 days.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT,

SATUD.D4.--Y--.178—ef0;13. Alderman Sutton (in the chair), Coun- cillor Voisey, and Mr. John Geddes. DISORDER IN A LODGING Houss.—Eliza Anderson was charged on remand with being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street, on Wednesday afternoon, and also with assaulting her landlord, William Preston. The case was before the magistrates on Thursday last, and was re- manded in order that the complainant, who was then too ill, might appear. P.C. Corbett stated that he went to Bank-street on the day in question, and there found the defendant, who was drunk and bleeding from the mouth —William Preston said that the defendant lodged at his house, and in consequence of what he heard, he found he could not allow her to remain in the house. He ordered her out, but she would net go. Be tried to put her out, but she threw a cup at him which struck him on the head. She also tore his new hat into ribbons. The complainant's son corroborated the above evidence.— The defendant said that Preston abused her "something awful." He stabbed her with a fork in the shoulder. It appears that a short time ago a robbery was committed at Preston's common bodging-house, and the defendant and a man named Howard were suspected. Mr. Hunt said that he should apply to the Sanitary Committee to withdraw Preston's license.—Alderman Sutton said he I did not think the complainant was altogether blameless. He was disposed to take a rather lenient view of the case and would bind the defendant over in £5 to keep the peace for six months. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) and Aldermen Harrison and Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—DonaId Munroe, drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-St., on Saturday afternoon, ss. and costs.—Mark Kelly was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Berry in Bridge- st. en Saturday night. P.C. Berry deposed that the pri- soner came up to him drunk and said he was the man that locked him up before, and challenged him to do so again. Witness told him to go away and that he was not the constable who had locked him up, and the pri- soner struck him. Witness pushed him down, and he got up and kicked him. P.C. Amson came to his assist- ance.—P.C. Atnson corroborated, and the prisoner was sent for a month's hard labour.—Thomas Monoghan was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Crown-st., and assaulting Esther Lawranson, a little girl, on Satur- day night. He went into a shop where the girl was in charge and paid only a halfpenny for a penny cake. The girl followed him through the street requesting him to give her another halfpenny or return the cake, but he would do neither, and struck her. She, however, kept following him. He wa4 taken into custody for being drunk and disorderly. In reply to the Mayor the child said the prisoner did not hurt her when he struck her. The Mayor said she was a very plucky little girl to fol- low a drunken man about like that for a halfpenny.— The prisoner was fined ss. and costs.—George Hopkins, 25th appearance, drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket- st., on Saturday night. a month's hard labour. DRUNK.—Patrick Callen, drunk in Bridge-st., on Sat- urday night, was discharged with a caution. BEGGING.—WiIIiam Brown, was charged with begging in Horsemarket-st., on Saturday afternoon. The con- stable proving the case said the prisoner went into Mr. Fleming's boot shop,to beg,and was very abusive. 11d. and a quantity of meat were found upon him. The Chief Constable said the man's hands showed that he did not work, but he hal a bad leg which incapacitated him for work. He was discharged on promising to leave the town immediately. CARD-PLAYING FOR MONEY.—Peter Callaghan, aged 16, employed at Cockhedge Factory, was charged with play- ing with cards for money in Bank-st., on Sunday after- noon. It was stated that a number of other boys were playing in his company, and would be brought up on Monday. The defendant was bound over to appear with them.

ASSAULT.—Peter Fox, puddler, Aikin-st., for assault- ing a man unknown on Monday last, was bound over in the sum of £5, and ordered to pay the costs, 7s. THE STONE-THROWING NUISANCE.—Thomas Knight, William Lilford, Arthur Parker, Robert Ashworth, and Edward Narroway, boys, were charged with throwing stones, to the danger of passengers, in Stamford-st., on the 17th Aug.—lt was stated in evidence that the hus- band of a woman who appeared against them had thrown the bed out of his window at the defendants and acted in such a manner as to cause boys to come about the street.—The wife of the man complained of said the bed was put by her through the door not the window. She said the boys even dragged the petticoat off her back. Her husband was very noisy with them when in drink.—The defendants were fined 2s. 6d. each. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (chairman) and
E. M. Crosfield.

DRUNK AND DISORDRRLY.-Thos. Baguley was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-st, the pre- vious night, and assaulting P.C. Amson. The constable said a man was carrying the prisoner in his arms, Bagu- ley's face being covered with blood. He was drunk, and

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 5, 1891.

had been fighting with a man named Maloney. Wit- Kass got the prisoner's face washed, and he ran out and wanted to fight again. Witness got hold of him and he butted him in the chest with his head and struck him, and then kicked him several times.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month in jail with bard labour.— Bridget McDonough, drunk and disorderly in Hill-street, on Monday night, was dismissed on the intercession of Mr. Hunt.

DRUNlC—Patrick Walsh was charged with being drunk in Bank-st., at ten minutes to one that morning. P.C. Bell appeared against him, and he accused this constable of coming up and seizing him by the neck and knock- ing him on his face without provocation, and remarked, "I will have a case anyhow to-night." The defendant was fined ss. ScHoor. CASES.—Elizabeth Bate, milliner, Orford-lane, John Divine, labourer at Cockhedge Factory, Henry Forster, foreman fustian cutter. Lythgoes'-lane, John Glynn;labourer, Oliver-st., were each fined ss. for not sending children to school.—William Lawrenson, forge- man, Pierpoint-st. was charged with a similar offence as to his son. dr. Garnett having heard what Mr. Riley, school attendance officer, and the boy's mother had to say, showing that the fault was on his part, Mr. Garnett remarked : I wish we had the birch rod here every morning, instead of fetching it.—A constable then brought in the birch rod, and laid it on the table in front of the Chief Constable.—Mr. Garnett (to the boy) : Would you rather be punished with that birch rod, or have your father punished ?—The boy: My father has punished me.—Mr. Hunt repeated the question to the lad, and he replied that his father would pay the ss. Mr. Garnett (to the mother) : You will be fined ss. this ' time. Next time, we shall very likely try the birch.— Mr. Hunt: The next time he misses going to school, bring hisn down here.—Elizabeth Moores, labourer, School Brow, 2s. 6d. ; William Quinn, tanner, School Brow, two boys, had an order to send one boy to Father Nugeot's School, and was dismissed as to the other.— Henry Syers, forgeman, Bank Quay, two children, 2s. 6d. in one case, and ordered to send the other child to school.—James Ward, labourer, Ship-yard, 2s. 6d.— An order was made for a lad named Wm. Dunbabbin, son of George Dunbabbin, Ship Canal labourer, who was now charged the fifth time in respect to the boy, to be sent to the ship Clio, although the mother, the sister, and the boy himself objected, but the Bench told them he had been allowed plenty of chances to reform. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison.

DRUNK.—Thomas Higgins, drunk at Friars-green, the previous morning, ss. ; Henry Davies, in Buttermarket- st., on Thursday night, ss.—John Adams was charged with being drunk at Friars-green and wilfully damaging the window of Alfred Bruchemite's lodging-house there, about a quarter to 12 on Thursday night. P.C. Har- rington deposed to being called to the defendant and finding him drunk, and also a big stone in the lodging- house which he had thrown through the window. John Murray said the man came for lodgitts, and though he told him the house was full, would not go, upon which he put him out. He then threw the stone through the window falling to the ground with the force of the throw. The lodging-house keeper said after the defen- dant throwing the stone they found him hidden among the coals at the back, and gave him into custody. He was fined 55., and the damages. _ _

CRUELTY TO Honsis.—Thomas Rowley, waggonette proprietor, 333, Knutsford-road, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state, on the 29th of August. A constable and Inspector Dowty, R.S P.C.A., proved the case. 10s. and costs. ABSENCE FROM SeHooL.—John Garton, for not sending his son Richard regularly to school, was fined ss. CHARGE OF ASSAULT.—Mary Jane Battersby, married woman, was charged with assaulting and beating Mary Ann Hankinsen on Saturday afternoon last. The com- plainant said her husband was in America and defendant taking advantage of her being by herself came and quarrelle3 with her about 20. which she falsely declared witness owed her. The defendant called her a thief and struck her and made the blood fly. The defendant said the complainant was drunk and abused her and witness struck her, upon which the complainant assaulted her with a poker and seized her by the halr.—The defendant was bound over in the sum of £5 for six months, and had to pay 7s. costs. NON-PERFORMANCE OF SERVlCE.—Elizabeth Lee, em- ployed at Platt's fustian cutting mills, was summoned by Messrs. John and Joseph Wilkinson, fustian cutters, for nonfulfilment of duty while in their employ. She was ordered to pay is. a week till the costs and debt, 14s. in all, were paid.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNII SDAT.—Before Captain Withington (chairman) and Z. Armitage. ___ _ .

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Mark Turner, drunk and disorderly in Warrington-road. Penketh, on the night of the 13th ult., 2s. 6d. and costs. ASLEEP IN CHARGE OF LURRIES.—Gibert Hankiason and George Dumbell, for being asleep in charge of their lurries at Rixton on the 15th of August, were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

CHARGE OF DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Wm. Frederick Pennington, charged with being guilty of disorderly con- duct in Lord-st., Southworth-with-croft, on the night of August 19th, was dismissed. CRUELTY To HORSES.—Nathan Taylor, aged 71, was charged with working a horse while in an unfit state at Poulton, on the 17th August. P.S. Barns and Inspec- tor Dowty proved the case. The animal was being worked while in a very poor condition, and suffering from a very severe wound under the saddle, but had since been destroyed. The defendant had been fined the costs for similar treatment of the animal some months ago, and was now fined 2s. 6d. and costs. ILLBoaL SCALES.—John Aspinall, grocer, of Croft, was charged with having in his possession on August 17th, a pair of scales one drachm out of balance and a pair of scales unstamped. Mr. Jenkins defended.—lnspector Spencer proved the cases, and the defendant was mulcted in costs in each case. VAGIO,NCY.—WiIIiam Fletcher and David Deegan, charged with sleeping in a barn belonging to Mr. Massey, farmer at Martinscroft, on the Ist inst., were dismissed on promising to leave the district. A FARM RAID BY JOYBNILES.—James Parry, Thomas Drew, John Burnett and William Burnett, all boys were charged with stealing, on the 23rd of August. seven .eggs, a quantity of apples, and a fowl from the farm of Joseph Pownall, Great Sankey. Parry had been prey- , iously convicted, and was sentenced to 12 strokes of the birch rod, and the other boys to six stzokes each.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. H. Reynolds ond Mr. J. Handley. A JOKE.—Jas. Downs, a Ship Canal navvy, was charged with having on the previous night stolen a pair of boots the property of a fellow lodger, named James Walker. The prisoner said he intended to return the boots which he had only taken in joke. He was fined 10s. and costs. He had been several times convicted, including for burglary at Chester. WEDNESDAY.—Befere Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. L.
Davies.

AN UNSUSTAINED CHARGE.—Thomas .6 Peggy "was charged with indecently assaulting his daughter, Betsy, 16 years of age, on the previous day. After hearing the evidence the bench considered the charge unsubstantiated and discharged the prisoner. DRUNEENNESS.—Thomas Welsby and Ellen Whitby, were fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. For a like offence John Mitchell and Wm. Moran were each fined 2s. 6d. and costs. WILFUL DAMAGE.—Elizabeth Clayton, a stranger to the town was charged with being drunk and also with wilfully breaking two panes of glass in the window of the Railway Hotel, doing damage to the amount of 10s. Mr. E. Griffiths, the landlord, proved the damage and said the prisoner deliberately broke the window be- cause he refused to supply beer.—The defendant said she was excited and drunk. She had found her husband who was connected with theatrical people, with another woman.—A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed, and she was ordered to pay the damage.

div.head: RINCORN PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: RINCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. Henry Reynolds. DRUNKENNESS .—James Robinson was charged wit h being drunk on the towing path of the Bridgewater Canal and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. For a similar offence a boatman named James Fleming was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed on John Burns, who had been found drunk and asleep in Mersey-st.—Annie Hampson, a young woman, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Regent-st., and was fined ss. and costs:

THE OBSTRUCTION NUISA.NCE.—Thomas Boote, and James Howard, young men were each fined /s. and costs for obstructing Bridge-st., by loitering on the footpath; for a like offence committed in Church-st., Jas. Finegan was fined ss. and costs, Mr. James Reynolds remarking that this obstruction in Runcorn was a lwrrible nuisance and must be put down. YOUNG, THlEVES.—Patrick McDonald (11), Henry Ball (I 2 Thomas Connell (18), Thomas Morrison (15), and Thos. Wesley (39), were charged with having on Friday night stolen a cap and a cardigan jacket from the shop of Thomas Fox, draper, Church-st. On the application of Superintendent Large, Connell was discharged in order to give evidence. Connell stated that he saw Morrispn take the jacket from the shop door and hand it to Wesley, who afterwards gave him 10d. saying he had got is. for it. When apprehended by P.C. Shaw McDonald admitted having stolen the cap and handed it to Ball, in whose possession it was found. With the exception of Wesley the prisoners pleaded guilty. Wesley was discharged, Ball and McDonald were each sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod, and Morrison was sent to gaol for 14 days.

STEALING A FARMER'S OATS.-Wm. Donovan, and Geo. Swan,of Runcorn.were charged with stealing three sheaves of oats value 6d., the property of, John Frod- sham, of Aston by Sutton, on Sunday evening.—Henry Rosbottom farmer, deposed to seeing the defendants driving along Chester-road. They stopped near Mr. Frodsham's field and one of them went through the hedge and threw three sheaves in the cart.—P.C.Griffitlas stated that he found the oats in the cart at Dutton Dean. The prisoners were each fined 10s. or seven day's impri- sonment,

div.head: Total THE WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS
div.p: Total THE WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS

The officers of A, D, and F Companies of the Warrington Volunteers joined together on. Saturday to give the men under their command some oppor- tunity of practising extended manceuvres, after- wards entertaining them at a substantial tea, and concluding the evening with songs and the distri- bution of company shooting prizes. Both in the instruction in the afternoon and in the amusement in the evening the undertaking was very success- ful. At half-past four a considerable muster of the companies named, under Captain j. D. Buckton, Lieutenants J. A. Edelsten and F.M. Appleton, and 2nd Lieutenants R. S. Chorley and J D. Fairclough„, headed by the brass- and bugle bands,, started from the Drill Hall and marched at attention as far es. the Latchford Post Mee. Here the halt was sounded,. and patrolling parties were sent out by Grappenhall-rd, and Thelwall-lartei. the supposition being that an enemy had been reported somewhere Inthe neighbourhood, of Thelwall. Preceded by an advance guard, the remainder of the companies marched forward along the linutsford. rd. over the new bridge into the parkadjoining Thelwall Hall,the use of which had been generously lent for the oc- casion by Admiral Jones-Parry. The enemy was sapposed to have been found in the groundsof the hall,and on their being rejoined by the patrolling parties, the companies were at once formed for. "the attack." A few files were to represent the defence. The movement was practised twice, terminating with the advance of the second line, which doubling through the firing line with loud cheer- ing, bugles sounding, and drums beating, might be sup- posed to have carried the position with the bayonet charge. The companies were next expanded for skir- mishing, but, finding no new enemy, they took up an echelon formation against an imaginary atack of cavalry. After a little practice in throwing out advance and rear guards, the companies marched to the Latchford Parish Room, where a very comfortable tea, kindly prepared by the lady friends of the officers, was awaiting them. Songs and recitations were given later by Sergeant Taylor, Lance-sergeant Gregory, Corporal Smith Private Rich-

ardson, and others, and money prizes were handed by Captain Buckton to the members of A Company who had been successful in the competition completed on the pre- vious Saturday. Captain Buckton briefly addressed the men, complimenting them on the work of the whole year and especially on the way they had performed their duties that afternoon. He explained that the company cup, presented by Major Pickmere, could not be pre- sented that night, as a question had arisen as to the winner, depending on a point still under the considera- tion of the commanding officer. Lieutenant J. A. Edels- ten handed the shooting cup of D Company to the winner, Private S. Flannagan, and said that he had been Qommb- sioned by the donor of the cup, Mr. J. Malin Edelsten, who he much regretted was unable to be present, to put a small packet inside the cup—the packet looked as if it contained a coin. Lieutenant Edelsten spoke briefly of tke work of the company during the year, and particu- larly of the praiseworthy conduct of the men on Whit- Monday, which was spent in class firing at Altcar. Lieutenant Appleton and 2nd Lieutenant Chorley followed with speeches, addressed especially to the men under their command, and at a quarter to ten the "fall in "was sounded, and the companies marched back to th 3 Drill Hall.
ST. MARY'S ATHLETIC SPORTS, WIDNES.

The fifth annual sports in connection with St. Mary's Young Men's Society, Widnes, was held on Saturday, on the ground of the St. Mary's Football Club, there be- ing a fair attendance of spectators. Mr. W. Platt was handicapper, Mr. E. Farrell starter, Messrs. T. Farrell, Healey, and T. Kelly judges, and Mr. T. Laws referee. Results-300 Yards Handicap, for youths: 1, H. Eaves, St. Helens, 73 yards start; 2, N. Whilley, Widnes,. 87; 3, E. Kelly, Widnes, 70. Members, 220 yards: 1, T. Mc Cafferty, 8 yards start; 2, J. Clarke, I; 3, J. Kelly, 3. 120 Yards Race: 1, J. Graig, Widnes, 6; 2, H. Peters, Widnes, 8; 3, J. Clarke, Widnes, 10. Mile Bicycle Race—Winners of Heats: W. H. Bellian, Warrington; W. Leatherbarrow, Warrington; W. V. Brown, Widnes; W. J. Maxwell, Roby, L. Ainsworth, Liverpool, and V. J. Swift, Widnes. Final heat: 1, Leatherbarrow, 150 yards; 2, Browne, 180'; 3, Bellian, 150. 220 Yards Made: 1, J. H. Tilley,Widnes,s9 yards; 2,J. J. WARRINGTON V. CHBETHAM HlLL.—This return match ; was played at Cheetham Hill on Saturday in dull and cheerless weather. Warrington were but poorly re- , presented, their team being made up by the inclusion of four players from the junior clubs of the town. The recent heavy rains had rendered the wicket in a sodden condition, and it was certainly a slice a luck on the part of Mr. Morgan to defeat Mr. Crosfield in the spin for choice of innings. Cheetham Hill batted first, and J. Morgan and Cadman took up the attack against Cros- field and Shaw. The home captain hit out brilliantly at the onset, forcing the game, but Cadman preferred to adopt defensive principles, with the result that with the score at 12, Crosfield completely beat him. S. Murray was the next on the list, and was content to see his partner do the bulk of the scoring. Runs came fast, and at 34, Ashton (a slow bowler) relieved Shaw. It was left to Crosfield to effect a separation, for Murray being tempted to hit, he missed, and Clark was a trifle too sharp behind the stumps. Morgan survived a confident appeal for being run out whilst he had a couple of lives in the'out-field, Yonge making a brilliant attempt to bring off a catch. Bothwell only added four when he fell at 60, but so well did Oates bat, that the score was taken to 76-, when ' Morgan was beaten by Brown. Pennington and Oates hit brilliantly, and a score was taken to 120, when the closure was applied. The Warringtonians had a little over an hour and a half in which to bat, but each player adopted strict defensive tactics, and at the close War- rington had lost but four wickets for 58 runs. Podmore, Crosfield and Clark were undoubtedly responsible for Warrington making the creditable draw. Score :

WARRINGTON V. CHRETTIAM HILL (2ND ELEVINS).-011 Arpley ground, on Saturday. The home team won the toss and took first innings. The commencement was anything but favourable, Adamson being caught and bowled with only three runs on the board. Wallington and Dutton took the score to 14-, when the latter was bowled by the fast bowler. When Smith was in things were very lively, the left-hander treating all the bowling alike, and but for the sodden state of the ground, his score would have been much larger,many of his big hita stopping dead, close to the boundary. While Smith and Bibby were together 34 were put on for the seventh wicket, of which the former obtained 29. Jolley and Parry again took the score to 106 for the ninth wicket, although the former should have been caught and bowled early in his innings. The innings finally closed for 114 runs, Jolley taking his bat out for a hard hit 22. The fielding of the visitors was anything but good, and if all the chances had been taken the score would pro- bably have not been more than 80. The visitors made a fairly good start; and,heiped by some indifferent field- ing and wild throwing in, 43 runs were notched before the fourth wicket fell. After this, fielding was much smarter, and Dutton brought off two fine catches in the out-field, the fifth and sixth wickets failing at 50. Within ten minutes of drawing time, Dutton went on to bowl a second time, the visitors then having three wickets in hand, but the change worked well, the fast bowler promptly clean bowling two batsmen.
