div.head: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: SANKEY BRIDGES WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
PRESENTATION TO THE REV. H. WATER WORTH.

A tea and social gathering were held in the above place by the members of Mr. Brough's society class, on Saturday evening. A large number of the mem- bers were present, and advantage was taken of the circumstance to make a slight recognition of the services of the Rev. H. Waterworth, who, after la- bouring here for a few months, has received a call to Edinburgh. After those present had done justice to the substantial repast provided. Mr. T. Woolley, who occupied the chair, opened the meeting by a few well-chosen remarks. Afterwards Captain Sum- nierfleld and Messrs. R. Highley, C. Pritchard, J. Corradine, Beddall, Walker, Schofield, Butler, and Foden addressed.tbe meeting, speaking of the great amount of good the Rev. H. Waterworth had done, and the loss that would be suffered by his removal. Mr. Brough was then called upon to make the pre- sentation. After explaining the object of the gathering, which he stated was decided upon almost at the last moment, he said he was pleased to see so many respond to the invitation. The 'Rev. Mr.Waterworth had during his short stay endeared himself to the hearts of the people. They loved him for his genial disposition and humility of spirit. His great success was owing in a great measure to his making himself one with the people. He had laboured hard among them, and his visitations had exerted an influence among the people that would neverdie. His eloquence as a preacher was very marked, and by his simplicity he had captivated the hearts of the children. The slight testimonial was not to Le regarded for its intrinsir value, but as the united expression of the love they bore him, and the es- teem in which he was held by the members of Mrs. Brough's class at Sankey Bridges. The present consisted of Tennyson's poems and Macaulars Essays.—The Rev. H. Waterworth, who was much moved by the expres- sions of the various speakers, said it gave him very great joy to labour among them. It had cheered, en- couraged, and benefitted him. This meeting would stimulate him ana encourage him to labour on, for he rejoiced to know that his labour was not in vain, and as he looked on those books in time to come it would bring back to his mind the generosity and the sympathy of the Sankey Bridges Wesleyans. He could not sufficiently thank them for their kindnessto him, but he trusted that in his future sphere he should eontinue to have the prayers of those gathered there. The meeting was then brought to a closein the usual way.
CIIA.RGE OF. ASSIITLT AGAINST A CORPORATION OFFICIAL.

At the Waryington County sessions, en Wednesday, Alfred Woodfall Howard, a clerk in the rate-collecting department under the Warrington Corporation, was charged with assaulting on the 25th of August, John Melor, keeper on the Arpley Meadows estate; and Melor was cross-summoned on a charge of assaulting Howard on the same occasion. Mr. Jenkins appeared for Melor, and Mr. Browne for Howard.—Mr. Jenkins said on the 25th of August, Melor was on duty in Arpley Meadows, and saw the defendant coming down an occupation road with a gun over his arm. He had permission to shoot over some fields in Arpley. The keeper met him and said "Good, morning, I see you are still coming sneaking down here with a gun," and Howard replied" I will come when I have a mind as long as I have permission to ga on the land." Melor said" Who has given you permission ?" Howard replied "Joseph Dobson." Melor retorted, " "don't believe it. In any caseyou are not going on to Joseph Dobson's land.' Howard said he should go across Mr. Dobson's field, and went in that direction. When he got into the field Melor went up to him and said, "Howard I an' surprised, looking at the position you. hold,, that you come sneaking down Arpley with your gun in that man- mer." Howard replied . I have got a living independent of my position." Meier said "I am very glad of that but you are worse than one of these common poachers." This excited the defendant, who struck Melor on the face, but he did not attempt to strike in return and went back, but told him he would summon him, and had done so by the instructions, of his employers.—Melor gave evi- dence confirmatory of Mr. Jenkins's-statement.—By Mr. Browne : Mr. Daniel Jones was not the prosecutor and had not paid for the summons nor had witness told anyone that he had. Witness knew Mr. Howard had a right 014 Mr. Owen's land. Mr. Howard said he would report witness to his superiors for insubordination, and he said " Are you any superior to me ? " Howard told him if he would put his stick up he would give him more.— Mr. Browne: A young thin fellow against you? ' Malor : And I a man 60 years of age.—Mr. Browne:. And you with a great thick stiek.—Melor If I had been a young man like him he would not have got away as he did.—Peter Collier and Wm. Thos. Schutt, milk dealer, havinggiven evidence,Mr. Browne addressed the Bench. He said ef all the paltry cases that were ever, trumped up this seemed to be one of the worst. The summons fon assault had been taken, out simply because the prosecutor found he had. no case under the game 5 laws. The assault was only imagined afterwards.—Mr. Norman, sanitary inspector, deposed to Melor telling him on August 26th that he was going to summon Howard for assault, and admitting having called him a, sneaking poacher, with a.profaue prefix to the word sneaking,. There was no mark on Melor. '— Joseph Dobson deposed that he had given Mr. Howard permission to shoot on his ground. —Mr. Strange son of the oecupier of ether land in the meadows, said his father had also given Mr. Howard per- mission.—Mr. Howard then gave evidence confirming that of one of his witnesses, who said he had no gun„only a thorn stick in his hand at the time in ques- tion. He was cutting it with his knife. He detailed veryprofane and, offensive language as used to him by Mekar,,and deniettassaulting him, but said Melor put up, hiastiek to him.—The Magestrates' Clerk said that was an.assault.—Mh. Browne-said he had forgotten to raise- the, point of law that the Bench had no jurisdiction in he case as a question of right of way was involved.— Tile- Chairman: I thought that half-an-hour ago.- IIIr. Jenkins thought the Court bad jurisdiction,. the ;charge being one of assault not trespass.—The Bench dis- missed the ease, Mr, Browne withdrawing :the charge against Meier.

A London and North-Western Railway guard named Thomas Allen is in. custody at Coventry on a charge of stealing large quantities of jewellery in course of transit. On ThArsday,, at a meeting of the Blackburn Town Council, attention was drawn to street betting in the town, and it was stated that children were often sent by their parents to make bets. At the woollen mill of Messrs. Berry-Taylor and Sons, Staniland, damage to the amount of £3,000 has been done by fire. On Thursday a cornmill and bakery occupied by Mr. William Mattock at Skipton was destroyed by fire, the loss being estimated at £5,000. THE NEGRO AND THE PIILLS.-At the Liverpool Court, the other day, before Mr. Kinghorn, deputy stipendiary magistrate, it came out in the course of cross-examina- tion of a witness in a trivial case of theft, that one of them, a young negro had been some time ago charged with stealing a lady's satchel, in which there was a box of Beecham's Pills. On looking at the box and seeing on it that they were "worth a guinea a box," be pro- ceeded to take them, and notwithstanding that several of his friends implored him to let them have one or two, he swallowed the contents of the box, The fine healthy appearance of the witness showed that the pills most certainly must have agreed with him.

div.head: RUMOURED RE-OPENING OF THE MAYBRICK CASE.
div.p: RUMOURED RE-OPENING OF THE MAYBRICK CASE.

"Lloyd's Newspaper" understands that during the last few days statements of a most important nature have been laid before the Home Secretary in connection with the Maybrick case. These statements throw new and, unexpected light on the matter, and they are now under consideration by the responsible advisers of the Home Secretary, who rook upon them as much more im- portant than the ordinary representations which in such cases are placed before them. Mrs. Maybrick's sympa- thizers hope they have submitted to the Home Secretary sufficient to cause him to reconsider the case as a whole.

div.head: HOURS OF RAILWAY SERVANTS..
div.p: THE HOURS OF RAILWAY SERVANTS..

At-h• demonstration of memliers of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants held on Sunday, in the St. James's Hall,Manchester,Mr. F. A. Charming, M.P., was the principal speaker. He said that personal examina- tion, as well as the recent evidence given before the Select Committee of the House of Commons, had con- vinced him that excessive hours were worked on eur railways. He therefatre urged all railway servants to combine acd form a strong union of their own, by whose aid they would be enabled to get direet represent— ation in the House of Commons. That would be the first step; towards securing for themselves a more just share - in the profits made from the public by the companies. Resolutions dealing with the hours of labour and calling • on all railway men to join the union were unanimoußly - carried.

div.head: "BEATING TIM E."
div.p: "BEATING TIM E."

How he once " beat time," or rather apparent time,. in a remarkable fashion is told by Mr. Archibald FOrbes in his article in " The Ninetoonth Century." It is a story of a telegrahic despatch from the battlefield. In the early morning of the 22nd of November, 1878, a British division under General Sir Samuel Browne, occupied the - Afghan fortress of Ali Musjid, up in the Khyber • Pass. Mr. Forbes rode back ten miles to Jumrood, where the field telegraph was, .and sent the news to England in a short message bearing date lga.m. There is five hours' difference of time between India and England in favour of the latter ; and "rho • Daily News" containing this telegram dated 10 a.m. was selling in Fleet-st. at 9 a.m. —one hour of apparent time before it was despatched. Its anticipation of time, however, did not end here. Owing to the five hours' difference between the clocks of London and New York, the message was in time for the regular editions of the New York papers that same :morning. It as thence, immediately wired across the ; American continent; and, owing again to the difference in time between the Atlantic coast and the Pacific slope, the early rising citizen of San Francisco, purchasing his morning paper at 6 a.m,, was able to read the announce- ment of an event whichactually occurred ever tw• hours later in apparent time some 13,000 miles away on the other side of the globe. Puck, as Mr. Forbes says, pro- fessed himself able to put a girdle round the earth in forty minutes, but this. telegram sped half round the globe in two hours less than no time at all.
WORK IN ST. HELENS CHEMICAL ThCTORIES. REMARKABLE STATEMENTS.

The "Manchester. Guardian" says:—" For some weeks past the "Trade Unioniat ' has been giving a remarkable account of the conditions under which the work at the chemieal factories of St. Helens is done. One case selected is that of the "saltcake men ".in the alkali works. Their work,' the Trade Unionist' says, 'is of such intensity that. only the finest powers of endurance can bear up against it. They work with rags or chunks of fib.unel be- tween their teeth in the hand-to-hand struggle with the flames and gas. The gas given off cuts into their arms and rots their teeth . . . very frequently bits get nibbled by the action of the acid out of the nien's hands and arms. Some of the hands at St. Helens have a corrugatedlook in con- seqmence. . . . Most saltcake men have teeth as black as coal. Their mouths get extremely tender. . . . Not only do the saltcake men suffer from their teeth and the .biting effects of the gas, but they begin to suffer from. chest complaints with deadly certainty after they have been some time at work. Of the 429 cases treated at the Providence P..bspital during last year, 74 came from, chemical works; and of the 2,000) eases treated since the little hospital was opened, 369 have been chemical workers," The "Trade Unionist" give the average working time of theseezen as eighty-. four houre a week, or fourteen hours a day for a week; of' six days. Another class of labourers„.the lime workers. are employed in sifting, beating, and slaking lime be- fore it is passed to the chlorine chambers to be used for. the making of bleaching powder. Here again the men either wear a muzzle or hold a piece of rag or flannel, tightly between their teeth, greasing the exposed parts. of the skin for a protection. "In spite of everything, however., the lime gets in somewhere and inflicts its. bite. All the time the work is carried on breathing is a, terrible, effort. To breathe through the nose wouldt have the direst consequences. A single inhalation,. Audi the lime particles would lodge • there. So the air has to. be inhaled through the muzzle and given out through the nose. Naturally, nose bleeding is a frequent coin - plaint at the works. Twenty minutes at a spell is as inr.cL as a man can stand ; after that he goes out to re- cover himself, and lay in a littleair for his inside and some grease br outside lining. These lime men, of course, are not able to wash;: they shun water as other people shun Ike. l'he. only wash they get,, some times for months together, is in the. grease." These men also, we understand from thaaccount, work for something like twelve houre a day,, in alternating day and night shifts. The writer hints that inione case at all events—that of the lime workers—some simple contrivance. " such as a fan to create a draught for carrying off the dust," would lessen the hardships of the employment, but that nothing of the sort is tried. If the account given by. ourcontemporary—whieh we have. no present means of verifying—is in. the main accuratei, then the chemical industry falls at once within the list of trades in which the exceptional. limitation of working hours by lava, is desirable. In the second place, it is desirable that the whole ques- tion of mechanical alleviations should be-looked into and that any which are found practicable should be made, compulsory. At all events it would be well to know in, the first place whether the " Trade Unionist's" descrip-. tion is strictly unexaggerated.; in the second place, if that be so, whether the omission of precautions ap‘ parently simple is due, as we should like to believe, and as certainly has been the case at Se.efheld, to the indiSer, ence of the workmen."

HOW A TAILOR GOT HIS MONEY.

A miserly nobleman—Lord Bath—who lived many years ago, owed his tailor some eight hundred pounds, which he utterly refused to pay. The tailor sent him many letters, stating that he had himself paid out a good deal of money for cloth, velvet, and trimmings of all sort, and could not afford to give so much away. But the dishonest nobleman never even so much as answered him. He called and told Lord Bath how many troubles he had had; how hard times were, and that nothing but necessity would ever make him press his bill. Lord Bath promised to pay him shortly, but only to get rid of him. Finally the tailor grew angry. He stood in the entrance way of Lord Bath's residence when he lrad company, and cried—" I want my money 1 The clothes you have are not paid fort" The servants turned him away. He followed his Lordship to places where he visited, forced his way into the hall, and insisted on being paid. The hosts had him arrested several times and he was charged with being insane. Finally he followed Lord Bath to church one morning, and seated himself in the pew beilind him. As the nobleman sat erect, leaning a little backward, there came a sharp whisper in his ear. "You call yourself a Christian, and cheat a poor tailor' do you ?" Lord Bath shifted his seat. The tailor followed him. "I want my money," he whispered. When in the course of the service the congregation arose, those at a distance who noticed the tailor, only saw a re- spectable man seemingly joining in the responses; but every time he opened his mouth the tailor whispered, "Pay me my money 1" in Lord Bath's ear.

Singularly enough, the sermon was on avarice. The tailor pointed every moral by whispering, "Just like you, my Lord 1" The clergyman hinted, as preachers of all denomi- nations were apt to do in those days, at the probable fate of the miser, and the tailor behind Lord Bath breathed, with great apparent earnest- ness, in his ears such words as these—" There, now, my Lord. See what is to happen to you if you're too fond of your gold not to be honest. I wouldn't risk it, my Lord, if I was you. The parson ought to know, and you see what he thinks of you." And when, in his peroration, the clergyman waxed eloquent, the tailor, lifting his voice higher than he had before, filled each pause with an earnest, "Ah I That's you to a certainty, my Lord. He's got you pat, my Lord. That's Lord Bath that never pays 414 debts, and sits in church with honest men."

The rector, in his high pulpit, heard nothing of all this, but the people in the pews all about were staring. Those home truths, perhaps, touched the miserly nobleman's conscience. At the conclusion of the benediction he requested the tailor to call on him the next morning, and, on his doing so, his Lordship gave him a cheque for the full amount of his debt.

div.head: SOME CURIOUS VOWS.
div.p: SOME CURIOUS VOWS.

A curious and somewhat ludicrous incident occurred in Belgrade in 1867. A body of well- known Servians, all members of the extreme patriotic party, marched through the streets with long beards down to their knees, escorted by a number of barbers, razors in hand, and in this way entered the fortress, when the barbers proceeded at once to strip those beautiful pards of their hirsute adornments, and sent them out clean shaved. The fact is that at the bombardment of Belgrade, in 1862, these Bervians vowed never to let a razor touch their faces until they could shave in the fortress itself on the day on which the Turkish troops abandoned it, and they completed their vow in the manner described. Vienna owes its Church of St. Charles to a vow made by the Emperor Charles VI. during an epidemic. In 1867, a handsome Spanish lady, attired in the garb of a pilgrim of the olden time, appeared in the streets of Toulon. She went on her way home to Madrid, having footed it from that city to Rome in fulfilment of a vow made when she fancied herself at death's door. In the like extremity an Italian princess vowed to undertake a journey to the Holy Sepulchre—no very arduous undertaking now-a-days to anyone. There is a story of a jovial waiter whom some kind friends sought to frighten into making a vow of sobriety. They told him a shocking tale of one who drank not wisely but too well, and was killed by blowing out a candle, the flame having ignited the alcoholic fumes of his breath. He listened, believed, and was duly horrified. Calling for a Bible, he then and there kissed the book, and solemnly swore that never again so long as he lived would he try to blow out a candle. The waiter was a wise man. He knew himself, and limited his vow aocordingly. Shrewder far was the Pittsburg man who swore never to touch another drop so long as he had a hair on his head, and the very same evening had his head shaved, and got drunk, with the proud consciousness of having kept him vow. • THE PLEASURES OF POVERTY.
When husband and wife are true-hearted, there IS Do greater aid to happiness than a few deprivations and hardships in the commencement of their married life. It is a great thing for each to realise

that he or she is sacrificing something for the other. The wife came with empty hands to a husband who had no rich gifts to bestow; but while she is straggling and saving, and he is toiling and deny- ing himself, the consciousness of doing it for the other's sake confers a happiness nothing can equal. It will be in more prosperous days alone, perhaps, that both will realise the pleasures of the poverty they endured in youth. In that grand new house there is nothing lacking that taste can devise or wealth procure. Yet, amidst the splendours and delights, the hearts of both—the wife's oftenest, without doubt—will turn with wistful affection to the little home of old times, poverty-stricken and Inconvenient as it was. The hardships and dis- comforts endured within its walls have passed away like mist before the sunshine, and memory only recalls the delights of contriving, managing, and arranging. The fun enjoyed over amateur attempts at carpentering and surprises in cookery; the brief, sweet holiday stolen from weeks of toil, saved for so anxiously, and looked for so eagerly—these and a hundred other simple joys, are the pleasures of poverty, in fact., undreamt of by the rich and worldly.

div.head: OUR JEWISH FRIEND.
div.p: OUR JEWISH FRIEND.

A man in want of a coat called upon a couple of enterprising German Jew clothiers. The senior of the firm soon found "a first-class fit." In answering the question as to the price, the response was "Tree- pound-ten." "Well, I like your coat very much," said the customer, "but I don't like the price." "Never mine, mine frent--ze price is nothing, so you like ze coat. Ve let you take 'em at tree- pound-five." The customer still complained of the price, saying that three-pounds-five was too dear. This was too much for the Jew, so, taking his cus- tomer to the extreme end of the shop, and drawing him into a dazker corner, he wispered in his ear, " Mine frent, I let you have zat coat for two-pound- fifteen." "Very good," said the customer, "I am satisfied with the price, but I should like to know the meaning of this mysterious performance." "Veil, mine frent, you see dat leetle man dere He was ray broler. He got ze heart disease, and, so help me gracious! if he vas to hear me tell you I take two-pound-fifteen for zat coat, he drop dead on ze spot I"

SOME one says that a remarkable imitation of black walnut may be manufactured from pure pine, the quality and appearance of the article being such as to defy detection, except upon close examina- tion. To accomplish this, one part of walnut peel extract is mixed with six parts of water, and with this solution the wood is coated. NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. FOOTBAI.L.

In South Africa on Saturday the English football team played their sixteenth match against a fifteen of South Africa, the game being by far the best contested ef the tour, as the result was practically an open question un- til the finish. The visitors, who played with four three- quarter backs, never succeeded in getting behind their opponents' goal line, and had not one of the English players succeeded in dropping a goal, the match would have ended in a draw. The Colonials pressed the visi- tors very hard, and several times only narrowly missed scoring, although they were slightly handicapped in the second half by one of their men having been hurt and compelled to retire. The match, which thus ended in favour of the visitors by one goal to nil, was witnessed by a large crowd of spectators, among whom the close- ness of the game created the greatest excitement.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

Referring to the reported retirement of the Lanca- shire captain, the" Athletic News" says I neve) knew a cricketer so universally respected and admired as Mr. llornby has been, and I feel convinced that if the ques- tion of a testimonial was mooted it would be enthusias- tically taken up, not only in Lancashire, but all over the country.

When the present captain of the Lancashire forces does retire he will have the satisfaction of knowing that he is likely to have a worthy successor in Mr. S. M. Crosfield, who on the few occasions he has had charge of the eleven has handled it with great skill, and he has yet to lose his first match. The Warrington amateur has any amount of enthusiasm for cricket, and Lancashire is indeed for- tunat.e in being able to command the services of so good and capable a player.

The Lancashire southern tour was a success, although wretched weather prevailed nearly all through the fort- night the cricketers were away from home. They beat Kent, Sussex, and Essex, and drew with Surrey. By the way, Lancashire have defeated every minor county they played during the season, and very easily too.

The county championship is now settled,and although Surrey are clearly at the top, it is not by such a major- ity of points as at one time appeared probable. Lanca- shire is a very good second, all things considered ; and Middlesex—who twice dofeated Mr. Hornby's team—is third. By comparing last year's table with that of the present season it will be found that Surrey and Lanca- shire occupy the same positions,although the champions have advanced four points, whilst Lancashire are con- tent with a similar number to 1890. The greatest falling off has been in Yorkshire, which tied for third place last year, and this season is eighth on the list, with five points behind nothing.

The final averages, so far as County cricket is con- cerned, show that Shrewsbury still heads the list by no less than 10, and not only so, but although he has batted in five innings less than Abel, he holds the record for the total of runs scored with 1,071. The only men to reach four figures are Shrewsbury, Gunn and Abel, although Bean is but 24 runs short. The first ten batsmen are made up out of the following counties :—Notts two, Surrey two, Middlesex two, Sussex two, Lancashire one, (A. Ward) and Kent one. The top score of the year was A. E. Stoddart's 215 v. Lancashire, and it is worthy of note that each of the ten batters have scored over 100 in one innings, whilst Stoddart has the honour of being the only second century man.

Turning to bowling, Hearne finishes off with a slight lead, although Lohmann is not far behind, and his is certainly the more creditahle performance, for he has taken 28 more wickets than the Middlesex man. Rawlin comes out very well, and Southern bowlers have evi- dently shown up much better than the Northern contin- gent, for out of the first ten they claim seven, the North being content with Mold, Briggs, and Attewell. The Notts man has sent down the most overs, but Lohmann has had the greatest number of runs scored off him. Not a single amateur appears amongst the first ten, and indeed the only one likely to do so was W. G. Grace.

div.head: CHAPTER OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.
div.p: A CHAPTER OF RAILWAY ACCIDENTS.
TRAINS RUNNING INTO ;THE STREETS.

Two or three serious railway accidents occurred on Saturday. The most disastrous took place at Facit, between Bacup and Rochdale, where a passenger train proceeding to the latter town was run into by a train of waggons laden with stone. The brakes of the engine attached to the stone waggons would not act on the slippery rails, and the train ran away down an incline at high speed, a collision being the result. The two rear carriages of the passenger train were broken to pieces, and the permanent way was much damaged. Esther Smith , aged 35, of Cheetham Hill, Facit, was so badly hurt that she died soon after being taken from the wreckage, and the injuries sustained by John Shepherd, of Lincoln, in the accident also proved fatal. Several *other persons were injured, including the driver of the stone train, who had a shoulder dislocated. Great dam- age was done to rolling stock at Bridge End, on the Wrexham and Connah's Quay line, and at Bradford goods station, in the former case by a collision between two goods trains, and in the latter by a runaway goods train knocking down a wall and falling into a public* street. A Midland express from London dashed into a North Western train at Leicester on Monday and telescoped the guard's van. Fortunately the guard and passengers had just quitted the North-Western train, and no one was injured. On the same day, an empty excursion train, running into Ramsgate to take passengers on to Luton crashed through the wall into the roadway leading to the sands, and killed a hawker and four other persons who were standing in the thoroughfare. The train was wrecked.

RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.

The annual meeting of the shareholders was held at the Public Hall, on Monday afternoon. Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., Chairman of Directors, presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Hayes, J. Simpson, W. Whittaker, W. F. Salkeld (Sec.), and W. Jones (assistant Sec.) In their half-yearly report the Directors state— "The Revenue Account shows a balance of £920 13s. id. including £167 14s. id. brought from the pre- vious half-year, out of which the Directors recommend a dividend to be paid of £4 10s. per centum, per annum, free from income tax, payable on and after the first day of October ; this will absorb £675, leaving a balance of £245 13s. id. to be carried forward. The Directors have ordered the Runcorn engine to be ,repaired at an esti- mated cost of £249 us. 6d. and the work is now satis- factorily progressing. The water in the well continues as previously and of good quality." The Chairman said it was pleasing to meet in an oc- casion like that with a growing revenue, and carrying forward a bigger balance than the company had ever done before in its history. The number of houses in Runcorn had increased by 74. and in Weston by one, so that this fact accounted to some extent for the improved demand for water. Extra expense had been incurred in service pipes, and taps in consequence of the severe frost of the past winter. He noticed that there was still a considerable waste of water in the town, much more than there ought to be, and during the past few months they had found out one or two flagrant cases. It was only through the good nature and 'kindness of Mr. Salkeli that strong measures were not taken, and he (the Chairman) wished it to be understood that in any future occurrences of a similar nature, prompt measures would be taken. He was also expressing the feeling of the other directors. With regard to the repair of the en- gine Runcorn, the Chairman said they were acting on the advice of their engineer, Mr. Hawksley, and when this was accomplished they would have two good en- gines, which would last for many years to come. The directors thought it best to do the work with a good balance in hand, and not pay a larger dividend than they were doing. If the works progressed as they were doing, the directors hoped to be able to declare a larger dividend next year. He moved the adoption of the re- port and accounts, and that the dividend suggested be declared.—Mr. W. Hayes seconded. Carried unani- mously.—On the proposition of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Whittaker, the retiring directors—Mr. W. Hayes and Mr. J. Simpson—werere-elected. Mr. Robt.Foulkes was re-appointed one of the auditors, on the proposal of Mr. Whittaker. seconded by Mr. Hayes.—Mr. Whittaker proposed a vote of thanks to the secretary for his excel- lent attention and interest in the company, and also to his assistants.—The Chairman seconded the motion, which was carried.—Mr. Salkeld thanked the meeting for their kindness, and remarked that he and the staff worked comfortably together, and tried to do their best for the company.

div.head: Zettero to tbe Obitor.
div.p: Zettero to tbe Obitor.
THE DRINK QUESTION AND ITS EVILS.

Sir,—lt was with great pleasure I read the letter from Mr. Guest in your last week's issue, written in such a manly style, and yet in such:a Christian spirit concern- ing the decision come to by the magistrates at the Brewster Sessions. I am persuaded it would be a great blessing to the town of Warrington if we had a few more such gentlemen on the magisterial bench. We have heard a good deal lately abont our locus standi in the Police Court, but we are proud that we can plead in the public Press, and again I appeal to every reason- able man who has the welfare of the town he lives in, and the welfare of his fellow creatures at heart, if the objections raised at the Brewster Sessions are not justi- fied by the results we see in our streets day after day, as was said. The public-houses are of no earthly use ; Gila I can certainly say they are of no heavenly use, for the front entrance to all those places that are lieensed to sell drink is the sure road to the asylum, workhouse, and goal. There are many reasons why all people, Christians especially,should help the Temperance Feder- ation to remove those stumbling blocks to all that is pod and pure, if only out of the paths of their growing sons and daughters. The voiceS Jc!'..n 12'A:ht.! a,dfl Richard Cobden have often been heard on this great question, and no nr:en have won greater respect for hon- esty of purpose and clearness of judgment. John Bright • declared that "a monster obstacle is in our way, remove this curse the drink traffic, for our way is upward and snward, and our labours will be blessed." Cobden said "Every day's experience tends more and more to con- firm me in the opinion that the temperance cause lies at the foundation of all social and political reform." Lord Coleridge declares" but for the drink we might shut up nine-tenths of our gaols." Stand at our own street corners for half an hour on any Saturday night and you will have no lack ef illustrations of what I write about. Look at the police record week after week and you will find ample evidence of the curse of this detestable traffic. There is scarcely a family even in the town of Warrington that can not count some of its branches or members as victims ofjthis drink, which like the destroying angel of Eg,ypt,scarcely leaves a home where there is not one dead. In conclusion, our:opponents charge us again and again with extravagance of language. 11l words may have fallen from earnest speakers, but really no words can be called too extravagant to describe such terrible sights as are to be seen daily in our public streets, and my advice to all interested in stemming this tide of iniquity, is go and see for youselves.—Yours truly, Liverpool-road, Warrington.
J.H.W.

div.p: DRINK TRAFFIC.

Sir,—The special sermon of Mr. John Yonge, the speeches of the great anti-licensing meeting of the in- habitants,and the Brewster Sessions have become things ef the past, and Warrington to-day remains, as before, cursed with its 209 licensed centres of drunkenness, crime and misery. The most ardent friend of social reform could hardly have expected a different result. The great "Beer and Whisky Ring," with its extensive and subtle influences for evil, and our manipulated Watch Committee are all powerful factors in upholding the pre- sent state of things.

As to the opposition of "the clergy," the less we say the better. Avowed drinkers themselves, and the per- sonal friends and spiritual guides of the big brewers and publicans, it would be absurd to attach much importance to their spasmodic utterances against drunkenness. They cannot, apparently, close their eyes to the evils resulting from the public-houses around them, some of them al- most at their doors, and so they must, for decency's sake, assume the role of temperance reformers, the bur- den of their prophesy being: "Just drink what will do you good and then stop." But how feeble, how tempo- rising, is their attitude in regard to "the trade!" Is not the great drink-made baronet of Wilderspool fame a lover of their Zion and a builder of synagogues? and does not the wife of another knight of the bung, of art gal- lery renown, come all the way from Liverpool to lay foundation stones for them? Why then should we expect Mr. Willis and bis friends to do anything to curtail the usefulness of these good men and women by clos- ing their springs of revenue, however objectionable these springs may be? Like reformers in another field, Mr. Willis would relieve the congested districts by transferring some of the licenses to localities as yet free from the blighting and demoralising influence of the drink shop. What a great reform that would be? -Just think of curing drunkenness by removing the pub- lic-house from one place to another! It is not in "the clergy" any more than in human nature to put obstacles in the way of their own interests. Charles Buxton, an eminent brewer, has left it on record that "the struggle, of the school, the church, and the library against the gin pa!ace and the beerhouse is only another development of the war between heaven and hell." Quite so; who can deny it ? But there is a great political power in the liquor traffic which may be relied upon when "the .church" is in danger. The noisiest, if not most potent, defenders of "Church and State" at election times are the publicans and their deluded clients. And so the struggle must be continued ad infinitum, no matter how disastrous the war may be to the peace and well-being of s, iety. And members of the " enlightened " party sat on the 'Bench with their traditional enemies the "stupid" Tories, an'', great things were expected from them by their ad- mirers and followers. But great was the disappointment they experienced. Whether the valiant champions of reform made any effort to close the floodgates of drunkenness in the town your report saith nct. If they

did it is to be regretted, on their own account, that it was not duly and fully reported. Another view maybe taken of their silence on the occasion. The near presence of Almighty God may have had a collapsing effect upon the good men. Their knees may have become feeble,and their tongues so cave to the roof of their mouths that they could not utter a wore in defence of the people's right to be delivered from the abominable nuisance of the .public-house.

The result of the proceedings was just what we ex- pected it would be. Despite the special sermon, the speeches, and the presence of friends of progress on the bench, the Tory alders and abettors of drunkenness had it all their own way. And, lixe the Philistines of old, they quitted themselves like men of war by re-licensing, without exception, the noble army of Bulls,'" " Dragoons," "Bear's Paws," "Stars," "Angels," &c., &c., with a supreme, if not contemptuous, disregard for public order and decency and the best interests of the inhabitants. And they seemed so satisfied with the day's work that, according to their mouthpiece, Mr. Justice Chandley, they were quite prepared to bear the respon- sibility of it. Poor men. We fear they have not very carefully considered what that responsibility would be, and how far it would extend into the future. But they may rest assured that for all the tears and groans, the oaths and blasphemies,and for all the disorder and crime which will undoubtedly result from their action they will bear the full measure of guilt before the law of God. Nor will they be able to shield themselves under the lying plea that intoxicating drink being "a good crea- ture of God," can only entail punishment upon the weak and foolish people who abuse it. Beer, whisky, rum, brandy and gin,are assuredly not good creatures of God, but vile decoctions produced by destroying some of the "kindly fruits of the earth."—Yours truly,
toRENZO.
THE SAVIOURS OF SOCIETY v. WARRINGTON PUBLIC MORALS COUNCIL.

Sir,—Warrington Teetotallers again hpad the column in London and provisional papers with " Extraordin- ary evidence" at the Warrington Brewster Sessions. One of the " Intemperate teetotallers" objected to the renewal of seven licenses, and astounded the bench, when cross-examined, in that he did not know what ac- commodation the said houses possessed. Good heavens; was ever so mean and depicable a bogus opposition offered? Yes, that witness was very badly drilled. What will Lord Bramwell's opinion be on such mean and cowardly objects? Sir, I tell the Rev. J. Yonge NO his agitators that they should practise what they preach. My letter—partly read at the Co-operative Hall—was well condensed. I charged several of the clergymen and laymen present with receiving money for their own benefit and use coming from that contaminating evil, drink. Can it be denied?

I notice advertisements in your "Borough Journals" furthering the sale of drink, and yet those who receive money from the said advertisements mount a public platform and condemn the trade and liquor, while ethers are interested as shareholders in household companies and receive rents &c., from this drink traffic! Ah ! Religion what a beautiful occupation, where is the con- sistency of such hypocrites? I notice one of your "Great unpaid "in adjudicating on a case wherein the man was charged with drunkenness recklessly asserted he never had a publican up for selling drink to drunken people! Surely a man can buy a bottle of spirits from other than the" Publican," namely, the wine-merchant, the grocer, his club, or the Crosby Hotel, and drink it in his own home or ois the road! All goes against the publican. The cowardly co..,duct of men who slander, libel, and abuse those engaged in a legal and legitimate trade, is disgusting to listen to. Does It matter if a publican or his wife purchase, a sofa or chair, or have bills printed atsay "Examiner,' or " Observer " Office? Will the money for what the bill may come to for such goods be refused even when erdered to be sent to the "Pig and Whistle " or the "Red-Cat ?" I refuse to supply any intoxicated person with drink. Will the cabinet-maker or printer refuse to sell their wares to an intoxicated person ? Query. Sir, in Ty opinion the publican who" knowingly" serves with in- toxicating drink an intoxicated man or woman, no tine or punishment is too heavy for the offender. Compare the Christian and honest example and speech of your worthy Rector to those of his fiery following at the Co operative Hall. He, the Rector, takes drink in modera- tion but does not abuse it. He does not want to anni- hilate all houses which moderate men may use for their "cakes and ale."

I would bring to your notice, Mr. Editor, a most glaring act of inconsistency on the part of a vicar not twenty miles from Warrington which occurred during the present month. The rev, vicar was the owner or trustee of "a pub." The tenant, who had spent years In the house, and who during that time never had his name or the house tarnished by report, was refused a renewal of lease at the same rent. It was then offered to a brewery company who gave the rental asked for to the rev, prelate, who presided at a "teetotal meeting" not a month ago for the purpose of urging magistrates to reduce, aye, annihilate the drink trade! If I see in the columns of your journal that a sermon will be preached on "Consistency" at Wycliffe, or any other place of worship, by any of the rev, gentlemen who met at the Co-operative Hall—your consistent rector ex- cluded—l will attend.

Have not Lord Bramwell, Mr. Justice Grantham, and other judges stated publicly from the judicial bench that the quips and oddities of the " cranks " denominating themselves teetotallers have done more to retard and harass them in their efforts in the path of true temper- ance reform, continued durln,9: many years both in and out, of Parliment than any other cause? • In cOnclualcm, I would warn those "Saviours of Society" to be more careful in the wilful slanderous as- sertions theymake. I commended theßishop of Bedford's advice at a recent Church Congress to the consideration of the Rev. J. Yonge, but ieseems it was of no avail as the rev. gentleman seems a power in himself. I note also, Mr. Editor, that the less sustained by those ratepayers of good character, whose " pubs " found accommodation for the continuous flow of troops who were billeted on them during the past week cannot be estimated at less than £l3O. Will the Rev. Mr. Yonge or Councillor Roberts or Mr. Walker volunteer to find accommodation for those horse-soldiers, and keep them away from the " contaminating influence of the pub," which first tempted the writer to drink, an incident I never have regretted, as I never yet have abused drink ; but practise and preach moderation.
LAWRENCE FLOOD. Crosby Hotel, Manchester.

div.head: LICENSING QUESTION IN WARRING-
div.p: THE LICENSING QUESTION IN WARRING-
TON.

Sir,—The licensing sessions are being held in various parts of the country, and the temperance agitators ap- pear determined to leave no stone unturned in trying to ruin the publicans ; and what, I ask, would be the result ? Drunkenness I detest—no man can defend it— but I contend that if all the public-houses were closed, unless drink was entirely banished from our midst and prohibited from being made, drunkenness would be far more prevalent than it is, and the last state would be worst than the first.; In arguing this drink question, those who are against us cannot find language too strong , to hurl at us, though we are dealing in a legitimate and , honest trade. There is nothing that I like better than to call a spade a spade, or to strike straight from the shoulder in whatever we have to say and as publicans, charged as we are by these teetotallers with everything that is loathsome, charged as we are as being the fore- runners of crime, charged as we are as being the insti- gators of every imaginable sin. I think it is high time to do our utmost and seize every opportunity we can to expose the dishonesty and hypocrisy of these men. I will not say for a moment that all temperance men are fana- tics. I know some who are sincere and earnest in their work trying to reclaim the drunkard from being a slave to his passion for drink, but their arguments are differ- ent to others; they say, do right and act justly, and thus they strive in season and out of season both by precept and example and not as it were by grasping at the pub- lican's throat to ruin him at one fell swoop. There are many things which appear strange to me in the various agitations that take place, which compel me to believe that many of our agitators work for that which will be most beneficial to them, even if it is not according to the honest dictates of their conscience, and I charge these teetotal fanatics with being both hypocri- tical and dishonest in their dealings with the publicans. This may appear to be strong language, but I will men- tion a few things, and if I fail to prove my charge let LI any of these men who ,are against my trade, from the highest to the lowest,tackle anything that I may say and prove to the contrary. I _believe that the motto of a real teetotaller in regard to drink is, neither touch, taste, nor handle,and I take this to mean,because every- thing connected with drink is corrupted. In my youth, at Sunday School, I was taught, "Thou shalt not steal, and that the receiver of stolen property, if he knew that it was stolen, was as bad as the thief." I can go to a teet)taller's shop where the owner knows I am a publi- can, I can order a suit of clothes and he will receive pay- ment for the same; I can go to one of our local coal merchants, order a few tens of coal which he will be pleased to send to me; he will receive payment, and the following Sunday I might hear him on the market square at a temperance meeting speaking against drink, the publican, and everything that emanates from his trade. I can go to other teetotallers in various branches of trade and without the slightest hesitancy or com- punction they are ever ready to receive my money, in fact, I have never yet found one to tell me that it was corrupted, and that they will neither touch, taste, nor handle it, and to carry this question to its logical con- clusion that if the receiver of stolen property is as bad as the thief, the teetotallers are as degraded and loath- some as the publican while they receive this money. This is a point that I submit to temperance agitators, and charge them that it is contrary to their teachings.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMI3ER 5, 1t391.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMI3ER 5, 1t391.

Some time ago I remember reading in a Manchester paper about a Methodist conference being held in that city,and some of the ministers who attended there found I fault with some of their brethren because they were pecuniarily interested as shareholders in some of the brewery companies of this country. Hard words were used about such conduct, and that was about all that was done, and I presume these men are receiving divid- ends from such companies to which they have a perfect right as shareholders. But what shall we say of such men? They will go to their place of worship and stand , up in their pulpits—they will speak against the drink trade in all its branches, telling their flocks that they must ever shun it because from its source the vast majority of sins and crimes flow, and after doing this, perhaps the following week or month these men will receive a dividend note from the breweries they are con- nected with, and with a quiet, but I hardly think an honest, conscience they will cash the same. Yes, these are our religious teachers professing to teach the pre- cepts their great master laid down, but I am satisfied of this, that such teachings instead of advancing the cause they preach will retard it; that such teachings as these, lacking as, they do a true example, instead of strengthening the cause of religion will have the opposite effect, by bringing it into contempt and ridicule. When we are charged by these men with such heinous sins, I think we can quietly sit down and calmly reflect. We can ask ourselves a few questions, such as the fol- lowing: Have we read of men in high positions in life committing criminal offences? Have we read of the Cleveland-st. scandals? Have we read of gas scandals? I Have we not read of many other sins being committed , by men who belong to this or that temperance move- ment, or to some religious body? Such cases as these we can fling to the leaders of temperance, and tell them that there is sufficient, ground for them to exercise some of their reclaiming talents on such cases as these, with- out wasting it all against drink. We hear of bigotry, , intolerance, and uncharitableness, and, I think, if there are any men in this country who ought to lay claim to such,it is the teetotal and temperance party. The more I think about the drink question, and the various ways and aspects I view it in, [become more convinced than ever that the teetotal way of settling this question is most dishonest. If teetotal manufacturers, tradesmen, and shopkeepers were honest they would not receive the labour of men who drink, but who work for them in helping them to make their fortunes. They, however, do not refuse this, but to practice what they preach they ought. If money comes to their coffers it is right. Their policy seems to be "Get money, honestly if you can,but get it." I will just mention another way amongst many that I look at this question. I do not think there are two men in the country, who speak more agaiast the drink traffip and public-houses than the Rev. Canon Farrer and the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes. I will suppose that these two ministers were each holding a bazaar for some religious object in connection with their church and school, and, for the sake of argument, I will assume that I am acquainted with them and that they know me to be a publican, and that I go to their bazaar with a few hundred pounds in my pocket and begin to spend it on different things to be bought there. Now I wonder if these two ministers would stop me and tell me that because I was a publican they would not have my money. This is a very simple way of putting it; no one can mistake it, and perhaps they will answer. It grieves me, and I am sure it grieves others who are interested in the same trade, to know that we are made the targets at which these teetotal fanatics fire their shots, while at the same time we believe ourselves to be far better citizens than they. I know men in this town who fight and work hard against the drink trade; they seem to make it their one aim to do so, but in their everyday life they are the meanest of men. Some of these will grind their workpeople down and drive them like slaves, occasionally cursing them till they nearly froth at the mouth, and these are the men who set themselves up to be the regenerators and purifiers of society. Total abstainers have a right to be such; what they wish to eat and drink let them have it, and I, as a pub- lican, would be the last to object or forcibly prevent them from having it, but at the same time I must claim the same right for myself that I give to them. But they have the impudence to Say no ; they will not even allow this ; to their own faults, failings, and shortcomings they are wilfully blind, but those of the poor publican they magnify like a huge mountain. The sooner temperance men banish such bigotry and intolerance from their minds and believe that the publican is like themselves in the great ocean of life, a man and a brother, the better will it be fork's alt. He that is without sin let him first cast the stone, but none of us dare respond to this, and I do think that if instead of forcibly trying to thrust our opinions down other people's throats we did but exercise a little more charity, we should be doing more good in a just, honest, and truthful way, by assisting those who are weaker and feebler than ourselves, in helping them to fight and struggle successfully against the frailties and pitfalls of human existence which appear to sur- round us on every hand.—Yours, &c.,
A RADICAL TEETOTAL SHAREHOLDER IN A WARRINGTON BREWERY.

of the licence of the Exchange Vaults, Oldfield-street, tenant Ebenezer Clare.—Objection was also taken to the renewal of the license of the Victoria Hotel, Market- place (tenant, Charles Harrison). Mr. Swift elicited that the notice of objection had been posted too late, and on that ground the objection was struck off. Mr. Seger intimated that the decision affected objections to three other houses, and those objections would be withdrawn. The landlords were James Gregory, Churn Inn, Tontine- street ; William Battersby, Volunteer Inn, Bridge-street; and Thomas Milne, Nelson Arms, Bridge-street. The renewal of licenses tot the Royal Standard, Market-place (James Lathom); Moss Rose Inn, Brook-street (Patrick Brennan), Star Inn, Merton Bank-road tMrs. Margaret Ellen Ridgley), and an off-license held by Mrs. Jane Twist in Peasley Cross-lane, were afterwards opposed, the principal ground of objection in each case being that the license ; was not required in the neighbourhood. After a brief retirement of the magistrates, the Chairman said the Bench had decided not to renew the license to Mrs. Twist, as the license had not been used for some years. With regard to the other cases, the magistrates did not see their way to refuse renewals of any of the licenses, but they wanted it to be particularly understood that that decision must not be considered as showing that they thought there were not too many licensed houses in the town, and that occasion would not be taken to refuse a renewal whenever an opportunity occurred.
BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE,
(MIXED)
BY TIM/ 0' DICK 0' BOBS.
It s a gradely good ovvd beverage, is brimstooan an, traycle !

Yigh, although id isn'd served up i' cups at th' swell 'pubs' an' station refreshment rooms, a dose o' this owd-fashioned spring remedy abeawt th' back end is a grand thing ayther for young or owd or middle-aged o' booath sexes. Aw speyk fro' experience, though there is fooak at fratches o' things as they've ne'er tasted on theirsels, an' among thad lot yo'll happen recollect Owd Squeers an' th' wife i' Nicholas Nickleby, and heaw fond they wor on id—for th' skollars. Dudn'd th' owd geezer say: "They hay.e. their brimstone and treacle partly because if they hadn't something or other in the way of medicine they'd be always ailing or giv- ing a world of trouble ; and partly because it spoils their appetites, and comes cheaper than breakfast and dinner."

There is times, yo' know, when yo'r blood gets eaw t o' order, un' yo've heeat-lumps, or boils, or segs botherin' yo', an' yo' say to yor'sel : " Aw mon tek, summat to werk me a bit ; so yo' begin studyin' th' pill advertisements th' noospappers, an' then yo' chuck thirteenpence hop'ny away on one o' th' quack remedies. Aw say yo' chuck th' brass away, becose th' stuff does yo' no good; id'll gi' yo' th' back door trot, but nowt else--unless id gi's yo' a lesson for th' future. An' o' th' time yo' could ha hod thia fine tonic for a penny!

Well it's just th' same wi' th' mind as id is wi' th' body. Id geds eawt o' order at times, an' then there's heeat-lumps, an' boils, an' segs on id ; then th' owner sterts thinkin' abeawt dosin' id, an' he gooas to the quacks, too. He'll swallow a lot o' pills ae is covered wi' sugar, an' neglect th' good hawsome dose of brimstooan an' traycle as wxl do him ten times more good nor th' dearer artickle will.

Aw darsay yogi hey some like aim wod aw'm drivin' at bi this, an' aw hooap yo'll nod look on me as a quack as is puffin' up his own pertickler brew o' brimstoan an' tracyle. To tell th' truth aw'm nob- but new to th' job, an' it's possible aw may at times put rayther too much brimstooan in, an' at other times happen a sooap moore tracycle nor aw owt; but bP done for th' best. There'll be some natures as id'll act on an' do good, some as aw'm deawtful abeawt, an' others as id'll nod touch at o' —moore's th' pity. Yo' know therr's three soorts o' fooak among th' werkin' classes; th' fost is olez gooin' upparts, slowly, but surely, an' i' th' coourse ov a generation or sooa they become pert o' wod we co' th, middle class ; another soort is them as is olez sinkin' deawn'ards, an' th' last soort is between 'em booath, an' id occasionally adds to booath, happen:P equal proportions. As far as aw know this is mi own discovery, an 'id may torn eawt to be a mare's nest, but when aw gooa to a free lib- rary aw see a lot o' factory lads th' readin' room, on' ged a glent o' th' books they're werkin' at so herd, aw corn'd help but think o' th' hunderds as is at th' jerry-shops, an' low places o' every kind, squanderin' their herd-earned wage, an' their pre- cious time on—wod?

Nay, aw'm nooan a teetotal preycher, nod aw ; but wod pleasure con there be for mon or woman as sits suppin' drink o' fleet in a 'pub 'after bein' stewed up in a factory fro' mornin' to fleet? Or in a low music-hall, hearin' o' soorts o' nasty songs? An' these fooak hes childer at hooam as wants feedin' an' clooathin', an' bringin' up to play their pert i' th' history o' th' world. Will brimstooan an' traycle werk these fooak ? My opinion is as id hes'nd bin tried, for th' chaps as should be given th' medsun to 'em seem to ha' lost th' spoon. _

Like as iv everything's gooin' wrang, for welly everybody's dissatisfied abeawt summat or other; one lot will hey id as Christianity's played eawt, another as marriage is a failure, an' others as life isn'd wo'th livin'. An' there's a varra dangerous soort o' socialism flyin' abeawt, an' a noisy religion! as is disgustin' fooak, an' sich a mix up i' th' _poli- tical world as never war sin' politics were fost in- vented; an' drunkenness is on th' increase, an' crime.

0` Things is geddin' serious !" Nod so mich for us as for th' fooak as hes these ideas, an' does these things. An' th' remedy is a dose o' brimstooan an' traycle mooast cases; we o' on us know o' men an' wimmen as wants this treeatment, an' it's eawr duty to treeat 'em; we know exactly heaw mich brimstooan is wanted, an' heaw mich traycle, nobbut mony a time we're freekned o' vexin' th' body as wants id. Ay, we're a soft lot when we daren't risk thad for th' sake o' savin' booath him an' his wife an' childer, an' mony a time a bit o' eawtspokkenness bee browt a keer- less, thowtless chap to his senses, an' bin th' mek- kin' on him.

Id doesn'd olez do to co' a spade a spade, bi ony meeans, for them as co's id a agricultural imple- ment wod be as shockt as they possibly could be iv yo' dud. Aw wonst wrooat a tooathri verses on a innicent little babby, an' becose aw used th' word " ippin" th' wife ov a Alderman as read thad nowty word welly fainted. Hoo threatened to stop spendin' a penny a week on thad papper, an' aw'll nod be sure as hoo didn'd tell her husband as hoo'd hey a divorce iv he browt thad noospapper th' heawse ageean. These is th' lines as shockt her modesty soon:

EAWR BABBY. (BI MR. AN' MRS. TIIM 0' DICE 0' BOBS). Turn: Eh, bless tha lad, tha'rt bonny! Tha'rt th' grandest bab i'th row; Aw'm towd sooa bi thi gronny, An' surely hoo should know, There's not a mon feels preawder Except mi mam-F-law Mrs. : Turn, reych thad vi'let peawder, Th' poor thing, its welly raw. (Turn reyches it.) Turn: Thall soon begin wi' trouble, A lot too soon, aw deawt— Mrs. : Turn! Wilta reych thad double Ileaw oft hey aw to sheawt ? Turn: Neaw, iv thad bin a woman,: Istid o' bein' a chap— Mrs.: Well !iv this is'nd a rum un ! It's feelin' for id pap ! Turn : Tha'rt cross, but tha'll hi crosser When teethin' time comes reawnd ; An' th' vacksinatin's wosser—

Aw's catch id, aw'll be beawnd, An' when aw weean tha, laddie, (To think on't meks me glum), It's woe-be to thi Daddy— Mrs.: Another 'ippin, Turn! Turn: An' when tha zeds to clippin' TM daddy reawnd his neck Mrs.: Turn ! Turn ! ! Another ippin ; Wod messes id does mek ! Turn: An' when tha geds to walkin' Mrs.: Tha hesibin cram'd to-day. Turn: An' when tha sterts o' talkin' Mrs.: Turn! ! ! Mek some cinder tay.

There's nobbut one time when id isn'd wise to be eawtspokken, an' thad is when a strappin' chap as is a bit short tempered tells yo' a lie ; iv yo' vally yor skin doend yo' co' him a liar streyt eawt, but ax iv he isn'd descended fro'Ananias on th' mother's side, an' Baron Munchausen on th' fayther's. But at ony other time—an' to a less chap—yo' may god id off yo'r chest; for instance, there's th' little grocer at th' corner o' yo'r street as yo' con tell a tooathri things too, Bich as there bein' sixteen eawnce to th' peawnd, an' damp 'bacca bein' dear at fourpence an eawnce. Tell him it's for his own good, an' as he'll be gedd!n' fined iv he gooas on, an' that sooart of' tawk ; id'l.l be a dose o' brim- stooan an traycle as'll do him good—an' yo' to, i' th' long run. Well that's heaw we mon act together, an' iv th' mixter isn'd wod it should be, or seems to be a bit quackish aw hooap to heir ont ; soon wi' these tooathri words o' hintroduction, Aw'm yo'rs truly, TUM 0' DICK 0' BOBS.

div.head: ST. HELENS LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: ST. HELENS LICENSING SESSIONS.
STRONG OPPOSITION.

The annual licensing sessions for the borough of St. Helens were opened on Tuesday, before Celonel D. Gamble, C.B. (in the chair), Alderman D. IlTechnie, C. J. Bishop, J. Hairisen, Dr. Gaskell, Dr. Twyford, Messrs. A. Sinclair, and W. J. Thom- son. Very great public interest was manifested in the proceedings. The courtroom was crowded, and Mr. Seger, barrister, instructed by Mr. W. Hutchen, solicitor, Liverpool and Prescot, appeared to oppose the renewal of certain licenses and the granting of new licenses on behalf of the clergy and minis- ters of the town and the St. Helens and District Temperance Union. Among those present were the Revs. W. Edmund Eon, G. B. Thurston, W. Richard- son, 11. S. Bolton, G. Lakeman, W. T. Hancock (Church of England); Revs. R. J. Ward, A. G. Bridge, D. Clayton, and G. White (Congregational) ; J. Brown (Presbyterian), G. Hammond (Wesleyan), F. Smith (Primitive Methodist), W. liolroyd (Bap- . tist),D.Pnngoe (Ragged School Mission)Mr.R.Shaw (president of the St. Helens Temperance Union). Chief Constable Wood reported that the total popula- tion of the district was 71,288 giving one beerhouse to every 512 and one public house to every 484 inhabitants. There were 147 public-houses and 139 beerhouses and nine grocers had wine and spirit licenses. During the year 541 persons had been summoned, and 813 arrested for drunkenness, making a total of 1,354, against 1,216 in 1890, 1,587 in 1889, and 1,726 in 1888. During the past year 8 publicans had been proceeded against, of whom 4 had been convicted, and 2 beersellers had been proceeded against, both being convicted. In 1890 4 beersellers only were convicted, and in 1889 5 publicans and 14 beersellers were convicted. The following license- holders had been convicted during the year :—Licensed Victuallers: John Cross, Rifle Corps Hotel, Windle,sell- ing adulterated whisky, fined ss. and costs ; Margaret Sherwin, Star Hotel, Eccleston, supplying drink to a drunken man,fined 10s. and costs ; James Dennett,Black Horse Hotel, Parr, selling drink to a drunken man ,fined 10s. and costs ; William Dyson, Victoria Vaults. Parr, selling intoxicating liquor without a license. Beersellers : William Cook, Old House at Home Inn, Windle, supply- ing drink to a drunken man,fined 40s. and costs ; Henry John Parr, Royal Oak Inn, Parr, keeping open a lottery called the "Doncaster Spring Handicaps,'” fined £5 and costs. _ _ _

Chief Constable Wood intimated that he objected to the renewal of all the licenses for the houses where con- victions had taken place during the past twelve months and Mr. Segar said he was instructed to oppose the re- newal of 14 beerhouse licenses and one off-license. Two of the licenses referred to were included among those mentioned by the Chief Constable.—The Chairman stzted that in accordance with the custom of the Court they would adjourn all the licenses to which the police authorities had given notice of objections made against other houses by the clients of Mr. Segar. The licenses would be renewed in all other cases. The Rev. G. Lake- man (St. Mark's Church)asked the Bench if they would receive a memorial on the general subject.—The Chair- man intimated that they would do so.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, said he appeared for the majority of the publi- cans against whom notice of objection had been given, and he strongly objected to the magistrates receiving any such memorial. —The Chairman said the Bench would receive the memorial and hear any objection against it. The Rev. G. Lakeman then handed to the Bench a petition signed by 22 clergymen and ministers of the town, pointing out thatethe number of licensed houses in St. Helens was greatly in excess of legitimate requirements ; that the large proportion of the , houses had no accommodation for travellers, so that they did not fulfil the original I design of the licensing system, and were consequently mere " tippling " houses..—Mr. Lakeman remarked that he had been asked to present the petition as the chairman of a: meeting of representative ministers, clergy, and priests, who had considered that they should express their opinion that there were too many public houses and beerhouses in the town. The objections against renewals were then heard, the first case called being that of Thomas Walter Jones, of the Millstone Inn, College-s. Mr. Segar contended that there were too many licensed houses in the neighbour- hood of College-st., and that it was the scene of frequent drunkenness.—Evidence in support of the ob- jection was then given ny Thomas Stevenson, glass packer; William Parker, insurance agent; and Chief Constable Wood, who remarked that there was no doubt the number of public-houses increased the difficulties of the police force in regard to their duties.—Mr. Swift sub- mitted that the objections were of a frivolous nature. —After evidence had been given by the landlord and by Mr. Joseph France, miller, the bench intimated that they had decided to grant the renewal of the license, but in all other cases they would give their decision at the end of the proceedings.—The next case was that of Joseph Bridge, of the Clarendon Hotel, College-street, and the objection was practically the same as in the Millstone case.—Similar objection was also taken to the renewal

div.head: TRH NEW APPLICATIONS,
div.p: TRH NEW APPLICATIONS,

The licensing sessions were resumed on Wednesday, when the applications for new licenses were considered. The magistrates on the bench were Colonel D. Gamble, C.B. (in the chair), Alderman J. Harrison and C. J. Bishop, Dr. Gasket!, Mr. A. Sinclair, and Mr. W. J. Thomson. Mr. Segar, barrister, instructed by Mr. Hutchen. Liverpool and Prescot, again appeared to oppose the applications and among those present wcre the Revs. H. S. Bolton, R. J. Ward, J. Brown, P. B. Newall, F. Smith. and G. White.— The first application on the list was one by Mr. George James Robins, Garwood, estate agent, for the provi- sional grant of a victualler's license for premises to be erected at the corner of Birchley-st. and Tolver-st. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the applicant, and applied for the adjournment of the application until the adjourned licensing day. Since notice of the application was given the applicant had received an intimation that the site might be wanted, and probably would be wanted, by the new railway company. The site adjoined the site of the proposed new railway station, and applicant was anxious to make inquiries before proceeding with his application.—Mr. Segar opposed the ad- journment and asked for it to be dismissed.—The bench did not think anything would be gained by dismissing it, and adjourned the application. Mr. Ross Brown, of Liverpool, instructbd by Mr. R. W. H. Thomas (St. Helens) applied on behalf of Mr. John Henry Barton, bookkeeper, Cooper-st., for a license for the Peel Arms Hotel, corner of W'estfield-st., and Water- st.,now closed.—Mr. Segar remarked that it was refresh- ing for them as teetotallers—he was a teetotaller for the time being—(laughter)—to know that the owner was willing to give up two other licensed houses for the Peel Arms, but that he thought, was being done asa business transaction. The offer was in the nature of a bribe,and he asked the bench to refuse the application. He added that he had a petition many yards long against the application —Evidence was then given by the Rev. R. J. Ward (Congregational) and the Rev. F. Smith (Primitive Methodist) to the effect that the license was not wanted in the vicinity.—The Bench intimited that they would reserve their decision until the applications had been heard.—Mr. J. 0. Swift next applied on behalf of Alfred Hardy, of Norman's-road, Sutton, for a full license for the Boilermakers' Arms. If the full license was granted to the Boilermakers' Mans the owners would give up the license of the Mechanics' Arms beerhouse.— Evidence in support was given by several residents, and Mr. Fouldes, Secretary of the Sutton Football Club, said the full license was required for the convenience of foot- , ball players and their friends.—Mr. Segar, in opposing the application, remarked if football players would play more and drink less it would be much better for the game. 'lt was a great pity that drink was so much associated with football, as it led to rowdyism and betting.—The Rev. J. Ward protested against the granting of the license and said he was opposed to the association of football with drinking. Me believed that the best football players and athletes all round were teetotallers.—Mr. Swift afterwards applied for a full license for the Britannia Vaults, 94, Duke-street, on behalf of Thomas Salts ; and also for a full license for the Robin Hood Inn, 58, Crossley-road, Sutton, on behalf of James Ash- ton. These were opposed by. Mr. Segar.—These concluded the applications by publicans, and the bench retired. On their return the Chairman stated that they had decided to refuse all the applications.— After an adjournment for lunch, Mr. J. 0. Swift sup- ported an application by William Dewfall for a wine license for the White Rose Inn, 92, Park-road; and also , an application by William Mercer, of 44, Vincent-street, ' for an off-license.—Mr. J. P. Mearns appeared onjbehalf Mrs. Sarah Littler, of 81, North-road, who applied for an off-license, and also supported a similar application by Thomas Jenkins, of 75, Charles-street.—Mr. Segar opposed all these applications.—The only unopposed application was one by Mr. James Lewis, grocer and provision dealer, 20, Market-place, for a wine, spirits, and liquors license. Mr. R. W. H. Thomas appeared for the applicant, and it was stated that the application had been rendered necessary by the removal of Mr. Lewis from his former premises in Church-street. The bench again retired, and on their return it was stated that they refused the applications.—Mr. Thomas pointed out that they had no power to refuse the application by Mr. Lewis, and, after a brief consultation, , the chairman said the bench would grant that application.

div.head: SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.
div.p: SHOCKING DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.
MURDEROUS ATTACK ON A CHESHIRE LADY.

The New Zealand papers just to hand bring detail; of a shocking domestic tragedy at Ashburton, near Christ- church, New Zealand, a few months back. Miss Ella Hall, daughter of the late Mr. Joseph Hall, of Audlem, Cheshire, left England to become the wife of Albert Ed- ward Moss, eldest son of a Leicestershire gentleman, who occupied a responsible position in the house of Messrs. Friedlander, of Ashburton. They were duly married, and appear to have settled down happily, when young Moss sustained some serious finan- cial losses, which affected his brain. On the 7th July he seized a hatchet used for crushing coal, and attacked his bride with it. He inflicted two dreadful wounds with the weapon on the left side of her head, and two in the neck. Her thumb and two fingers of the left hand were nearly severed in endeavouring to protect her head. Her screams brought assistance, when Moss was found lying on the floor with his throat shockingly cut. On the way to the hospital he jerked out, "Man swindled me. How is my wife? Swindled." No expectations were entertained of his recovery, but Mrs. Moss was progressing satisfactorily when the mail left.
GOLBORNE. MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT GOLBORNE.

On Saturday afternoon, the members of the Pride of Golborne Miners' Lodge, held a demonstration at Gol- borne under favourable circumstances. A meeting was held in the Liberal Club, when Mr. W. Billington pre- sided.—Mr. Henry Twist moved the following resolution: —" That in the opinion of this meeting the time has fully , come when a larger staff of efficient Mines inspectors must be appointed ; that better provisions must be made for providing timber, and the Mines Act made more definite in respect to the system of setting props and chocks, with a view of giving greater security to the lives and limbs of the workmen ; and we also desire to give our unqualified support to the Miners' Eight Hours' Bill, as the only practicable way of introducing unifcr- mity of hours in the mines."—Mr. Alfred Twist seconded the resolution, which was supported by 'Mr. S. Woods, who referred to the large number of accidents which oc- curedin the mines, these, he said, being caused by inex- perienced men being engaged to do the work which an experienced man ought to do. In regard to the eight hours' question, he would advise them that at the next election, whether he be Liberal ot Conservative, if the candidate would not vote for them they should not vote for him, and he was sure that the colliers could turn the election on either side. He was aware that they were on the look-out for a Liberal candidate for the Newton Divi- sion, but he would say vote for the member that would vote for them. Rome Rule was no more precious to the Irishman than the Eight Hours' Bill to the miner, and they would make this a test question at the next election. On being put to the meeting the resolution was unani- mously carried. EARLESTOWN RUGBY FOOTBALL CLUB.

A general meeting of the members of this club was held at the Prince of Wales Hotel, on Tuesday evening. Mr. A. Watkins presided, and he was support ed by Dr. Harold Watkins and the• whole of the Committee, there being also about 50 mem- bers present. The meeting was called for the pur- pose of electing a vice captain, for the first team, in the place of Mr. G. Baker, who has 'signified his inability to hold the position. On a vote being be- ing taken Mr. E. Sherrington was appointed. Mr. T. Crank,a member of the Committee, having left the neighbourhood, Mr. Jag. Mather was elected in his stead. A suggestion was made by Mr. A. Wat- kins, that Maltese crosses be presented at the end of the season to the 15 most deserving players, and after some discussion the suggestion wa s adopted It was decided to have a general practise on Satur- day and Monday next, and the season will he opened on the 12th inst. The prospects of the club are very encouraging, a couple of fairly strong teams having been got together. A good field had been secured, near the Sankey Sugar works, and being in a central position, they have fair hopes of being well supported. Matches have been ar- ranged with the following clubs :—Runcorn, Sut- ton, Wigan Temperance, Widnes Athletic, Walkden. "A," Putricroft, Red Rock, West Leigh, Widnes "A," Frodsham, Pendleton Trinity, Barton, Fails- worth Old Boys,llorwich,Stalelens " A," St. Helens Recreation "A." There is also a capital list of fix- tures for the" A" team.

div.head: NEW WARRINGTON STEAMER.
div.p: A NEW WARRINGTON STEAMER.

A steam barge is at the present time being built by Messrs. R. Smith and Son, of Lytham, for Messrs. Monks, flail, and Company, of Warrington. The steamer is a large one 90ft. long by 2lft. beam —and is being built for the purpose of carrying the rapidly-increasing quantities of iron which Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company send down to Liverpool and Birkenhead for export. In the building of the vessel care will be taken to adapt her for navigating the Ship Canal when the water- way is completed.
