div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The Secretary of the Runcorn Musical Society (Mr. R. W. Pierpoint), has just issued the prospec- tus of the Society for the ensuing season. Taken as a specimen of the printer's art the prospectus is of a unique description, a credit to Mr. Bellany the typographer. The concert arrangements are on the most complete scale, and show, in a marked degree, that the Committee and officials have lost none of their enterprise, nor any degree of their capacity of making a selection to meet all the musical tastes.

The first concert on Outober 12th, is ".ballad and instrumental." The vocalists engaged are Miss Dews and Signor Foli (the eminent basso), Senor Athos is solo violin and Senor Albeniz, solo pianist, both musicians of commanding talent. The second con- cert. is fixed for December 21st, when Rossini' s Sta- bat Mater will be performed in the first part and miscellaneous selections will fill the second part. The artistes will be Miss Monbeith, Miss Annie Richardson, Mr. E Houghton,and Mr. A. S. Kennel!. The third and last concert,on March 29th, will con- sist of Haydn's Creation and the principals are to be Madame Conway, Mr. Maldwyn Humphreys,and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint. This is a programme of a season's work that should satisfy, the most exacting and fastidious concert goers.

The Runcorn Waterworks Company is making progress. The dividend is steadily rising and at the annual meeting on Monday 4i per cent. was de- clared. The concern was stated by Mr. Brundrit to be in a highly satisfactory state, and the share- holders showed that they were of the same opinion by their unanimous absence. At various times there has been some talk of the town taking over the Waterworks, on the ground that the ratepayers, and not a private company, should have control of the water supply. It is quite clear that the longer such a project is delayed the higher will be the price.

The election of Runcorn Commissioners presented the usual f‘iatures on Thursday.. There was the same wrestling and jostling as of old, and the term " hear garden" 80 often applied to it is about the correct description. Mr. Grice had endeavoured as far as lay in his power, and as far as the antiquated and 4isgraceful mode of election would allow, to improve the arrangement,and he earned the thanks of numerous ratepayers by providing a private booth, where they were unmolested by the candi- dates or their more energetic and pressing agents. The other arrangement of the market, where, of course the poll took place, were an improvement upon those of previous years.

Widnes.does not yet get its charter of incor- poration. Government officials never so far forget their dignity as to hurry, and we shall have to wait patiently. The ratepayers will not be able to elect their Mayor on the historic ninth of November,that is certain, but he will be none the • worse for being placed in his chair in the spring..

One step is being taken towards the establish- ment Gf technical educaticn in Runcorn by the formation of Science and Art Classes during the coming winter. The School Board have the matter in hand, in conjunction with three representatives of the Board of Commissioners, the Commissioners having guaranteed £75 towards the cost. Mr. Moss, the clerk to the Board;. has published a long list of sciences which it is contemplated shall be taught if there be any demand by the youth (Ind young men of the town, and the Science and Art Department have also sanctioned the teaching of modern languages, shorthand,, and bookkeeping. It is to be hoped that the efforts of the Board in pro- viding these classes will be appreciated and that a large number of pupils will present themselves for instruction. The evening classes, under the control of Mr. Moulton; the head master at Greenway-road Schools, will also be continued.
BY AN EARLICSTOWN CORRESPONDENT.

We hear very little just now about the "pro- posed " Public Hall. It is now something like three months since the award was made for the best design. and HO far as the outside public are concerned, the affair may be buried in oblivion. I was in hopes that some sort of a start would be made with the building this year. but, judging from appearances, these hopes are more than likely to remain unfulfilled. I think we might have got as far as laying the foundation stone, which would at least have shown that the Commissioners meant business. Perhaps it would be as well if we were not kept so much in the dark on the matter.

On Monday, at the usual monthly Board meeting of the Commissioners, a member is to be elected to fill the vacancy caused by the retirement of Mr. B. B. Crlover. I have heard several names proposed, but the favourite,' understandS§ Mr. Peter Thomp- son, grocer, of Bridge-street, and if my information is correct, this is the gentleman who will be elected to the vacant seat. A meeting of a certain section of ratepayers has been held this week, and although their deliberations were held in camera, I understand the gentleman' have named was generally accepted. This selection will give Earlstown a decided majority over Newton in the voting.

The appointment of ex-Police Constable Bowes as Relieving Officer for the Newton district appears to have given general satisfaction. There can be no two opinions as to his fitness for the post, and I think the Guardians have made a wise selection.

The Flower Show at Newton on Saturday, was not quite so good as it has been in previous years, but the attendance was up to the average, and in this respect the Committee have no cause to com- plain. The weather was all that could be desired, but the grass was a trifle damp under foot. The entries were above the average, but all those who entered in the various classes did not exhibit, and well it was that they did not, as some inconveni- ence would have been caused, owing to want of sufficient space for staging. The Committee, how- ever,deserve every praise for the excellence of their arrangements, and I hope next year, they may put forward still better attractions for the public.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. - The market is very strong all roubd, and producers ge'Aeratly quoting higher prices, but few are able to report satisractory progress at the advanced rates. Cotton goes ; the estimate of "spot" was 15,000 bales later 18,000, and later still the estimate was raised to 20,000, and quotations generally advanced I-16d. Yarns are very strong at extreme quotations, and those who need have to pay, but not many large lines are reported, either in twist or weft. Bundles are not in great request, and no doubt spinners would be willing sellers. Min cloths are not moving at present quotations. There is fair inquiry for Indian fabrics, but high prices stop brwiness. The. miscellaneous demand is seldom for large lines at she higher rates now quoted._

this is the overflow of four migkty inland seas that is gradually edged in until it surges over the Falls at the rate of 15 million cubic feet per minute into the eighty feet abyss below, then it is that you are IMPRESSED WITH THE GRANDEUR and power of the scene. Then it is that your thoughts go back to the priest-explorer, Father Hennepin, and you try to realise what must have been his thoughts when for the first time he caught sight of this great and glorious cataract. "Just my view" observed Mr. Jones. "I had very similar impressions and reflections myself." I rambled all over the reservation, and photographed upon the prepared plates of my memory views that will be recalled with pleasure for many years to come. I lingered about the spot until other sensations reminded me that it was a long time since I had breakfasted, and it was well on in the afternoon ere I sat down to dinner. But Niagara was the sight I had crossed the ocean par- ticularly to see, and I have to admit that, when all pre- conceived ideas of what it was like had been effaced by the reality, it was worth a voyage of three thousand miles to behold. NIAGARA VILLAGE, through which I walked back, consists principally of hotels, restaurants, and curio shops. In a very pleasant and prominent place there is a monument to the dis- coverer whose "find" has given the village a well deserved world-wide reputation, and one on which the straggling village lives. At the foot of the Falls, the river is fairly tranquil, but about two miles further down the stream the waters burst out most furiously and form the equally-famous WHIRLPOOL RAPIDS. It is a fearfully agitated mass of water, and the won- der is that any sane person should even think of passing through it. This portion is private property, and th,. proprietors all along the route advertise their views as the best from which to see the spot where Captain Webb lost his life. But you are soon satisfied with your view of these rapids, and you return towards the roaring cataract which seems to lure you to it with an irresis- tible attraction.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. Mownar.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. W. Deacon. • DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—A fine of 55. and costs was imposed upon the following for being drunk :—Thomas Leigh, Ellen Smith, Brian Eavers, Andrew Nolan, Ed. Matthews, and John Hannon. Alfred Sateliffe was fined 7s. 6d. and costs for a like offence. For being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, David Blinstone, of Warrington, was fined 103. and costs. Thomas Jones, Warrington, was mulcted in a similar sum for a like of- fence. ASSAULT ON A CONSTABLE.—John Hannon,Water-street, was charged with assaulting P.C. Ward, on Saturday night, by striking him on the arm with a poker. A fine of 105. and costs was imposed. Thar', BY BOYS.—Michael Dunn, Christopher O'Neil, and Patrick Kelly, boys, were charged with stealing a quantity of articles, valued at 204., the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. On Sun- day night a girl named Mary Spencely saw the prisoners coming from the railway goods yard with cans of con- densed milk under their arms, and information being given to P.C. Strickland they were apprehended. The goods were found to have been taken from a wagon. As this was their first offence, the boys were bound over to be of good behaviour for six months, and also to come up for judgment when called upon. PIGEON STEALING.—NichoIas Maroney, of St. Helens, was convicted of stealing two pigeons from the Black Horse Inn, Farnworth, the property of F. Simcock. The prisoner, who was caught in the act, :was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days. PASSING COUNTERFEIT COIN.—Eda Bedford, no fixed abode. Fred Lloyd, St. John-st., Edinburgh, and Thos. Morris, Liverpool, were brought up on remand, charged with uttering counterfeit coin at several shops in the town. The evidence having been repeated,the prisoners were committed to the Assizes for trial.

A POST OFFICE THEFT OF £20,000. Henry Rhodes, a General Post Offics sorter, was com- mitted for trial at Bow-st.,. London, yesterday, charged with stealing letters. At his lodgings 2480 letters were found. The cheques and money- orders stolen repre- sented £20,000. CAPTAIN O'SHEA AND. HIS REPORTED ENGAGE- MENT. Captain O'Shea writes to the "Freeman's Journal :" "With reference to the statement in your newspaper that I am about to remarry, allow me just sufficient space to say I am a Catholic." MURDEROUS ATTACK" ON A CARETAKER. On Thursday night John Collins, caretaker of an evicted farm at Rewls Nunan, near Meelin,, was attacked by five masked and armed moonlightere,. who beat him savagely, knocked him down, broke several of his teeth, burnt his lips, and then decamped. ASSAULT ON IRISEI HARVESTMEN AT HAWARDEN. HEAVY FINES. At Hawarden, on Thursday evening, four Irishmen named Joyce, farm labourers, summoned eight men from Saltney, near Chester, for an atrocious assault. They met the Irishmen on the road, knocked them down, and kicked them about most cruelly. The bench. said they were determined to stamp out these outrages, and fined the two ringleaders named Knight and Reynolds £5 and costs, and six other men £2 10s. and costs.. The total fines amounted to £25.
